CONCLUSION: Current evidence does not demonstrate a statistically significant overall association between ambient air pollution and KD. However, associations may vary by pollutant, exposure timing, geographical setting, and meteorological conditions. Future studies should use standardized exposure windows and account for key meteorological factors to clarify these potential context-specific associations.

articles.title: Service Availability and Readiness for Essential Health Services in Somalia: A Narrative Review of Facility Evidence and Health-System Priorities.
articles.abstract: Essential health services are central to universal health coverage; however, nominal service availability does not necessarily indicate that facilities are ready to deliver care safely, continuously and equitably. In Somalia, evidence on service availability and readiness remains dispersed across facility assessments, policy documents, programme reports and peer-reviewed studies, limiting its use for planning and equitable resource allocation. This narrative review synthesizes Somalia-specific evidence on service availability, facility readiness, readiness-related delivery constraints and health-system priorities for strengthening essential health services. Evidence was classified as direct facility-readiness measures, readiness-related delivery-system indicators or coverage, programme-performance and outcome indicators to distinguish structural readiness from indirect signals of delivery-system performance. Available evidence suggests important readiness gaps across emergency and critical care, surgical services, maternal and newborn health, immunization, nutrition, communicable diseases and selected non-communicable disease services. These gaps are reinforced by donor-dependent and geographically uneven financing, fragile supply chains, workforce shortages and maldistribution, weak referral and emergency transport systems, fragmented public, private, NGO and humanitarian service delivery, and limited routine use of facility-assessment data. Rural, displaced, nomadic, pastoralist and conflict-affected populations experience substantial access barriers. Institutionalizing readiness monitoring and linking facility-assessment evidence to planning, budgeting, supervision, supply allocation, donor coordination and accountability could help Somalia move from nominal service availability toward effective, continuous and equitable essential health-service coverage.

articles.title: Prevalence and Associated Factors of Thyroid Dysfunction Among Clinical Populations in Bangladesh: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
articles.abstract: Thyroid dysfunction (TD) is a significant endocrine burden with profound implications for systemic health; however, consolidated epidemiological data within the clinical landscape of Bangladesh remain sparse. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to estimate the pooled prevalence and identify clinical factors associated with TD among Bangladeshi clinical populations using data published between 2010 and 2025. Following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines and PROSPERO registration (CRD42025116168), six electronic databases were searched without language restrictions. Data from clinical populations (aged ≥12 years) were synthesized using a random-effects model. Subgroup analysis and univariable random-effects meta-regression were employed to explore drivers of heterogeneity, whereas publication bias was assessed via Peters' regression test. The pooled prevalence of TD was 23.72% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 17.90-30.72) across clinically heterogeneous populations, with hypothyroidism identified as the predominant abnormality (20.55%) over hyperthyroidism (4.93%). Meta-regression identified clinical profile as the factor most strongly associated with heterogeneity, revealing that patients with metabolic-inflammatory disorders (e.g., diabetes, metabolic syndrome) exhibited a markedly higher prevalence (34.77%) than endocrine-reproductive groups (19.14%). Furthermore, comprehensive biochemical assessments (thyroid-stimulating hormone [TSH] with free hormones) yielded higher prevalence estimates (28.31%) than limited TSH-only testing (18.31%). Peters' regression test showed no significant asymmetry (p = 0.384), though this should be interpreted cautiously given the small number of studies (k = 8). These results underscore a critical "dual burden" of endocrine and systemic disease in Bangladesh. The high prevalence within metabolic high-risk groups necessitates the integration of routine, comprehensive thyroid screening into standard clinical management protocols to optimize endocrine care and mitigate long-term systemic complications.

articles.title: Spatial and Sociodemographic Distribution of Predicted 10-Year Cardiovascular Disease Risk Among Hypertensive Adults in Bangladesh: Evidence From BDHS 2022.
articles.abstract: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is a major public health problem in Bangladesh, especially among adults with hypertension, yet the sociodemographic patterning, wealth-related inequities, and spatial distribution of their predicted CVD risk are poorly understood. Using the 2022 Bangladesh Demographic and Health Survey (2544 adults aged ≥18 years; 1412 in the propensity score-matched sample), we estimated predicted (not overserved) 10-year CVD risk among adults with hypertension and examined its sociodemographic correlates, wealth-based inequalities, and geographical clustering. Risk was categorized as low, medium, or high, using a matrix adapted from the World Health Organization/International Society of Hypertension (WHO/ISH) approach, which requires no cholesterol data, and combines hypertension grade, age, sex, recent tobacco use (within 30 min), obesity, and diabetes. Analyses included descriptive and bivariate tests, ordered logistic regression, propensity score matching to assess covariate imbalance across wealth groups, and Global Moran's I and Getis-Ord Gi* spatial analyses. Overall, 44.7% had low, 18.7% medium, and 36.6% high predicted risk. Older age, female sex, overweight/obesity, recent tobacco use, and higher household wealth were associated with higher predicted risk, although some associations partly reflect the classification rules rather than true differences in risk. In the matched sample, nonpoor participants were slightly more likely than poor participants to have elevated predicted risk (adjusted odds ratio [AOR]: 1.25; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.00-1.57), with a stronger association among those with secondary or higher education (AOR: 1.97; 95% CI: 1.09-3.56). Excluding adults under 35 years left most associations and the wealth-education interaction unchanged but altered the education and age effects. Spatial autocorrelation was significant (Global Moran's I = 0.133, p = 0.027), with hotspots in Comilla, Dhaka, Narayanganj, and Narsingdi. These findings concern predicted risk rather than observed cardiovascular events and may support integrating absolute CVD risk assessment into primary care and geographically targeted prevention for hypertensive adults in Bangladesh.

articles.title: Trends in acute myocardial infarction mortality with diabetes mellitus as a contributing cause of death in the United States, 1999-2025, with forecasts through 2030 and exploratory projections for 2031-2040.
articles.journal: Journal of diabetes and metabolic disorders
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Diabetes mellitus (DM) is a major risk factor for acute myocardial infarction (AMI) and is associated with increased mortality. Despite substantial advances in the management of both conditions, the population-level mortality burden involving AMI as the underlying cause and DM as a contributing cause remains insufficiently characterized. This study aimed to evaluate national trends and disparities in mortality involving AMI as the underlying cause and DM as a contributing cause among U.S. adults aged ≥ 25 years from 1999 to 2025 using CDC WONDER data, forecasts were generated through 2030, with exploratory projections extending through 2040, stratified by DM type, age, sex, and race and ethnicity.

METHODS: A retrospective analysis of U.S. national mortality data from 1999 to 2025 was conducted to identify deaths among adults aged ≥ 25 years in which AMI; ICD-10 code I21 was the underlying cause and DM; ICD-10 codes E10-E14 was a contributing cause. Age-adjusted mortality rates (AAMRs) and crude mortality rates (CMRs) were calculated. Temporal trends were assessed using joinpoint regression to estimate annual percent changes (APCs) and average annual percent changes (AAPCs). Time-series methods were used to forecast mortality through 2030, with exploratory projections through 2040 .

RESULTS: Trend analyses were conducted using observed mortality data from 1999 to 2025, whereas projections extended from 2026 to 2040. A total of 762,802 deaths were attributed to AMI, with DM documented as a contributing cause, among U.S. adults aged ≥ 25 years from 1999 to 2025. Overall mortality significantly declined (AAMR: 18.9 to 9.16; AAPC: -3.05; 95% CI: -3.3 to -2.9; P < 0.001). Males showed higher AAMRs (23.32 in 1999 to 12.72 in 2025) when compared to females (15.74 to 6.2). Older adults aged ≥ 65 years carried the greatest mortality burden, with CMR decreasing from 72.9 in 1999 to 32.4 in 2025. NH Blacks had the highest AAMR (29.95 to 12.68). Forecasts projected a decline in overall AAMR from 8.17 in 2026 to 6.72 in 2030. Exploratory projections suggested a further decline to 3.08 by 2040, although substantial uncertainty surrounded these long-term estimates. The AAMR for deaths involving AMI as the underlying cause and T2DM as a contributing cause increased from 3.34 in 1999 to 4.15 in 2025, whereas the corresponding AAMR for T1DM decreased from 1.90 to 0.23.

CONCLUSION: Mortality involving AMI as the underlying cause and DM as a contributing cause has significantly declined and is projected to continue declining through 2040. Disparities among males, NH Blacks and older adults require refined strategies to improve outcomes.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s40200-026-02124-x.

articles.title: Cold-Inducible RNA-Binding Protein Alleviates Hypertensive Renal Injury Through the KEAP1-NRF2 Pathway.
articles.abstract: Angiotensin II (Ang II) plays crucial roles in renal dysfunction, fibrotic changes, apoptosis, and oxidative stress. CIRBP, a cold-inducible RNA-binding protein, functions to maintain cellular homeostasis. However, its role in renal damage elicited by Ang II remains unclear. Here, we investigated the mechanisms through which Cirbp overexpression alleviates renal damage caused by Ang II, and Cirbp deletion induces basal renal injury. Transcriptomic analysis identified the involvement of Cirbp in hypertension-related renal injury. Across the animal and cell models, Cirbp overexpression attenuated Ang II-induced renal dysfunction, fibrosis, apoptosis, and inflammation, whereas Cirbp deficiency aggravated basal injury and increased renal susceptibility to injury. CIRBP activated the KEAP1-NRF2 antioxidant pathway to mitigate redox stress. This renoprotective effect was reversed following the application of the NRF2 inhibitor ML385, but was resumed by the NRF2 agonist RA839. Together, CIRBP modulates redox imbalance during Ang II-mediated renal damage through KEAP1-NRF2 signaling.

articles.title: Cardiovascular diseases and guideline-directed medical therapy in low socio-economic status patients: A single center experience.
articles.journal: Journal of Taibah University Medical Sciences
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Patients with a low socio-economic status (SES) exhibit high cardiovascular risk factors (CVRFs) and a high burden of cardiovascular disease (CVD), but they are under-recognized in clinical practice. In this study, we explored CVRFs and CVD in low-SES patients, and estimated the guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) prevalence for each CVD.

METHODS: Consecutive individuals with low-SES who attended the primary care and cardiology clinics within a single charitable medical center between 2024 and 2025 were retrospectively recruited. Data on SES, symptoms, CVRFs, CVDs, and treatment strategies were collected and analyzed descriptively. GDMT comprised class I medications reported by patients and documented in their medical records at the time of data collection for each CVD.

RESULTS: Among the 2374 patients, the mean age was 58.7 ± 6 years (57.2% females). Common CVRFs included hypertension (39.5%), diabetes (28.6%), and hyperlipidemia (27.4%). Common CVDs included coronary artery disease (CAD) (12.4%), heart failure (HF) (6%), and atrial fibrillation (AF) (1.7%) (mean ages: 55.79, 63.12, and 62.4 years, respectively). CAD patients had a high prevalence of acute coronary syndrome (74.2%), with most managed noninvasively (87%), but 38.5% received GDMT. HF with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) exceeded HF with preserved EF (HFpEF) (63.6% vs. 32.8%). Prevalent HF causes included CAD, hypertension, and valvular disease (33.6%, 27.3%, and 26.6%, respectively). GDMT rates for HFrEF and HFpEF were 18.7% and 34%, respectively. The mean CHA2DS2-VASc score was 3.5 for AF patients, with 42.8% on GDMT (78% on warfarin).

CONCLUSIONS: Low-SES patients had a high prevalence of CVRF, where CAD, HF, and AF were most common. The patients were relatively young and managed conservatively, but GDMT rates were low. These findings may guide policymakers to improve cardiovascular care in low-SES individuals.

articles.title: Stem cells for hepatic regeneration: Evaluating mechanisms, sources, and clinical outcomes.
articles.abstract: Despite rapid advances in regenerative medicine, the clinical translation of stem cell-based therapies for end-stage liver disease remains limited. These approaches seek to promote hepatic repair through cell replacement, paracrine signaling, and immunomodulation, but differ substantially in their mechanisms, functional capabilities, and translational readiness. The distinctive contribution of this review is a mechanism-based and translation-oriented framework that links the biological properties of different stem-cell sources to the requirements for clinical application. We critically compare mesenchymal stem cells, embryonic stem cells, induced pluripotent stem cells, hematopoietic stem/progenitor cells, and liver-resident progenitors according to their predominant regenerative mechanisms, differentiation capacity, immunogenicity, safety, manufacturing feasibility, and clinical evidence. Particular attention is given to distinguishing direct hepatocyte replacement from paracrine support and stimulation of endogenous repair, while separating preclinical findings from evidence obtained in human studies. We also examine MSC-derived extracellular vesicles as an emerging cell-free approach and assess how organoid-based differentiation, three-dimensional encapsulation, and scalable bioreactor systems may address limitations in hepatocyte maturation and functional stability. Importantly, hepatocyte-marker expression is distinguished from mature metabolic function when evaluating the therapeutic potential of stem-cell-derived hepatic cells. By integrating these biological and engineering considerations with product heterogeneity, tumorigenic risk, manufacturing reproducibility, and the need for validated, mechanism-linked potency assays, this review identifies the principal barriers to clinical translation. Rather than providing a descriptive catalog of therapeutic platforms, it offers a comparative framework for evaluating how regenerative mechanisms, functional maturity, and manufacturing constraints shape the clinical readiness of stem cell-based strategies for hepatic regeneration.

articles.title: A rare neurovascular complication of Lemierre syndrome: Skull base pachymeningitis and reversible inflammatory stenosis of the petrous-cavernous internal carotid artery.
articles.abstract: Lemierre syndrome is a septic thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein that follows an oropharyngeal infection, most often caused by Fusobacterium necrophorum. Its intracranial complications are predominantly venous; arterial involvement is uncommon and its nature is rarely characterized on imaging. We report the case of a 22-year-old woman admitted with fever, headache, left cervical pain and vomiting 1 week after an acute pharyngitis treated with azithromycin. Blood cultures grew F necrophorum, and contrast-enhanced cervical computed tomography showed thrombosis of the left internal jugular vein extending to the jugular bulb. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) on day 3 showed skull base pachymeningitis with patent dural sinuses. On day 7, the patient developed raised intracranial pressure and diplopia. Time-of-flight angiography showed segmental narrowing of the petrous and cavernous segments of the left internal carotid artery, and contrast-enhanced black-blood 3D T1-weighted fast spin-echo images showed circumferential thickening and enhancement of its wall, absent before contrast and on the contralateral side, consistent with an inflammatory arteritis contiguous to the infected jugular foramen; the dural sinuses remained patent. Treatment combined 21 days of intravenous antibiotic therapy active against anaerobes, therapeutic anticoagulation and acetazolamide. On day 15, MRI with the same sequences showed resolution of the mural enhancement, a normal arterial caliber, regression of the pachymeningitis and partial regression of the jugular thrombosis, and the patient had fully recovered by day 28. This case illustrates how vessel wall MRI, even with a routine sequence interpreted against internal controls, can characterize arterial involvement in Lemierre syndrome and document its reversibility.

articles.title: Multi-Analytical Characterization and Taxonomic Distinction of Australian Plant Exudates.
articles.abstract: Plant exudates have been used worldwide for millennia in broad applications due to their unique physicochemical properties. Indigenous Australians have used exudates in long-standing cultural and technical practices, including hafting adhesives and paint binders. Chemical characterization and botanical identification can provide important insight into the origin, properties, and usage of exudate materials from the archaeological past to the present. However, Australian exudates and cultural heritage materials have been far less examined compared to European, Asian, and North African counterparts. Here, we report combined Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy, X-ray Raman scattering (XRS) spectroscopy, nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy, and pyrolysis gas chromatography mass spectrometry (py-GC-MS) analyses for atomic- to molecular-level characterization of over 20 genera of Australian exudates. This research contributes to fundamental understanding of the chemistry of exudates that drives their usage as natural binders. Integration of all four techniques and multivariate statistics reveals chemical differences at both the genus and species level. We establish correlations between taxonomic groupings and chemical composition to identify key features for distinction of exudates. Our multi-analytical approach provides new insight into the unique chemistry of less well-studied Australian exudates, with impact on the characterization of exudates in important cultural and archaeological materials worldwide.

articles.title: Immunogenicity of the 9-Valent Human Papillomavirus Vaccine in Occupationally-Exposed Adults.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: HPV is the most common sexually transmitted infection and has a well-established role in the pathogenesis of recurrent respiratory papillomatosis (RRP) and oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (OPSCC). HPV DNA is detectable in surgical smoke, and case reports have linked occupational exposure to laryngeal papillomatosis in healthcare workers. In 2026 a joint European Laryngological Society/Union of European Phoniatricians Delphi consensus agreed that occupational exposure is plausible and that vaccination should be offered to workers at risk, but stronger recommendations were not issued due to absence of transmission and immunogenicity data. Immunogenicity data in adults over 26-particularly men-remain minimal in the literature.

METHODS: In a single-center prospective study, 9-valent HPV vaccine naïve operating room staff and surgeons within otolaryngology, general surgery, urology, and obstetrics-gynecology aged 27-69 were recruited to receive the standard three-dose 9-valent vaccine. Antibody titers for HPV 6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, and 58 were measured at baseline (Month 0) and after the completion of their vaccine series (Month 7).

RESULTS: Of 33 enrolled adults, 21 completed the study (18 male, 3 female; mean age 36 years, range 27-61; 4 aged > 45 years). At Month 7, all 21 seroconverted for all nine types of HPV (100% seroconversion).

CONCLUSION: The 9-valent HPV vaccine produced 100% seroconversion in a predominantly older, male, occupationally-exposed cohort that has been under-represented in prior research. This data suggests that offering vaccination to at-risk workers, addressing the immunogenicity gap identified by the ELS/UEP consensus.

LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: 3.

articles.title: Impact of BMI on Ramadan fasting in individuals with type 2 diabetes mellitus: Insights from the DaR Global Surveys 2020-2022.
articles.journal: Journal of Taibah University Medical Sciences
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Fasting during the holy month of Ramadan is a central religious practice for Muslims worldwide, including individuals living with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). Managing diabetes during prolonged fasting presents significant clinical challenges, particularly balancing glycemic control and preventing complications such as hypoglycemia. The body mass index (BMI) is a widely used surrogate marker for metabolic status and may significantly influence the physiological response and tolerance to fasting in individuals with T2DM. However, data are limited regarding the relationship between BMI and fasting experiences among diabetic individuals in diverse Muslim-majority populations. This study used data from the Diabetes and Ramadan (DaR) Global Survey, conducted via SurveyMonkey, to examine the associations between BMI and fasting-related outcomes among adults with T2DM in Muslim-majority countries. The findings may support more personalized risk stratification and clinical guidance for safe fasting practices in this population.

METHODS: Using a specifically designed SurveyMonkey questionnaire, Muslim individuals with T2DM were surveyed in several countries in different geographical regions and stratified by BMI. Basic demographic, clinical, and fasting-related data were collected and analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistics to explore differences between subgroups.

RESULTS: Among 6530 participants, 42.4% were overweight and 37.7% were obese, and obesity was more prevalent in females and the Gulf region. Individuals with obesity were younger and had a slightly longer duration of diabetes. Glycemic control (mean HbA1c ∼ 8.2-8.4%) was similar among BMI groups. Obesity was associated with higher systolic blood pressure, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and microalbuminuria. Pharmacologic management patterns varied little, although use of GLP-1 receptor agonists was greater among individuals with obesity, and Ramadan fasting intentions and practices remained consistent across BMI groups. Self-reported hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia rates were comparable, although overweight participants had higher rates of emergency visits (p = 0.01). Most participants received Ramadan-specific diabetes education, but self-monitoring of blood glucose adherence varied.

CONCLUSION: Individuals with T2DM in all BMI categories were able to fast safely during Ramadan, with no significant differences in fasting behavior or adverse events. Despite a higher burden of cardiometabolic comorbidities among obese participants, glycemic control and complication rates during fasting were comparable. These findings highlight the importance of structured education and individualized care for supporting safe fasting among people with diabetes, regardless of BMI.

articles.title: Regional and national variation in donor and recipient characteristics, transplant practice, and outcomes after liver transplantation (the IMPROVEMENT collaborative): a multicentre cohort study.
authors: de Fatima Santana Ferreira Boin I
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Outcome variability in liver transplantation remains globally driven by differences in donor-recipient characteristics and in risk-mitigation strategies. Prediction models lack geographic balance and fail to account for current disease classification and advanced organ preservation methods. The IMPROVEMENT study (ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT05289609) aimed to characterise the donor-recipient risks and to develop and validate global prognostic algorithms (mortality and complication rate).

METHODS: This non-competitive, international, cohort study involved 61 centres across Europe, Asia, North and South America, Oceania. Centres provided 83 balanced data series. 5218 patients were enroled in retrospective (2017-2019) and/or prospective (2022-2023) cohorts to avoid COVID-19 confounding. A four-step analytical hierarchy process (world maps, radar graphs, donor versus recipient risk plot, and mixed-effects generalised models) enables visualisation of risk propensity, namely, "aggressiveness", and risk-mitigation balance, namely "coverage adequacy". Outcome measures were 90-, 365-, and 730-day mortality and high complication rates.

FINDINGS: Overall survival rates at 90 days, 1 year and 5 years were 93, 90 and 80, respectively. Predictors of mortality included recipient age, CAD, pre-operative complex portal thrombosis, preoperative ventilatory life support, MASLD, MELD 3.0 > 30, packed red blood transfusions (PRBC), and cold ischaemia time ≥360 min. The high complication rate resulted dependent from preoperative ventilatory life support, complex portal thrombosis, TIPS and PRBC. Notably, donor factors had a low impact on outcomes, reflecting successful donor-recipient matching and new graft perfusion modalities. Transplant at high-volume centres (>65 transplants/year) was a significant protective factor (mortality and complication rates). C-statistics of 90-day mortality and high complication rate models were 0.78 and 0.77, respectively.

INTERPRETATION: The IMPROVEMENT study shows that, unlike before, recipient and system-level factors now appear to account for the largest proportion of outcome variability. Implementing risk-mitigation strategies can offset high-risk profiles. These findings provide a robust framework for equitable health resource allocation and clinical decision-making worldwide.

FUNDING: Italian Ministry of Health #RF-2021-12372422 grant.

articles.title: Health-care burden of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease in European tertiary-care outpatient clinics (CONSTANS): a prospective multicentre cohort study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Despite modeling-based epidemiological studies of MASLD, precise estimates of the prevalence and health-care resource utilization in outpatient clinical practice are unknown. We assessed, in a real-life setting, the prevalence of suspected/confirmed MASLD and described health-care resource utilization.

METHODS: A prospective, observational study of patients attending the outpatient hepato-gastroenterology clinics of eight European tertiary care centers during three months. Follow-up data of patients with suspected/confirmed MASLD were recorded 12 months after the screening visit: final diagnosis, disease stage, diagnostic work-up and the use of health-care resources.

FINDINGS: 5240 outpatients from Germany, France, United Kingdom, Switzerland, Italy, Spain and Slovakia were screened. The main reasons for visit were: chronic viral hepatitis, 33.4% (1749/5240), miscellaneous hepatobiliary conditions including neoplasms, 32.9% (1725/5240) and known/suspected MASLD, 24.7% (1293/5240) (pooled prevalence of 26.1% (95% CI: 19.1-34.7)). 1134 suspected/confirmed MASLD patients were included, the diagnosis was confirmed in 80.2% (909/1134). Significant fibrosis was documented in 22.7% (257/1134) and cirrhosis (including burn-out MASLD) in 21.3% (241/1134). Procedures performed differed between countries, overall 66.4% (753/1134) had imaging studies, 65.3% (740/1134) non-invasive fibrosis tests, 20.4% (231/1134) liver biopsy, while referral for further cardiometabolic assessment or therapy was minimal (144/1134, 15.8%). The cost of all procedures and visits was in the range of that recommended for exploring hepatitis C before treatment, although highly variable between countries.

INTERPRETATION: MASLD was the second most frequent single cause for outpatient visits in eight European tertiary care centers. Significant fibrosis including cirrhosis was diagnosed in 44% of patients. The cost of required additional visits and procedures was equivalent to that recommended for hepatitis C before antiviral treatment.

FUNDING: IMI2-Grant Agreement 777377-LITMUS.

articles.title: Development and External Validation of an Updated Nomogram Including Both MRI and Local PSMA PET/CT Information for the Prediction of Side-specific Extraprostatic Extension in Patients Treated with Radical Prostatectomy.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVE: The predictive value of prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) for extraprostatic extension (EPE) in prostate cancer remains unclear.

OBJECTIVE: We assessed whether adding PSMA PET/CT to magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and clinical factors improves side-specific EPE prediction.

METHODS: Patients undergoing PSMA PET/CT and MRI before radical prostatectomy were analysed retrospectively. The endpoint was side-specific EPE (≥pT3a). Predictors were selected by backward elimination, and the final nomogram was fitted using generalised estimating equations to account for clustering of lobes within patients. Discrimination, calibration, and net benefit were assessed, with external validation in an independent single-centre cohort.

RESULTS AND LIMITATIONS: Development and validation cohorts included 801 and 287 lobes. The final model comprised prostate-specific antigen density (odds ratio [OR] 1.54 [95% confidence interval {CI} 0.94-2.50]; biopsy International Society of Urological Pathologists grade group (2 vs benign/1: OR 2.01 [95% CI 1.27-3.19]; 3 vs benign/1: OR 3.82 [95% CI 2.30-6.35]; 4 vs benign/1: OR 2.50 [95% CI 1.54-4.08]; 5 vs benign/1: OR 4.05 [95% CI 2.18-7.53]), MRI T-stage (organ-confined with a lesion [OC] vs organ-confined with no lesion [NL]: OR 1.31 [95% CI 0.86-1.99]; EPE vs NL: OR 4.11 [95% CI 2.56-6.60]), PSMA T-stage (OC vs NL: OR 1.67 [95% CI 1.07-2.61]; EPE vs NL: OR 2.59 [95% CI 1.49-4.49]), PSMAtotal (OR 1.72 [95% CI 1.33-2.23]). In development, the PSMA-MRI nomogram showed superior discrimination (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUC] 0.80 vs 0.71, p < 0.001). On validation, the updated model demonstrated discrimination comparable to the reference model (AUC 0.85 vs 0.86, p = 0.9), with minor risk overestimation and similar net clinical benefit. Limitations include a relatively small validation cohort.

CONCLUSIONS: The PSMA-MRI nomogram appeared to outperform the MRI-only model in development, but this was not confirmed in validation, indicating limited, context-dependent incremental value.

articles.title: Erratum to "Regulatory roles and translational potential of the Kruppel-like factor family in liver disease" [iLIVER 5 (2026) 100252].
