TRIM13 (tripartite motif-containing 13) improves mitophagy of dendritic cells via promoting SESN2 (sestrin 2)-induced K63-linked ubiquitination in sepsis.
articles.abstract: Sepsis constitutes a life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection. SESN2 (sestrin 2), an evolutionarily conserved stress-responsive protein, is a pivotal regulator of cellular homeostasis. Here, we identified TRIM13 (tripartite motif-containing 13) as a regulator that modulated the stability of SESN2 at the post-translational level. Specifically, TRIM13 promoted K63-linked ubiquitination of SESN2 with subsequent upregulation of its functional activation. Ubiquitinated SESN2 initiated a selective macroautophagic/autophagic program that facilitated the recruitment of SQSTM1/p62 (sequestosome 1/p62) to mitochondrial surfaces. The enhanced interaction between ubiquitinated SESN2 and the mitophagy receptor FUNDC1 (FUN14 domain-containing 1) at mitochondria-associated membranes (MAMs), facilitated by this modification, potentiated the mitophagic clearance of damaged mitochondria. In addition, it inhibited the interaction between FUNDC1 and RIPK3 (receptor-interacting serine-threonine kinase 3), which in turn ameliorated dysfunction and necroptosis of dendritic cells (DCs) upon sepsis. Thus, our findings establish that TRIM13 mitigates septic responses by activating SESN2-mediated mitophagy through ubiquitination, offering new insights into potential immunomodulatory strategies for sepsis.Abbreviations: AF: AlphaFold; BECN1: beclin 1, autophagy related; CLP: cecal ligation and puncture; co-IP: co-immunoprecipitation; DAMPs: danger/damageassociated molecular patterns; DCs: dendritic cells; DEGs: differentially expressed genes; FUNDC1: FUN14 domain containing 1; IL: interleukin; LPS: lipopolysaccharide; MAMs: mitochondria-associated membranes; MAP1LC3B/LC3B: microtubule associated protein 1 light chain 3 beta; MHC: major histocompatibility complex; MLKL: mixed lineage kinase domain-like; Nec-1: necrostatin-1; PBMCs: peripheral blood mononuclear cells; RIPK3: receptor-interacting serine-threonine kinase 3; SESN2: sestrin 2; SIRT1: sirtuin 1; SQSTM1/p62: sequestosome 1; TEM: transmission electron microscopy; TLR: toll-like receptor; TNF: tumor necrosis factor; TRAF6: TNF receptor-associated factor 6; TRIM13: tripartite motif-containing 13; ULK1: unc-51 like kinase 1; UPR: unfolded protein response; UPS: ubiquitinproteasome system; WT: wild-type.

articles.title: Targeting Kynurenine Synthesis Attenuated Cigarette Smoke-Induced COPD-Like Lung Injury Driven by TALDO1-Mediated Metabolic Reprogramming.
articles.abstract: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a devastating condition characterized by airflow limitation, inflammation, and structural lung damage. Metabolic dysregulation is recognized as a critical feature, but the key metabolic drivers remain unclear. This study identifies transaldolase1 (TALDO1) as a previously unrecognized metabolic regulator in cigarette smoke (CS)-induced COPD pathogenesis. TALDO1 is markedly upregulated in airway epithelial cells by CS exposure. Elevated TALDO1 promotes mitochondrial dysfunction, whereas its genetic knockdown attenuates CS-induced lung function decline and pulmonary inflammation. Mechanistically, TALDO1 activation redirects tryptophan metabolism toward the kynurenine pathway, leading to L-kynurenine accumulation. Genetic or pharmacological inhibition of this pathway significantly alleviates mitochondrial damage, while L-kynurenine supplementation exacerbates injury. Treatment with the IDO inhibitor Epacadostat ameliorates CS-induced lung impairment and inflammation in vivo. These findings define a TALDO1-kynurenine-mitochondrial injury axis linking airway epithelial metabolic reprogramming to COPD, providing translational evidence for targeting this pathway as a therapeutic strategy.

articles.title: Metal-independent effects of calprotectin on cocultures of Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus involve alkylquinolone production.
articles.abstract: The current working model of the innate immune protein calprotectin (CP) focuses on its metal-sequestering activity, which contributes to host defense against infection. Recently, CP was reported to enhance the survival of Staphylococcus aureus in coculture with Pseudomonas aeruginosa in a metal-independent manner. This prior work indicated that the CP protein scaffold, even in the absence of its metal-binding sites, possesses activities that impact interspecies dynamics between these bacterial pathogens. In this study, we employ ΔΔ, a CP variant lacking both functional metal-binding sites, to investigate metal-independent activities of the CP protein scaffold. Using dual-species transcriptomics, we report that ΔΔ treatment induced gene expression changes indicative of cell envelope modifications for both P. aeruginosa and S. aureus during coculture. The presence of the CP protein scaffold also attenuated the production of the quorum sensing molecule C4-homoserine lactone and the anti-staphylococcal alkylquinolone (AQ) metabolite 2-heptyl-4-hydroxyquinoline N-oxide. Cocultures with S. aureus and P. aeruginosa mutants defective in AQ biosynthesis demonstrated that AQ production was required for ∆∆ to impact expression of membrane remodeling genes in both species during coculture. Furthermore, we showed that in the absence of AQ production, the effect of CP on S. aureus in coculture resembled that of Fe depletion. Collectively, our findings demonstrate that the functional versatility of CP extends beyond multi-metal sequestration and that its intertwined metal-dependent and -independent activities have important consequences for bacterial physiology and polymicrobial interactions.IMPORTANCERecent studies of the innate immune protein calprotectin (CP), which is known for its metal-sequestering ability and contributions to nutritional immunity, uncovered that the protein also exerts metal-independent activities on bacterial pathogens. In this work, we investigate the metal-independent effects of CP on the interspecies dynamics of Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus, two high-priority pathogens that co-colonize various polymicrobial infection sites. We report that the ability of the CP protein scaffold to attenuate the anti-staphylococcal activity of P. aeruginosa results from perturbed quorum sensing and reduced production of alkylquinolone (AQ) metabolites. We further show that pseudomonal AQs contribute to cell envelope remodeling responses exhibited by both pathogens in the presence of the CP protein scaffold. As such, this study is the first to interrogate the CP protein scaffold absent its metal-binding sites, demonstrating that both canonical metal-dependent and non-canonical metal-independent activities of CP elicit physiological changes that perturb coculture dynamics.

articles.title: Management and Outcome of Paediatric Septic Shock Requiring Vasoactive Therapy: A Multicentre Prospective Observational Study.
articles.abstract:
AIM: Although vasoactive drugs are recommended for paediatric septic shock requiring vasoactive therapy (PSSRVT), evidence on optimal agent selection remains limited. This study aimed to describe clinical characteristics, vasoactive drug use, adjunctive treatments, and outcomes of patients with PSSRVT.

METHODS: This multicentre, prospective study was conducted between 1 October 2024 and 30 April 2025, across 16 Paediatric Intensive Care Units (PICUs).

RESULTS: The study included 225 PSSRVT patients treated with vasoactive agents, with a PICU frequency of 5%. Normal saline was administered in 93% of cases (mean 29.6 ± 14.0 mL/kg). A single vasoactive drug was used in 23% of patients, while 45% received two. Epinephrine was the most common first-line drug (70%), followed by norepinephrine (27%). Corticosteroids were used in 53% of vasopressor-resistant cases, with a median vasoactive inotrope score (VIS) of 60 (40-100). Among patients requiring intubation due to escalating sepsis severity, the median (IQR) VIS at the time of intubation was 50 (30-70). Overall mortality was 59%.

CONCLUSION: Multiple vasoactive drugs were required in most patients, with usage patterns differing from previous reports. The median VIS at corticosteroid initiation was close to the VIS threshold associated with increased mortality. Further studies are needed to optimize vasoactive agent selection and sequencing.

articles.title: Inpatient Cognitive-Communication Interventions Following Traumatic Brain Injury: An International Survey of Speech-Language Pathologists.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: Speech-language pathologist (SLP) management of adult cognitive-communication disorders (CCDs) is recommended following traumatic brain injury (TBI). However, there is limited evidence to guide inpatient cognitive-communication interventions, and previous investigations into SLP clinical practice are multidisciplinary. This current study aimed to investigate the clinical activities, barriers, and needs of SLPs who provide inpatient cognitive-communication interventions for adults with TBI.

METHOD: An international, anonymous, mixed-methods survey was designed with reference to the "Consensus-Based Checklist for Reporting of Survey Studies." Participants were recruited via convenience and snowball recruitment. Descriptive statistics were used for quantitative data, and inductive content analysis was employed for the qualitative data.

RESULTS: Thirty-seven SLPs from seven countries participated. Participants reported intervention activities and resources that prioritized patient function and contexts. Reported barriers included SLP priorities, patient variables, and service-setting factors. Key reported needs were setting-specific resources, a stronger evidence base, and professional development.

CONCLUSIONS: Clinicians in this survey reported practices that aligned with some of the broader CCD guidelines. Inpatient SLPs emphasized functional intervention activities and personally salient resources. However, in comparison to guidelines, groups and Goal Attainment Scaling were not frequently used. The limited awareness and adaptation of existing community treatment protocols, unique hospital context, and participants' call for setting-specific intervention materials suggest that further investigation and resource development for cognitive-communication interventions within inpatient rehabilitation is warranted.

SUPPLEMENTAL MATERIAL: https://doi.org/10.23641/asha.34872597.

articles.title: Spirometric Phenotypes in Schoolchildren: Longitudinal Study of Preschool Wheezers and Controls.
articles.abstract:
AIM: Knowledge of spirometric patterns beyond obstruction with low forced expiratory volume in 1 s (FEV1) remains limited. We assessed the prevalence, characteristics, and transitions of unimpaired spirometry, preserved ratio impaired spirometry (PRISm), dysanapsis and obstruction with low FEV1 (Obst-low-FEV1) at 7 and 11 years.

METHODS: We included former preschool wheezers (cases; n7 = 102 and n11 = 97) and healthy controls (37 at both ages), of whom 87 cases and 20 controls had spirometry at both ages. Assessments comprised questionnaires, clinical examinations, spirometry, bronchodilator responsiveness (BDR), fractional exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO) and blood sampling.

RESULTS: PRISm was the most common pathological phenotype in cases (17.6%/14.4%, age 7/11) and controls (13.5% at both ages). Among cases, Obst-low-FEV1 was more common (8.8%/11.3%, 7/11 years) than dysanapsis (5.9%/8.2% age 7/11). Phenotypes changed in 54% of participants between 7 and 11 years. BDR > 10% occurred across all phenotypes but was significantly associated with dysanapsis (ORadj = 2.88, CI 1.00-8.27) and Obst-low-FEV1 (ORadj = 16.14, CI 4.89-53.30) among cases. Higher FeNO was associated with Obst-low-FEV1 (ORadj = 1.03, CI 1.00-1.07), whereas lower FeNO (ORadj = 0.90, CI 0.82-1.00) and sensitization (ORadj = 6.22, CI 0.97-39.77) were associated with dysanapsis in cases.

CONCLUSION: PRISm and dysanapsis are common, dynamic phenotypes differing from Obst-low-FEV1 in their clinical and inflammatory profiles.

articles.title: Understanding the Training of Bilingual Providers: The Spanish and English Speech Therapy Education, Practicum, and Services.
articles.journal: Language, speech, and hearing services in schools
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: The Speech Therapy Education, Practicum, and Services (STEPS) program was established to improve the training for bilingual providers and the services for bilingual individuals with and without speech-language disorders from a Latino background. This article describes the program and its components, presents preliminary data on its impact, and discusses future directions, highlighting how STEPS contributes to training bilingual providers and promotes patient-centered, linguistically and culturally responsive practices.

METHOD: Participants were 37 STEPS alumni who completed the Multilingual Service Providers Survey. Statistical analyses included a theme-by-theme internal consistency analysis to examine the measurement model and descriptive statistics of the participants' survey responses. Additionally, a qualitative theme analysis examined responses to open-ended questions.

RESULTS: The findings suggested that the STEPS program may equip speech-language pathologists with linguistic and cultural competencies necessary to serve multilingual populations. Despite strengths, the evidence to elucidate its specific impact in terms of components and academic structure remains limited. Future research should use experimental designs to evaluate training impact, address systemic barriers to clinical competence and patient-centered care, and incorporate bilingual communities' perspectives to facilitate meaningful change.

CONCLUSIONS: The STEPS program offers a promising model for training bilingual speech-language pathologists and meeting community needs. This study contributes to documenting the impact of the STEPS program and thus increases the understanding of bilingual clinicians' education and professional practice in the field.

articles.journal: Journal of agricultural and food chemistry

articles.title: Discovery of Structurally Unusual and Diverse Indole Diterpenoids with Antisteatotic Activity from the Endophytic Fungus Penicillium Paxilli BM-6.
articles.journal: Journal of agricultural and food chemistry
articles.abstract: Small molecule accurate recognition technology (SMART)-guided isolation of the endophytic fungus Penicillium paxilli BM-6 afforded 36 indole diterpenoids (IDTs) including eight new ones (1-8). Their structures were elucidated by HRMS and NMR data, DP4+ probability analysis based on calculated NMR chemical shifts, ECD calculations, and X-ray crystallography. Penipaxiline A (1) features an unprecedented 6/5/5/6/7/4 hexacyclic skeleton derived from the paspaline framework, representing a new carbon skeleton in the IDT family. Paxillindole A (2) possesses an unusual 10,30-γ-lactone moiety, whose formation introduces an extra five-membered ring, resulting in a novel 6/5/5/6/6/6/5 heptacyclic system. Antisteatotic activity screening identified 12 active compounds surpassing resmetirom, with compound 23 showing the highest inhibition rate (90.4% at 50 μM). Mechanistically, 23 reduced lipid accumulation by inhibiting lipogenesis and promoting fatty acid oxidation. These findings uncover a new pharmacological application of IDTs for the treatment of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD).

articles.title: Structural Characterization of LDP-1, a Polysaccharide from Lyophyllum decastes, and Its Protective Effects against PEDV-Induced Intestinal Inflammation In Vitro and In Vivo.
articles.journal: Journal of agricultural and food chemistry
articles.abstract: Porcine epidemic diarrhea virus (PEDV) infection causes severe intestinal inflammation and barrier injury in piglets. In this study, a purified polysaccharide fraction, Lyophyllum decastes polysaccharide-1 (LDP-1), was isolated and structurally characterized, and its protective effects against PEDV-induced intestinal injury were evaluated in IPEC-J2 cells and piglets. LDP-1 predominantly comprised glucose and exhibited a peak molecular weight of 30.56 kDa, with an α-(1→4)-glucan backbone. In vitro, LDP-1, particularly under pretreatment and whole-process treatment, attenuated PEDV-induced inflammatory cytokine expression. In vivo, LDP-1 pretreatment reduced diarrhea, alleviated intestinal pathological injury, and partially restored villus-crypt morphology. LDP-1 also decreased intestinal interleukin-6 (IL-6), interleukin-1β (IL-1β), tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) expression and restored zonula occludens-1 (ZO-1), Claudin-1, and Occludin expression. These findings indicate that LDP-1 protects against PEDV-induced intestinal inflammation and barrier injury and may serve as a potential natural protective agent.

articles.title: Effects of very early mobilization for post-stroke patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
articles.journal: European journal of physical and rehabilitation medicine
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Most stroke survivors live with long-term functional impairments. Although very early mobilization (VEM) benefits post-stroke recovery, the optimal intervention timing remains contentious and is tightly linked to intervention dosage. This study assesses the safety and efficacy of VEM initiated within 24 hours of acute stroke onset.

METHODS: A systematic literature search was performed in six electronic databases, including Medline (via PubMed), EMBASE (via embase.com), the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) in the Cochrane Library, CINAHL, APA PsycInfo, and APA PsycArticles (via EBSCOhost), with the search period concluding on August 31st, 2025. Eligible RCTs were screened and included in the analysis.

DATA ANALYSIS: Data were synthesized using RevMan 5.3 and Stata 15.0 software. Subgroup analyses were conducted based on different follow-up time points and intervention doses. The quality of evidence was evaluated using the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) system.

RESULTS: A total of 22 RCTs involving 3215 participants were included. The meta-analysis results indicated that VEM was significantly associated with lower favorable outcomes (mRS/RS 0-2, OR=0.86, 95% CI: 0.74-0.99, P=0.04) and higher mortality (OR=1.23, 95% CI: 1.04-1.46, P<0.05), with low heterogeneity. At 3 months, VEM had worse favorable outcomes (OR=0.84, P=0.02), but no difference at other follow-up times. High-dose VEM reduced favorable outcomes (OR=0.84, P=0.04), while low-dose had no difference. ADL outcomes revealed a nonlinear prognostic effect of VEM: beneficial effects emerge at day 7 (SMD=0.73, 95% CI: 0.09, 1.37; P=0.03), peak at 1 month (SMD=1.35, 95% CI: 0.72, 1.98; P<0.0001), and decline to statistical insignificance by 3 months (SMD=0.10, 95% CI: -0.09, 0.28; P=0.30), with greater functional recovery in patients receiving high-dose regimens (SMD = 1.48, 95% CI: 0.84, 2.13; P<0.00001). No significant differences were found in mortality (dose subgroups), complications, or ADL scores between VEM and CG.

CONCLUSIONS: In conclusion, high-dose VEM within 24 hours post-stroke is associated with poor functional outcomes, whereas low-dose VEM yields no between-group differences in functional recovery, mortality or complications relative to the controls. ADL benefits fail to present a linear pattern. The efficacy of VEM is modulated by multiple factors, including intervention timing, mobilization dosage, and patients' baseline clinical status. Constrained by the limited number of included trials and small sample sizes, the certainty of evidence was moderate for favorable functional outcomes, mortality and ADL, while evidence pertaining to complications was rated low. Further stratified research by baseline status, timing and dosage is necessary to define the prognostic influence of early mobilization in stroke patients.

articles.title: Incidence and Management of Ocular Hypertension Following the 0.19 mg Fluocinolone Acetonide Implant for Diabetic Macular Edema.
authors: Wills Eye Retina Service Study Group, The Wills Eye Retina Service Study Group additionally includes
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: To investigate the real-world incidence and management of ocular hypertension (OHT) following the intravitreal 0.19 mg fluocinolone acetonide implant (FAi, Iluvien) for diabetic macular edema (DME).

METHODS: Retrospective review of eyes treated with FAi (2015-2025) with ≥1 month follow-up. Primary outcome was OHT (IOP >25 mmHg). Secondary outcomes included IOP >30 mmHg, IOP rise ≥10 mmHg from baseline, and OHT management.

RESULTS: A total of 118 eyes (90 patients) were included with mean follow-up of 33.1 ± 1.3 months. Mean baseline IOP was 14.0 ± 3.0 mmHg. Pre-existing glaucoma or OHT was present in 32.2% of eyes, and 78.8% had a prior periocular or intravitreal corticosteroid injection. Overall, 11 eyes (9.3%) developed OHT (IOP >25mmHg) following FAi. Peak IOP >30 mmHg occurred in 6 eyes (5.1%), and 12 eyes (10.2%) had an IOP rise ≥10 mmHg above baseline. OHT developed at variable time points, with 36.4% of cases occurring between 6-12 months and 27.3% after 24 months; mean time to OHT development was 15.6 ± 13.1 months. Higher baseline IOP was associated with increased odds of developing OHT (OR per 1mmHg increase 1.32, p=0.02). Of the 11 eyes with OHT, most were managed medically (63.6%) or with observation (36.4%) alone, with only 1 eye (9.1%, 0.8% of entire cohort) requiring incisional glaucoma surgery.

CONCLUSION: FAi was associated with low rates of OHT, with most cases managed with observation or topical therapy, with surgery rarely required. This supports the safety of FAi and highlight the importance of extended IOP monitoring.

articles.title: People With Influenza Requiring ICU Admission During the 2025-2026 Season, Marked by the Emergence of Influenza A(H3N2) Subclade K: A French Prospective Nationwide Cohort Study.
articles.journal: Clinical infectious diseases : an official publication of the Infectious Diseases Society of America
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Intense influenza activity has been reported alongside the emergence of influenza A(H3N2) subclade K. While epidemiological studies have reported heterogeneous findings regarding public health impact, data remain lacking on its impact on clinical phenotype of people requiring intensive care unit (ICU) admission.

METHODS: Prospective, multicenter, observational SEVARVIR cohort study including people admitted in 42 French ICUs with laboratory-confirmed influenza infection during the 2024-2025 and 2025-2026 seasons. Primary end point was day-28 mortality.

RESULTS: Seven hundred twenty-six people were admitted for influenza in 2024-2025 (n = 360) and 2025-2026 (n = 366). In 2025-2026, influenza subtype was available for 265 people; 49% (n = 129) had A(H1N1)pdm09 and 51% (n = 136) had A(H3N2) subtype infection. Among the 40 people with A(H3N2) infection for whom whole-genome sequencing was available, 33 (82.5%) belonged to subclade K. In multivariable Cox analysis of the 2025-2026 season, age (adjusted hazard ratio, aHR = 1.04 [1.01;1.09]; P = .015), Clinical Frailty Scale (aHR = 1.59 [1.28;1.98]; P < .001), and sequential organ failure assessment score (aHR = 1.15 [1.05;1.26]; P = .003) were associated with an increased risk of death. In the 2024-2025/2025-2026 seasons or 2025-2026 season alone, influenza subtype was not associated with a significant risk of day-28 mortality. Phylogenetic analyses from our ICU cohort together with 600 contextual sequences from community-acquired influenza cases collected during the period showed no clustering according to severity.

CONCLUSIONS: There was no evidence of an increased risk of death among critically ill people with influenza during the 2025-2026 season, despite the emergence of influenza A(H3N2) subclade K.

TRIAL REGISTRATION: NCT05162508.

articles.title: Determinants of T Cell Exhaustion: How Far Back Can We Go?
articles.abstract: Over the past four decades, T cell exhaustion has been primarily associated with chronic infection and cancer and described as a late, adaptive response that limits immunopathology under chronic antigen exposure. Emerging evidence has revealed that exhausted T (Tex) cells are formed developmentally with distinct transcriptomic, epigenetic and phenotypic profiles, with progressive and hierarchical loss of effector functions. Recent reports show that exhaustion is not merely a late-stage phenomenon, but a multifaceted developmental trajectory that begins far earlier than previously thought. Intrinsic factors established at T cell priming synergize with extrinsic cues from the tissue microenvironment to drive T cell differentiation towards an exhausted state long before exhaustion becomes phenotypically fixed. This review presents an overview of recent knowledge that has reshaped our understanding of T cell exhaustion formation. Here, we discuss the genetic, epigenetic and metabolic determinants of T cell exhaustion, as well as the roles other soluble mediators and cell types may play in promoting exhaustion. Enhancing our understanding of early determinants of exhaustion has implications for the development and application of therapeutic strategies that adapt to the temporal evolution of exhaustion, which may be more effective than treatments aimed solely at reversing exhaustion.

articles.title: Edge-to-edge mitral valve repair for bileaflet prolapse in Barlow disease.
articles.journal: Multimedia manual of cardiothoracic surgery : MMCTS
articles.abstract: Barlow disease with bileaflet prolapse represents one of the most challenging lesions in degenerative mitral valve surgery. Multiple prolapsing segments, excess leaflet tissue, elongated chordae and annular dilatation often coexist, requiring a comprehensive repair strategy. The edge-to-edge technique, first introduced in 1991, provides a simple and reproducible method to restore leaflet coaptation in this complex setting. By approximating the free edges of the anterior and posterior leaflets at the site of regurgitation, a double-orifice mitral valve is created. This single manoeuvre effectively addresses bileaflet prolapse, reduces leaflet height, forces coaptation, restricts excessive leaflet motion and prevents systolic anterior motion of the anterior leaflet. A concomitant ring annuloplasty is strongly recommended to remodel the dilated annulus, stabilize the repair and ensure long-term durability. This video tutorial presents the key surgical steps of the double-orifice edge-to-edge repair combined with annuloplasty for the treatment of severe mitral regurgitation caused by bileaflet prolapse in Barlow disease. The procedure is performed through a anterolateral minithoracotomy at the fourth intercostal space under video assistance with peripherical cardiopulmonary bypass and cardioplegic arrest. Technical tips for patient selection, suture placement, leaflet assessment, avoidance of mitral stenosis and intraoperative competence testing are provided.

articles.title: Evaluation of a Rapid and Practical Deep Learning Framework for T1-weighted MRI-based Brain Age Estimation.
articles.abstract: Purpose To develop and evaluate a rapid brain-age estimation framework using freely available Python tools and assess the clinical relevance of brain-age gap (BAG). Materials and Methods In this retrospective study conducted from March 2025 to August 2026, T1-weighted MR images from cohorts of cognitively normal adults (n = 4,346) were divided into training, validation, and internal test sets; two cohorts (n = 315 and 209) served as external test sets. Clinical evaluation used the BICWALZS cohort (n = 954; cognitively normal and various dementias). Preprocessing used freely available Python tools only. The model was trained to predict chronological age as the reference standard. Associations of the residualized BAG with diagnosis, amyloid PET positivity, white matter hyperintensity (WMH) severity, stroke history, and longitudinal clinical worsening were evaluated using ANCOVA, logistic regression, and Cox models. Results The development cohort included 4,346 cognitively normal adults (mean age, 47.0 ± 21.2 years; 2,414 women). Chronological age prediction yielded R2 = 0.95 and MAE, 3.76 years in the internal test set and R2 = 0.69-0.90 and MAE, 4.82-5.15 years in external test sets. The residualized BAG increased across diagnostic groups (P < .001) and was associated with WMH severity (odds ratio [OR], 1.64; P < .001) and stroke history (OR, 1.46; P < .001), but not with amyloid positivity after full adjustment (P = .17), and predicted longitudinal clinical worsening (HR, 1.92). Conclusion The framework accurately predicted age, while residualized BAG was associated with diagnosis, cerebrovascular burden, and longitudinal clinical worsening. © RSNA, 2026.

articles.title: Sympathetic hyperactivity in hypertension via additional intraganglionic cholinergic collateral connections.
articles.abstract: Sympathetic hyperactivity in hypertension is classically attributed to altered central drive, yet peripheral synaptic mechanisms within autonomic ganglia remain poorly defined. We previously demonstrated excitatory cholinergic collateral synaptic connections between sympathetic ganglion neurons and showed that angiotensin II (AngII)-induced hypertension increases sympathetic activity in postganglionic neurons independent of the CNS by activating collateral connections. Here, we tested whether AngII-induced hypertension induces intraganglionic synaptic remodelling in stellate ganglia by quantifying excitatory postsynaptic current (EPSC) latency dynamics, including latency, jitter, response multiplicity and probability of failure. AngII-induced hypertension increased latency variability of evoked EPSCs, response multiplicity and synaptic failure rates, indicating reduced temporal precision and heterogeneous synaptic transmission. These changes are inconsistent with increased presynaptic release or postsynaptic receptor function and instead suggest altered synaptic circuit organization within stellate ganglia. Collectively, these data provide functional evidence that hypertension is associated with intraganglionic synaptic reorganization consistent with increased circuit complexity. Such peripheral remodelling represents a previously underappreciated mechanism that might contribute to sympathetic overactivity in cardiovascular disease.

articles.title: Between the Dings.
articles.journal: Pediatric critical care medicine : a journal of the Society of Critical Care Medicine and the World Federation of Pediatric Intensive and Critical Care Societies

articles.title: Low Physical Activity and Reported Barriers Among Survivors of Critical Illness: A Mixed-Method Study.
authors: Trajectories of Recovery after ACutE and cRitical illness (TRACER) study group
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To examine physical activity levels in survivors of critical illness across 6 months, and to understand the barriers and facilitators of physical activity.

DESIGN: Prospective, longitudinal, convergent mixed-methods study.

SETTING: Functional testing laboratory.

PATIENTS: Adults admitted to the ICU for at least 72 hours with acute respiratory failure or sepsis.

INTERVENTIONS: None.

MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: Patients wore an accelerometer starting at hospital discharge, at 3- and 6-month follow-up to quantify daily step counts. At 6 months, physical function and patient-reported outcomes were collected in-person, with a subset of participants completing semi-structured interviews. Eighty-two patients were enrolled, with 67 (82%) having physical activity data with median age of 60 years (interquartile range [IQR], 52-66 yr), 54% male, and ICU stay 9.0 days [IQR, 5.8-17.0 d]. The median daily steps were 1358 (IQR, 742-2799) in 50 patients at baseline, 2305 (IQR, 1081-3898) in 54 patients at 3 months, and 2826 (IQR, 1609-4781) in 44 patients at 6 months. Higher comorbidity burden and earlier measurement associated with lower step counts. At 6 months, patients walked a mean of 344 ± 169 meters on the 6-minute walk test and reported being sedentary a median of 300 min/days (150-480 min/d). Eleven participants completed interviews, yielding three themes: 1) "a marathon, not a sprint": the extended ICU recovery trajectory; 2) engagement in physical activity is highly regulated by personal context; 3) value-driven and motivation-informed physical activity decisions. Mixed-methods integration demonstrated that qualitative themes expanded upon quantitative findings to explain nonlinear recovery patterns, contextualizing persistent sedentary behavior, and revealing that motivational and behavioral gaps are not captured by accelerometry.

CONCLUSIONS: Survivors showed gradual improvement in daily steps over 6 months yet remained below recommended activity levels. Survivorship and attrition biases may lead to overestimation of step counts, further warranting larger studies. Integrating quantitative and qualitative data reveals modifiable contextual factors that may inform the design of pragmatic physical activity interventions.

articles.title: Evaluation of Sequential Organ Failure Assessment-2 Performance Across Demographic Subgroups: An External Validation Using MIMIC-IV.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the discrimination and calibration of the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA)-2 score for ICU mortality across demographic subgroups defined by age, sex, race and ethnicity, primary language, and insurance status.

DESIGN: Retrospective cohort study.

SETTING: Single academic medical center in the northeastern United States (Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston, MA), using the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care-IV database (version 3.1), 2008-2022, a dataset external to the SOFA-2 development cohort.

PATIENTS: Adult patients (≥ 18 yr) with at least one ICU admission. The first ICU admission of the first qualifying hospitalization per patient was analyzed.

INTERVENTIONS: None.

MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: First-day SOFA-2 scores were calculated from the worst values recorded during the first 24 hours of ICU admission across six organ systems, with ICU mortality as the primary outcome. Discrimination was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and calibration using intercept and slope, with subgroup differences in AUROC estimated by bootstrap resampling. Among 64,015 ICU patients (mean [sd] age, 64.6 [17.1] yr; 56.1% male; 66.1% White), overall AUROC was 0.77 (95% CI, 0.76-0.77). Discrimination declined significantly with age: AUROC, 0.85 (0.83-0.87) for ages 18-44 years vs. 0.72 (0.70-0.73) for ages 75 or older (ΔAUROC, -0.14 [95% CI, -0.16 to -0.11]), with systematic underprediction in older patients. Discrimination was significantly decreased among non-English speakers (ΔAUROC, -0.04) but did not differ across documented racial/ethnic groups. Patients with missing demographic information had markedly higher mortality than the overall cohort rate of 7.2% (14.1% for missing race/ethnicity; 23.1% for missing language).

CONCLUSIONS: SOFA-2 demonstrated good overall performance but with clinically meaningful variation across subgroups, particularly with age and language. Patients with missing demographic data experienced markedly higher mortality. These findings argue for routine equity evaluation as a complement to traditional validation of clinical prediction tools.

articles.title: The Quiet Struggle: Parental Perspectives on Sibling Well-Being During PICU Admission.
articles.journal: Pediatric critical care medicine : a journal of the Society of Critical Care Medicine and the World Federation of Pediatric Intensive and Critical Care Societies
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To identify the impact of PICU admission on parental perceptions of the well-being of patients' child-aged siblings and understand how families use hospital resources to support siblings.

DESIGN: Qualitative study using semi-structured interviews of parents of PICU patients with siblings to characterize sibling socioemotional changes during PICU admission and how the sibling interacted with hospital resources. Interviews were transcribed and thematically analyzed.

SETTING: Quaternary-care PICU at a level 1 trauma center in St. Louis, MO.

SUBJECTS: Parents of a child admitted to the PICU with at least one additional child living at home between the ages of 5 and 19 years.

INTERVENTIONS: None.

MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: Fourteen biological parents and one legal guardian representing 15 households and 17 siblings of PICU patients were interviewed. Four themes were identified describing parental perspective on sibling psychosocial well-being: 1) routine is important, 2) parents consider multiple factors when evaluating the impact of sibling visits on child well-being, 3) hospitalizations impacts sibling well-being in many ways, and 4) few siblings' physical well-being changed following hospitalization. Two themes were identified regarding parental perspective of hospital resources: 5) parents believed that hospital support was designed to cultivate a sense of normalcy, and 6) the provision and utilization of child life services was not uniform.

CONCLUSIONS: It is critical to prioritize the emotional and social well-being of siblings of critically ill and injured children through the maintenance of routine, balancing the needs of both patient and sibling when considering visitation policies, and providing hospital supports tailored to sibling's age and cognitive level.

articles.title: The Effect of Guanfacine on Delirium in Surgical and Trauma ICU Patients: A Pilot Randomized Clinical Trial.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the feasibility of conducting a randomized controlled trial investigating guanfacine for ICU delirium, including assessment of recruitment, retention, protocol adherence, and data completeness, while estimating treatment effects to inform future trial design.

DESIGN: Single-center, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled pilot trial conducted from November 2020 to February 2023.

SETTING: Surgical and Trauma ICUs at the University of Alabama at Birmingham Hospital.

PATIENTS: One hundred critically ill adults with Confusion Assessment Method-ICU-confirmed delirium randomized 1:1 to guanfacine or placebo.

INTERVENTIONS: Patients received 2 mg guanfacine or matching placebo nightly for up to 14 days, or until ICU discharge or delirium resolution.

MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: Primary feasibility outcomes included protocol adherence (target ≥ 90%), retention (target ≥ 80%), recruitment rate (target ≥ 2 patients/mo), and data completeness (target ≥ 95%). Most feasibility targets were achieved: protocol adherence was 100%, retention was 100%, and data completeness was 100%. Recruitment was significantly impacted by COVID-19 pandemic disruptions, achieving 0.9 patients/wk during active recruitment periods.For clinical outcomes, in unadjusted analyses, median delirium and coma-free days were higher with guanfacine than placebo (2 [interquartile range [IQR], 0-6] vs. 1 [IQR, 0-4]; p = 0.02); however, this association was not statistically significant after adjustment for prespecified baseline covariates. ICU and hospital length of stay and duration of mechanical ventilation did not differ significantly between groups. No hemodynamic differences or safety concerns were observed.

CONCLUSIONS: This pilot study successfully supports feasibility for a definitive trial, with excellent protocol adherence, adequate retention, and preliminary signals that warrant further evaluation. Although adjusted analyses were not statistically significant, the observed unadjusted difference in delirium and coma-free days and favorable safety profile support progression to a multicenter trial informed by these pilot estimates.

articles.title: Composite Endpoints in Critical Care Delirium Trials.
articles.abstract: Delirium is an abnormal mental status, commonly occurring among critically ill patients, in which a person's attention and awareness change acutely. Delirium is associated with negative outcomes, including death. Furthermore, a longer duration of delirium is associated with long-term cognitive impairment in survivors of critical illness. Hence, there is a need for novel interventions that reduce the duration of delirium; however, measuring and analyzing "duration of delirium" as an endpoint in randomized trials is challenging due to the episodic nature of delirium and the competing events of coma and death, which can bias analyses of duration of delirium. Given these challenges, delirium trials have adopted one of two composite endpoints: delirium- and coma-free days, defined as the number of days alive without delirium or coma for both survivors and nonsurvivors, and an alternative composite that ranks death as the worst state and orders days alive without delirium or coma among survivors. To date, these composite endpoints have not been rigorously evaluated. Hence, herein we use data from the Maximizing Efficacy of Targeted Sedation and Reducing Neurologic Dysfunction (MENDS) trial to motivate the use of composite endpoints in critical care delirium trials, discuss how to define the effect of treatment on each composite endpoint and their clinical interpretability, and present a method for visualizing how the treatment effects accrue over the course of follow-up. Based on these analyses, we provide practical recommendations for the use of composite endpoints in critical care delirium trials, which could be extended to other randomized trials that rely on similar composite endpoints.

articles.title: Normocapnia Versus Mild Hypercapnia During Lung Protective Ventilation in Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome: A Target Trial Emulation.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: This trial emulation aimed to answer the question: Among patients with acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) who receive lung protective ventilation with low tidal volume, is normocapnia through an increase in respiratory rate associated with lower mortality than mild hypercapnia?

DESIGN: Target trial emulation.

SETTING: Hospitals of the ARDS Network and Prevention and Early Treatment of Acute Lung Injury (PETAL) Network.

PATIENTS: Patients with ARDS enrolled in seven ARDS Network and PETAL Network randomized controlled trials.

INTERVENTIONS: None.

MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: A target trial was emulated, assigning participants in a 1:1 ratio to normocapnia (target Paco2 35-45 mm Hg) or mild hypercapnia (target Paco2 50-55 mm Hg) for 4 days following the initiation of lung protective ventilation. The primary outcome was 90-day in-hospital mortality. Of 5367 potentially eligible subjects, 292 patients were assigned to normocapnia and 292 to mild hypercapnia. Separation in Paco2 values was preserved over the 4-day period of emulated intervention. Both groups had median pH greater than or equal to 7.33. Bicarbonate levels, driving pressure, tidal volume, and dead-space fraction did not differ clinically significantly between groups, while median respiratory rate was 33.0 breaths/min in the normocapnia vs. 28.0 breaths/min in the mild hypercapnia group (p < 0.001). Death within 90 days occurred in 84 of 292 patients (28.8%) in the normocapnia group and in 84 of 292 patients (28.8%) in the mild hypercapnia group (log-rank p = 0.842). This result persisted in subgroups such as older (≥ 65 yr) and obese (body mass index ≥ 30 kg/m2) patients.

CONCLUSIONS: Among patients with ARDS who received lung protective ventilation, normocapnia through an increase in respiratory rate was not associated with lower mortality than mild hypercapnia. As this finding is derived from a trial emulation, it should be interpreted cautiously given the potential for significant residual bias.

articles.title: The Serum Proteomic Signatures Associated With Organ Dysfunction Based on Phoenix Criteria in Pediatric Sepsis: A Pilot Study.
articles.journal: Pediatric critical care medicine : a journal of the Society of Critical Care Medicine and the World Federation of Pediatric Intensive and Critical Care Societies
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To investigate the serum proteomic characteristics linked to sepsis-induced organ dysfunction, as defined by the Phoenix Pediatric Sepsis (PPS) criteria.

DESIGN AND SETTING: We conducted a serum proteomic study using data-independent acquisition mass spectrometry in pediatric patients with sepsis, admitted to the PICU at a tertiary, university-affiliated children's hospital in China.

PATIENTS: Thirty-eight patients with sepsis and 19 healthy controls were included from November 2020 to June 2022.

INTERVENTIONS: None.

MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: A total of 403 differentially expressed proteins (DEPs) were identified in the serum of pediatric sepsis patients compared with healthy controls. Gene Set Enrichment Analysis revealed that DEPs across the four PPS-defined organ dysfunction were enriched in the antimicrobial humoral response, negative regulation of inflammation, plasminogen activation, and cytokine-mediated signaling pathways. Weighted Gene Co-Expression Network Analysis (WGCNA) showed that the MEgreen module was highly associated with the PPS score and was enriched in neutrophils. Further analysis identified seven hub proteins (tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinase-1 [TIMP1], cathepsin L peptidase 1, β-1,4-galactosyltransferase 1, carbonic anhydrase 3, interleukin 1 receptor like 1, olfactomedin 4, and cathepsin G [CATG]) as candidate serum proteomic markers of organ dysfunction risk. We used the expression of these seven hub proteins in a least absolute shrinkage and selection operator regression model to predict organ system dysfunction. It achieved an area under the curve of 0.857 for the coagulation system and 0.769 for the cardiovascular system. All seven hub proteins were significantly correlated with lactic acid and the international normalized ratio (all p < 0.05); CATG was positively correlated with mean arterial pressure (p = 0.005), TIMP1 displayed a positive correlation with d-dimer (p = 0.021) and a negative correlation with platelet (p = 0.005).

CONCLUSIONS: We identified seven hub proteins that constitute a novel proteomic signature for predicting sepsis-associated organ dysfunction based on the Phoenix criteria. It is particularly relevant to the coagulation and cardiovascular systems.

articles.title: Postoperative Infection Mediates and Modifies the Effect of Risk Adjustment for Congenital Heart Surgery-1 Category on Hospital Stay in Pediatric Cardiac Surgery: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
articles.journal: Pediatric critical care medicine : a journal of the Society of Critical Care Medicine and the World Federation of Pediatric Intensive and Critical Care Societies
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To investigate whether postoperative infection mediates and/or modifies the effect of surgical complexity, as defined by the Risk Adjustment for Congenital Heart Surgery (RACHS-1) category, on hospital length of stay (LOS) in pediatric cardiac surgery patients.

DESIGN: Retrospective cohort study.

SETTING: Tertiary pediatric cardiac center at Xinhua Hospital, Shanghai Jiao Tong University.

PATIENTS: A total of 1244 children who underwent congenital heart surgery between October 2020 and July 2024.

INTERVENTIONS: None.

MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: Multivariable regression and causal-mediation analyses were performed to estimate the direct and infection-mediated effects of surgical complexity on LOS. Higher-RACHS-1 categories and postoperative infection were independently associated with prolonged LOS (all p < 0.001). In negative binomial mediation analysis, infection mediated 17.4% of the total RACHS-LOS association for RACHS-1 category greater than or equal to 5 vs. 1, corresponding to an infection-mediated increase of 3.87 expected LOS days (95% CI, 1.70-6.42). Infection also modified the association between surgical complexity and LOS, with infection-associated excess LOS increasing to +16.73 days in RACHS-1 category greater than or equal to 5 vs. 1. Mediation was strongest among infants less than or equal to 1 year (28% for RACHS-1 category 3 vs. 1).

CONCLUSIONS: Postoperative infection both mediates and amplifies the impact of surgical complexity on hospital LOS, particularly in high-risk infants. Targeted infection-prevention strategies are essential to reduce postoperative morbidity in this population.

articles.title: ROS-Responsive Selenocysteine-Releasing Nanozyme for Targeted Ferroptosis Suppression and Pancreatic β-Cell Protection in Type 2 Diabetes.
articles.abstract: Pancreatic β-cell ferroptosis, driven by oxidative stress and impaired glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) activity, has emerged as an important contributor to the progression of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). However, persistent reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation and insufficient selenocysteine (Sec) availability limit GPX4-dependent antioxidant defense, making effective ferroptosis intervention challenging. Here, we engineered a ROS-responsive Sec-loaded copper-based single-atom nanozyme (Se@CuSAzyme) that combines catalytic ROS scavenging with Sec supplementation. Benefiting from its intrinsic superoxide dismutase- and catalase-like activities, Se@CuSAzyme efficiently eliminated excessive ROS, while oxidative stress-triggered Sec release enhanced GPX4 expression. As a result, Se@CuSAzyme markedly suppressed high glucose and erastin-induced ferroptosis, reduced lipid peroxidation, and preserved mitochondrial integrity in pancreatic β-cells. In high-fat diet/streptozotocin-induced diabetic mice, Se@CuSAzyme demonstrated therapeutic efficacy comparable to that of metformin in ameliorating hyperglycemia, alleviating insulin resistance, and increasing energy expenditure. Importantly, Se@CuSAzyme outperformed metformin in protecting against hepatic steatosis and glycolipid metabolic dysfunction.

articles.title: Circulating Cell-Free Mitochondrial DNA, Delirium, and Long-Term Cognitive Impairment in Critically Ill Adults With Sepsis: A Prospective Cohort Study.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: During sepsis, circulating cell-free mitochondrial DNA (ccf-mtDNA) is released and elevated due to cell injury, augments the immune response, and may contribute to organ dysfunction. Delirium is common and deleterious during sepsis, but little is known about the relationship between mitochondrial injury and delirium during sepsis. We sought therefore to examine associations between ccf-mtDNA and delirium and other clinical outcomes during sepsis.

DESIGN: Multicenter, prospective cohort study.

SETTING: Medical and surgical ICUs in university and community hospitals in Nashville, TN.

PATIENTS: Four hundred eighty patients with sepsis plus shock and/or acute respiratory failure.

INTERVENTIONS: None.

MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: We measured ccf-mtDNA in plasma collected on multiple days (study days 1, 3, and 5) during sepsis and assessed participants bid for delirium and coma using the validated Confusion Assessment Method for the ICU and Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale. We then assessed survivors' cognitive function 3 and 12 months after hospital discharge using the Repeatable Battery for the Assessment of Neuropsychological Status. During sepsis, the adjusted odds of delirium were 7% lower for individuals at the 75th percentile of ccf-mtDNA compared with those at the 25th percentile (odds ratio [OR], 0.93; 95% CI, 0.86-0.99; p = 0.048). ccf-mtDNA was marginally associated with in-hospital mortality (hazard ratio, 1.09; 95% CI, 0.99-1.20; p = 0.08), but was not associated with coma (OR, 0.98; 95% CI, 0.90-1.05; p = 0.31) or 3-month (beta, 0.23; 95% CI, -1.58 to 2.05; p = 0.80) and 12-month (beta, -0.36; 95% CI, -2.13 to 1.42; p = 0.69) cognitive outcomes.

CONCLUSIONS: In this multicenter, prospective cohort study, higher levels of ccf-mtDNA were associated with lower odds of delirium, a result that contradicted our hypothesis. This provocative finding should be interpreted cautiously until replicated and explained by future studies.

articles.title: Alarm Fatigue Across Critical Care Domains: Comparative Insights and Independent Predictors From a Cross-Sectional Multicenter Survey Study.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Alarm fatigue, the desensitization to excessive false alarms, threatens patient safety and staff performance across critical care domains. It is unclear whether alarm fatigue differs between hospital departments. This study compared alarm fatigue among staff in the ICU, cardiac telemetry ward (CTW), and operating room (OR), and, secondarily, identified its independent determinants.

DESIGN: Cross-sectional, multicenter survey study.

SETTING: ICUs, a CTW, and ORs.

PATIENTS: A total of 514 healthcare professionals working in the ICU, CTW, and OR.

INTERVENTIONS: None.

MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: Alarm fatigue was assessed using the Dutch-translated Charité Alarm Fatigue Questionnaire, which includes alarm stress and alarm coping subscales. Participants also rated their self-perceived alarm fatigue on a 1-10 scale and the percentage of perceived false alarms. Telemetry staff reported the highest self-perceived alarm fatigue (B = 0.65; 95% CI, 0.06-1.24; p = 0.032) and perceived false alarms (B = 0.77; 95% CI, 0.23-1.30; p = 0.005), while OR staff reported the lowest (B = -1.01; 95% CI, -1.59 to -0.43; p < 0.001). Second, physicians (B = -0.13; 95% CI, -0.25 to -0.01; p < 0.031) and less experienced staff (< 3 mo; B = -0.34; 95% CI, -0.68 to -0.01; p = 0.046) reported lower alarm fatigue.

CONCLUSIONS: Alarm fatigue varied significantly across departments and professions, being highest in telemetry staff and lowest among physicians and less experienced personnel. Targeted department-specific interventions and longitudinal research are necessary to mitigate alarm fatigue and enhance patient safety.

articles.title: Fish TRAF6 shapes interferon antiviral response by targeting the background MAVS for protein degradation.
articles.abstract: The interferon (IFN)-mediated antiviral immune response is tightly regulated to prevent insufficient or excessive immune activation. In mammals, the E3 ubiquitin ligase tumor necrosis factor receptor-associated factor 6 (TRAF6) is generally considered a positive regulator of IFN signaling although its role in fish may differ. In this study, zebrafish TRAF6 showed opposing regulatory effects on different retinoic acid-inducible gene I (RIG-I)-like receptor (RLR) signaling components in overexpression assays, but knockdown and knockout experiments further supported its overall negative regulatory role in the fish IFN response. To investigate this inhibitory mechanism, we uncovered a previously unrecognized role of zebrafish TRAF6 in promoting the degradation of mitochondrial antiviral-signaling protein (MAVS) under basal conditions in an E3 ligase activity-dependent manner. Zebrafish TRAF6 bound to the N-terminal caspase recruitment domain (CARD) of MAVS in the cytoplasm and promoted lysosome-dependent MAVS degradation. Lys286 and Lys293 contributed to this degradation and were required for TRAF6-enhanced K48-linked polyubiquitination of MAVS. Simultaneous mutation of both residues increased basal MAVS protein levels and enhanced its ability to activate the IFN response. Our data also suggest that TRAF6 may promote MAVS degradation through a proteasome-dependent pathway involving the C-terminal region of MAVS. TRAF6 knockout (TRAF6-KO) zebrafish exhibited significantly enhanced resistance to spring viremia of carp virus (SVCV) infection. Basal MAVS protein levels were also significantly higher in TRAF6-KO tissues than in wild-type (WT) zebrafish. Collectively, our results reveal a critical role of zebrafish TRAF6 in regulating basal MAVS expression to fine-tune IFN-mediated antiviral innate immunity.IMPORTANCEInterferon (IFN)-mediated innate immunity is essential for protecting fish against viral infection, but excessive IFN activation can also be harmful to the host. Here, we identify zebrafish TRAF6 as a dual regulator of IFN-mediated antiviral signaling. In overexpression assays, TRAF6 enhanced RIG-I-mediated signaling and increased K63-linked ubiquitination of the RIG-I signaling complex while suppressing MAVS-mediated signaling by promoting MAVS degradation through distinct degradation pathways. In vivo, TRAF6 deficiency enhanced antiviral gene expression, reduced infectious viral titers, and significantly improved survival following SVCV infection. These findings reveal a previously unrecognized dual regulatory role for TRAF6 in fish antiviral immunity and highlight the importance of TRAF6-mediated MAVS degradation under basal conditions in regulating IFN-mediated antiviral responses.

articles.title: Echo-Guided Ventilator Management in Critical Care: A Physiology-Based How-To Approach to Heart-Lung Interactions.
articles.journal: Turk Kardiyoloji Dernegi arsivi : Turk Kardiyoloji Derneginin yayin organidir
articles.abstract: Mechanical ventilation profoundly influences cardiovascular physiology through complex heart-lung interactions that affect preload, afterload, right ventricular (RV) function, ventricular interdependence, and forward flow. Despite these interactions, bedside hemodynamic assessment in mechanically ventilated patients often remains fragmented and predominantly pressure-oriented, potentially obscuring the underlying physiological mechanisms of circulatory instability. This article presents a physiology-based, flow-oriented echocardiographic framework for hemodynamic assessment during mechanical ventilation. The proposed approach integrates cardiopulmonary physiology with bedside echocardiography, prioritizing RV geometry, ventricular interdependence, and serial assessment of forward flow using the left ventricular outflow tract velocity-time integral (LVOT VTI). Within this framework, ventilator settings are interpreted according to their dynamic effects on ventricular loading conditions and effective circulation rather than as isolated respiratory variables. The article discusses the physiological effects of positive-pressure ventilation on RV loading, ventricular interdependence, and effective forward flow. It also addresses the limitations of static preload indices and the contextual interpretation of dynamic preload responsiveness tests, highlighting the role of echocardiography in bedside hemodynamic decision-making during ventilator adjustment and weaning. A shift from pressure-based assessment to a structured, flow-oriented echocardiographic approach may improve the interpretation of ventilator-associated hemodynamic instability. By aligning ventilator management with real-time cardiovascular physiology, this integrated framework may support individualized bedside management and help prevent inappropriate interventions, particularly unnecessary fluid administration. The proposed framework should be regarded as a physiology-based conceptual model intended to support bedside reasoning rather than as a validated clinical management algorithm.

articles.title: Combat Diver Training Shifts Autonomic Balance and Increases Vigor Without Cardiac Remodeling.
articles.journal: Turk Kardiyoloji Dernegi arsivi : Turk Kardiyoloji Derneginin yayin organidir
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the effects of a six-month intensive combat diver training program on autonomic function, cardiac structure, and psychological mood.

METHOD: Seven elite male combat diver candidates (median age, approximately 23 years) were assessed before and after a six-month program incorporating static and dynamic apnea, freediving drills, and high-intensity aquatic conditioning. Heart rate variability (HRV) was recorded using a Polar H10 device and analyzed with Kubios software. Resting transthoracic echocardiography was performed in accordance with the American Society of Echocardiography guidelines. Mood was assessed using the validated Turkish version of the Brunel Mood Scale (BRUMS). The Wilcoxon signed-rank test was used for all comparisons.

RESULTS: Training significantly increased parasympathetic tone, as demonstrated by a reduction in resting heart rate (from 68 to 62 bpm; P = 0.045) and increases in RMSSD (from 43 to 57 ms; P = 0.028), HF% (from 19.2% to 34.2%; P = 0.018), and the PNS index (from -0.17 to 0.54; P = 0.018), together with a marked decrease in the LF/HF ratio (from 4.20 to 1.92; P = 0.018). All echocardiographic parameters remained unchanged (P > 0.05). The BRUMS Vigor subscale score increased significantly (from 8 to 15; P = 0.017).

CONCLUSION: Six months of combat diver training enhanced parasympathetic dominance and psychological vigor without inducing cardiac structural remodeling, suggesting improvements in operational readiness and resilience to stress.

articles.title: Gut-hormone receptor systems in the eye: Pharmacological, local and putative endocrine signalling.
articles.abstract: The neural retina has traditionally been viewed as a downstream target of systemic metabolic disease, yet experimental and clinical evidence suggests that ocular tissues may also respond directly to peptide-hormone signalling. This review critically examines gut-hormone-related receptor systems in the eye across three biologically distinct evidence streams: endogenous circulating gut peptides, pharmacological receptor agonism, and locally synthesised ocular peptides. Physiological retinal access of native gut peptides remains poorly characterised, while receptor localisation is highly dependent on species and detection methodology. Mechanistic evidence is strongest for pharmacological GLP-1 receptor activation and local NPY and ghrelin systems, particularly in relation to neuroprotection, immunomodulation, metabolic and oxidative homeostasis, and neurovascular regulation. Human evidence remains disease-specific: diabetic retinopathy findings vary with glycaemic trajectory and endpoint definition; age-related macular degeneration associations are heterogeneous; glaucoma studies suggest a possible reduction in incidence without establishing protection against progression; and dry-eye evidence remains preliminary. Semaglutide also carries a regulatory safety signal for non-arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy. Future research should establish physiological ligand access and receptor engagement, validate ocular receptor localisation, characterise retinal and optic-nerve-head microvascular responses, and incorporate prospective ophthalmic phenotyping into metabolic-drug trials. Overall, current evidence supports pharmacological and local ocular peptide-receptor signalling, whereas direct physiological endocrine communication between the gut and eye remains unproven.

articles.title: Non-classical human astrovirus VA1 induces cell line-specific increases in intestinal epithelial permeability associated with claudin remodeling.
articles.abstract: Astroviruses are non-enveloped viruses with a positive-sense, single-stranded RNA genome. Human astroviruses (HAstVs) are classified into classical strains (HAstV-1 to HAstV-8) and non-classical strains (VA1-6 and MLB1-3). These viruses typically cause self-resolving acute gastroenteritis, but symptoms can be more severe, including extraintestinal infections and viral encephalitis, especially in vulnerable groups, such as children and the immunocompromised. Despite being one of the leading causes of pediatric gastroenteritis worldwide, little is known about the pathogenic mechanisms, and no vaccines or antivirals currently exist. Tight junctions are formed by multiprotein complexes, including claudins and occludin, that separate the intestinal lumen from the host interior and play an important role in intestinal barrier maintenance. HAstV-1 disrupts these tight junctions in polarized Caco-2 monolayers by degrading occludin and E-cadherin, thereby decreasing intestinal barrier permeability. In contrast, this study demonstrated that VA1 decreases transepithelial electrical resistance in polarized T84, but not Caco-2, cells by altering protein levels and localization of select claudins. Specifically, western blot analysis of T84, but not Caco-2, protein lysates showed that protein expression of the pore-forming claudin-2 increased in infected cells, while protein levels of sealing claudins-4 and -18 decreased. In addition, immunofluorescence imaging indicated a relocalization of claudin-3 into the cytosol. Butyrate, a short-chain fatty acid bacterial metabolite found in the intestine, attenuated these barrier changes. These data demonstrate that VA1 induces cell type-specific claudin remodeling associated with decreased epithelial barrier permeability in T84 cells and highlight the differences between classical and non-classical HAstVs in the mechanisms underlying intestinal barrier remodeling.IMPORTANCEHuman astroviruses are prevalent enteric viruses that are a leading cause of pediatric gastroenteritis worldwide. However, little is known about their pathogenic mechanisms, and no vaccines or antivirals are available to treat or prevent infections. Herein, we demonstrate that VA1 infection induces changes in the electrical conductance of polarized T84 cell monolayers and alters claudin protein levels or their cellular localization. This phenotype is attenuated by pre-treatment with the bacterial short-chain fatty acid butyrate and is not observed in infected polarized Caco-2 monolayers. Collectively, these data suggest that VA1 induces cell type-specific barrier alterations through claudin remodeling that differ from the HAstV-1-induced alterations in tight junction complex proteins occludin and E-cadherin, highlighting virus-specific differences in pathogenic mechanisms of classical and non-classical HAstVs.

articles.title: A human sensory neuron model for varicella-zoster virus latency and reactivation in vitro.
articles.abstract: Varicella-zoster virus (VZV) is a ubiquitous human neurotropic alphaherpesvirus that establishes lifelong latency in sensory ganglionic neurons. Subsequent viral reactivation causes herpes zoster, a morbid disease often complicated by neuropathic pain. Mechanisms underlying VZV latency and reactivation are not understood, mostly due to the lack of permissive animal models and challenges of current in vitro latency modeling. Here, we evaluated HD10.6 cells, a simplified and easily expandable human sensory neuron line to model VZV latency and reactivation. Differentiated HD10.6 (dHD10.6) neurons supported productive VZV infection, viral DNA replication, production of infectious progeny, and viral spread in cultures. VZV infection was associated with limited cytopathic effects and ultrastructural changes. Infecting dHD10.6 neurons with cell-free VZV in the presence of antivirals resulted in a quiescent-persistent state, characterized by persistent VZV genomes with restricted VZV gene expression and absence of infectious virus. Importantly, VZV could be reactivated by treatment with capsaicin, as evidenced by increased lytic viral transcription and virus spread. In conclusion, this study establishes human HD10.6 neurons as a novel and expandable in vitro model for studying VZV latency and reactivation to identify virus and host factors governing latency that may serve as therapeutic targets to restrict VZV reactivation.IMPORTANCEMost individuals carry latent varicella-zoster virus (VZV) in their dorsal root ganglia (DRG), which can reactivate to cause shingles and chronic pain. The mechanisms by which VZV establishes latency and triggers of reactivation are incompletely understood. Current platforms for the study of VZV latency do not easily support functional experiments (ganglia) or are difficult to expand and complicated by mixed neuronal populations (stem cell-derived neurons). Here, we demonstrate that differentiated HD10.6 cells derived from immortalized human DRG-derived neurons provide a clonal and easy-to-expand platform for studying lytic, latent, and reactivated VZV infection in sensory neurons. We propose that the HD10.6 platform could provide the basis to conduct studies on the viral latent state that have hitherto not been possible.

articles.title: Salty virus-host interactions: infection mechanisms of haloarchaeal viruses HRTV-7 and HRTV-10.
articles.abstract: Archaea can be infected by morphologically diverse viruses, and the study of these viruses is important for understanding viral evolution in general. Archaeal tailed viruses make up the largest group of isolated archaeal viruses and the major class of isolated viruses infecting haloarchaea. Yet, little is known about the infection strategies of these viruses. In this study, we focus on archaeal myoviruses and investigate their infection cycles. HRTV-7 and HRTV-10 are both capable of infecting multiple Halorubrum strains, including Halorubrum salinarum B2-2, which is well suited for light microscopy. Virus lifecycle experiments combined with plaque assays and time-lapse microscopy showed that both viruses have a predominantly lytic life cycle, with complete lysis occurring between 9 and 12 h post-infection. Cells swell considerably just prior to lysis, indicating that the cell envelope becomes compromised. Whole-genome sequencing of virus-insensitive strains suggests that HRTV-10 likely uses the S-layer, the main cell envelope component of these archaea, as a receptor. Interestingly, we observed full-length integration of HRTV-7 in virus-resistant cells, as well as parts of the viral genome within the host genome, suggesting viral resistance based on superinfection exclusion. Together, these findings contribute to our understanding of archaeal virus-host interactions and provide insight into their infection strategies.IMPORTANCEViruses of archaea are important to understand the diversity and evolution of all viruses. However, they are little studied. Archaea are ubiquitous microorganisms, of which some thrive at extreme conditions, such as high salt concentrations. Salt-loving haloarchaea are excellent models to study archaeal virus-host interactions due to the high availability of viral isolates and suitability for microscopy. Bacteria and archaea are both infected by tailed viruses; however, in archaea, their infection mechanisms are largely unknown. We used two tailed archaeal viruses infecting the same host to compare their infection strategies. Both viruses induce cell lysis of the host, which is preceded by cell bloating. Interestingly, one of the viruses can integrate into the genome of the host, which renders the strain resistant, suggesting a mechanism of superinfection exclusion. This work provides insight into archaeal virus-host interactions, thereby contributing to the exploration of the unusual archaeal virosphere.

articles.title: Machine learning-driven ECG screening for early coronary artery disease detection.
articles.abstract: BackgroundElectrocardiography (ECG) is inexpensive and widely available, yet its ability to detect early and nonobstructive coronary artery disease (CAD) is limited when interpreted using conventional criteria. We evaluated whether a deep learning model applied to standard 12-lead-ECG images can identify angiographically confirmed CAD and enable clinically meaningful risk stratification in a real-world population.MethodsIn this multicentric study, 15,890 ECG-angiography pairs (12-lead ECG paired with coronary angiography [CA] or coronary CT angiography [CCTA]) were included between November 2021 and January 2024. A DenseNet-121 convolutional neural network was trained to predict CAD from ECG images. Temporal validation was performed on a prospectively collected, independent cohort of 2168 samples from February to May 2024. Model performance was assessed using receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC), PR-AUC, and standard diagnostic metrics. Robustness across varying disease prevalence was evaluated using simulation, and prevalence-dependent predictive performance was summarized using PPV and NPV prevalence curves (AUCppv and AUCnpv).ResultsThe model was trained on 13,299 samples, validated on 1,002, and tested on 1339 (CAD prevalence 52.9%). On the test set, ROC-AUC was 0.80 and PR-AUC 0.83. At the optimal 0.50 threshold, sensitivity was 87% (618/708 CAD cases detected) and specificity 50% (317/631 non-CAD correctly classified). On the temporal validation set (n = 2168; 64% CAD), ROC-AUC was 0.81 and PR-AUC 0.83, with sensitivity 0.67, specificity 0.78, PPV 0.84, and NPV 0.57. Simulated prevalence analyses demonstrated robust PPV/NPV trends across distributions.ConclusionDeep learning analysis of routinely acquired ECG images can identify patients at increased risk of CAD and may support low-cost, scalable CAD risk stratification.

articles.title: Analytical performance and workflow impact of the FASTinov QUICKprep kit for direct bacterial identification and antimicrobial susceptibility testing from positive blood cultures.
articles.abstract:
UNLABELLED: Rapid pathogen identification and antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) from positive blood cultures are essential for the timely optimization of antimicrobial therapy in patients with bloodstream infections. The FASTinov QUICKprep kit enables recovery of viable microorganisms directly from positive blood cultures, allowing both identification and AST without prior subculture. We evaluated the analytical performance and workflow impact of the FASTinov QUICKprep kit using 112 positive blood cultures processed in a routine clinical microbiology laboratory. Direct identification was performed by matrix-assisted laser desorption ionization-time of flight mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF MS), and AST was performed using the automated RADIAN system. Results were compared with those obtained using the laboratory's standard subculture-based workflow. Identification accuracy, categorical agreement for AST, reporting times, and turnaround times (TATs) were assessed. Overall, the sensitivity and specificity of direct bacterial identification were 93.4% and 100%, respectively. The QUICKprep workflow enabled same-day identification for all evaluable samples and reduced the median TAT from 7.75 h to 3.0 h. Direct AST performed from QUICKprep-derived pellets demonstrated high categorical agreement with the reference method across 86 isolates. Most discordant AST results involved heteroresistant gram-negative subpopulations and were adjudicated in favor of the QUICKprep results by Etest. Importantly, AST results were consistently available within 24 h irrespective of sample arrival time, whereas the conventional workflow showed substantial delays for cultures received later in the day. In conclusion, the FASTinov QUICKprep kit provides reliable direct identification and AST from positive blood cultures while substantially reducing turnaround times. Integration of this approach into routine clinical microbiology workflows may facilitate earlier optimization of antimicrobial therapy and support antimicrobial stewardship efforts.

IMPORTANCE: Bloodstream infections remain a major cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide. Thus, efficient pathogen identification and antimicrobial susceptibility testing are critical to optimizing targeted therapy and antimicrobial stewardship. Despite advances in laboratory automation, routine procedures for positive blood cultures remain dependent on secondary subculture growth. Our study proposes relevant and practical benefits regarding the integration of a subculture-independent workflow for bloodstream infection diagnosis and its potential contribution to improving clinical outcomes.

articles.title: A review of tuberculosis diagnostic guidelines: identification of areas of consensus and divergence to support diagnostic access decision-making.
articles.abstract: Tuberculosis (TB) remains a leading cause of infectious disease morbidity and mortality worldwide despite substantial advances in diagnostic technologies. Multiple international and national organizations have developed evidence-based recommendations for TB diagnosis; however, differences in guidance can create uncertainty for laboratories, clinicians, and policymakers implementing diagnostic services. Understanding areas of consensus and divergence may facilitate evidence-informed decision-making and improve access to appropriate TB diagnostics. This minireview compares major TB diagnostic guidelines from the World Health Organization and organizations in Canada, the United States, Europe, the United Kingdom, and Australia, highlighting areas of consensus and divergence. While substantial agreement exists regarding the core components of TB diagnosis, recommendations differ in the positioning of molecular diagnostics, specimen selection, biomarker use, sequencing technologies, and treatment monitoring. Understanding the factors underlying these differences, including epidemiology, laboratory capacity, resource availability, and approaches to evidence appraisal, can support context-specific implementation of diagnostic strategies, improve equitable access to high-quality TB diagnostics, and identify priorities for future research and guideline harmonization.

articles.title: Metabolic Health Modifies the Obesity Paradox in Critically ill Patients: A Phenotype-Based Risk Stratification Tool from the MIMIC-IV Database.
articles.abstract: BackgroundThe prognostic significance of obesity in critically ill patients remains controversial, partly due to the simplistic use of body mass index (BMI) without considering metabolic heterogeneity. We aim to evaluate whether combining BMI with metabolic health status provides superior risk stratification for all-cause mortality in ICU patients using the MIMIC-IV database.MethodsThis retrospective cohort study analyzed 31 171 adult ICU patients from the MIMIC-IV database. Patients were classified into six phenotypes based on BMI categories (normal, overweight, or obese) and metabolic health status (healthy vs unhealthy, defined by hypertension, diabetes or hyperlipidemia). The primary outcomes included 7-day, 30-day, and 90-day all-cause mortality. We applied survival curve analysis and Cox proportional hazards regression, with subgroup analyses stratified by sex, age, and illness severity.ResultsAmong metabolically healthy patients, BMI category did not significantly affect mortality. However, in metabolically unhealthy patients, a clear graded protective association emerged: the metabolically unhealthy obese (MUO) phenotype conferred the strongest survival benefit (adjusted HRs: 0.63, 0.65 and 0.64 for 7-day, 30-day and 90-day mortality, respectively), followed by metabolically unhealthy overweight (MUOW, adjusted HRs: 0.73, 0.70 and 0.69 for 7-day, 30-day and 90-day mortality), while the metabolically unhealthy normal weight (MUNW) patients showed the weakest protection. Such a survival benefit was significantly amplified in males and in patients with higher illness severity.ConclusionsAmong ICU patients, metabolic health status, rather than BMI alone, is the key determinant of prognosis. For metabolically unhealthy patients, higher BMI was associated with a graded survival advantage, particularly in those with greater illness severity.
