CONCLUSIONS: All HBsAg positive individuals should be screened for HDV. All adults with chronic HDV and compensated liver disease are candidates for HDV therapy. Recent advances in HDV treatment offer hope for meaningful improvement in clinical outcomes.

articles.title: Industrialization restructures the domestic dog gut microbiome while preserving host specificity.
articles.abstract:
UNLABELLED: Industrialization has reshaped human gut microbiomes, but its effects on other human-associated mammals remain poorly understood. Domestic dogs provide an informative comparative system because they have shared human environments and food systems for millennia yet retain distinct host biology. However, most canine microbiome studies have focused on industrialized companion, colony, or controlled-feeding dogs, limiting our understanding of the ecological range of the domestic dog gut microbiome. We analyzed fecal 16S rRNA gene profiles from 261 dogs sampled across Nepal, Thailand, the United Arab Emirates, and the United States, spanning forager, agrarian, pastoralist, urban, and industrialized lifestyles; 257 dogs remained after excluding those with reported recent antibiotic exposure. Lifestyle was the strongest measured correlate of canine gut bacterial composition, and this association persisted in restricted analyses of mature, non-shelter dogs sampled from temperate regions. Industrialized dogs differed from non-industrialized dogs through directional genus-level shifts, prevalence-defined VANISH-like and BloSSUM-like bacterial guilds, coabundance structure, and shifts in predicted functional potential. Non-industrialized dogs were not microbiologically uniform: pastoralist dogs showed non-industrialized gut bacterial community profiles but diverged from a simple forager-to-industrialized continuum. Cross-species comparisons with humans sampled across matched lifestyle categories showed parallel lifestyle-associated restructuring in both hosts, but host species remained the dominant axis of variation, and genus-level responses were largely host specific. These findings expand the ecological baseline for canine gut bacterial communities and identify industrialization-associated lifestyle change as a major axis of gut bacterial community restructuring in a long-term human-associated mammal. More broadly, they show that shared lifestyle transitions can impose parallel ecological pressures across host species without overriding host-specific community assembly.

IMPORTANCE: Domestic dogs are one of the closest animal companions of humans, yet we know surprisingly little about how their gut microbiomes vary outside industrialized pet populations. This study shows that industrialization-associated lifestyle change is not only relevant to human microbiomes but also a broader ecological force that reshapes gut microbial communities in animals living alongside us. By comparing dogs across diverse human lifestyles, we show that shared environments can impose parallel pressures on the gut bacterial communities of humans and dogs, while each host maintains a distinct microbial identity. These findings suggest that gut microbial communities are shaped by the interaction between host biology and changing ecological conditions. Expanding microbiome research beyond industrialized settings is therefore essential for understanding what microbial diversity has been retained, altered, or lost during recent lifestyle transitions.

articles.title: Detoxification of host-relevant H2O2 shapes Pseudomonas aeruginosa population gradients in flow.
articles.abstract:
UNLABELLED: During infection, bacterial populations need to overcome low levels of host-generated H2O2. However, experiments almost always use high H2O2 levels that are rarely found in hosts. Here, we use microfluidics to investigate how host-relevant H2O2 impacts populations of the human pathogen Pseudomonas aeruginosa PA14 in flow. Using long-channel microfluidic devices, we establish that cells at the front of a population remove H2O2 and protect their downstream neighbors. Population-level protection is mediated by three OxyR-regulated scavenging systems (KatA, KatB, AhpCF), which are each sufficient to detoxify host-relevant H2O2. Mutants lacking all three systems are sensitive to H2O2, but can be cross-protected by resistant cells when co-cultured. Cross-protection is abolished in higher flow regimes, where H2O2 is delivered faster than cells can remove it. Our results demonstrate how local detoxification provides global protection, which results in spatial gradients across bacterial populations in flow. Together, our findings highlight how biological, chemical, and physical factors collectively determine the fate of bacterial populations in host-relevant environments.

IMPORTANCE: Bacteria experience chemical and physical stresses during infection. For example, bacterial pathogens encounter low levels of host-generated H2O2 in the bloodstream, urinary tract, and lungs. However, almost all laboratory experiments use much higher H2O2 levels, which are uncommon in host environments. In this study, we used microfluidics to deliver host-relevant H2O2 into populations of the human pathogen, Pseudomonas aeruginosa. We establish that P. aeruginosa uses three systems to detoxify H2O2, and strains lacking all three systems are highly sensitive. By co-culturing sensitive and resistant strains, we demonstrate how cells protect each other and form spatial gradients across mixed populations. Strikingly, we discover that cell-cell protection is lost in higher flow regimes, as flow-based delivery outpaces detoxification. Thus, our experiments reveal how host-relevant chemical and physical stressors combine to inhibit growth of bacterial populations.

articles.title: Incidence and risk factors of acute respiratory illness associated with influenza, COVID-19, and respiratory syncytial virus within a birth cohort study.
articles.abstract:
UNLABELLED: Influenza virus, severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) are leading causes of acute respiratory infections (ARIs). New Zealand's coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) public health measures disrupted the circulation of these viruses in 2020-2021, creating a rare opportunity to explore the impact of potential immunity gaps on age-specific infection risk. We analyzed data from 843 participants aged between 0 and 4 years enrolled in the Southern Hemisphere Influenza and Vaccine Effectiveness Research and Surveillance 3 (SHIVERS-III) birth cohort, a longitudinal community-based study in New Zealand, during 2020-2024. During the respiratory season, weekly surveillance captured ARI symptoms and severity. Nasal swabs were collected from symptomatic participants and tested for viral RNA by RT-PCR. Incidence rates (IRs) and incidence rate ratios (IRRs) were estimated for the surveillance period and adjusted for age, sex, ethnic group, socioeconomic status, and influenza vaccination status. No influenza or SARS-CoV-2 infections were detected in 2020 and 2021. From 2021 to 2024, RSV had the highest IR during the surveillance period (63.2/100 person-years [PY]; 95% CI, 56.6-69.8), followed by SARS-CoV-2 (39.3/100 PY; 95% CI, 34.5-44) and influenza (35.7/100 PY; 95% CI, 29-42.3). Age influenced infection risk: infants <6 months had the lowest incidence of influenza and RSV, potentially reflecting maternally derived immunity and limited exposure. Risk increased after 6 months of age, peaking at age 1 year for RSV and at age 2 years for influenza. Influenza vaccination lowered symptomatic influenza risk (IRR 0.66; 95% CI, 0.44-1.00). In the New Zealand community setting in the post-COVID-19 era, individual respiratory virus illness patterns differ in children aged 0-4. Influenza vaccine shows protection, and age influences virus-specific risk.

IMPORTANCE: Influenza virus, severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) are major causes of acute respiratory illness in early childhood, yet current understanding is largely reliant on hospital-based surveillance that underestimates the broader community burden. This study addresses this limitation by providing comprehensive, community-based estimates of incidence, severity, and symptom profiles across these viruses within a single longitudinal birth cohort. By leveraging the unique epidemiological context created by pandemic-related disruptions, it offers important insights into how changes in exposure influence subsequent infection risk and virus circulation. The direct comparison of three major respiratory viruses within the same population highlights distinct age-related risk patterns and disease characteristics. In addition, our research provides real-world evidence of the reduced risk of influenza-associated acute respiratory illness among vaccinated children. These findings strengthen the evidence base for age-targeted immunization strategies and improve understanding of early-life respiratory virus epidemiology.

articles.title: Evaluation of a new assay for the detection of IgM in recent and congenital Toxoplasma infections.
articles.abstract:
UNLABELLED: Toxoplasma gondii infection is usually asymptomatic in immunocompetent individuals. However, primary infection during pregnancy can lead to severe fetal manifestations. Consequently, accurate diagnosis of maternal infection is essential for prompt treatment. Currently, diagnosis mainly relies on detection of anti-T. gondii specific IgM and IgG in serum. If detection of IgM can be indicative of acute infection, it may also reflect the presence of persistent or non-specific antibodies. The Toxo-ISAGA IgM assay (bioMérieux, France), formerly considered a gold standard for anti-T. gondii IgM detection, was discontinued in 2024. New and reliable assays are, therefore, needed to support risk assessment and clinical decision-making, particularly in maternal and neonatal settings. A new generation of the VIDAS TOXO IgM assay (bioMérieux, France), one of the most commonly used commercially available assays for the detection of anti- T. gondii specific IgM in serum, has recently been developed: the VIDAS TXMN assay (reference 424641). This study aimed at evaluating its clinical performance. A retro-prospective study was conducted in two French clinical parasitology-mycology laboratories in 2024. Performance was determined on 1,275 single sera from patients with recent or chronic postnatal Toxoplasma infection and non-infected patients and on serial serum samples from both women who seroconverted during pregnancy and neonates with and without congenital Toxoplasma infection. In addition, qualitative results were compared to those obtained with frequently used commercially available comparators and ISAGA. Sensitivity and specificity of the VIDAS TXMN assay were 98.77 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 93.31-99.97%) and 100.00% (95% CI: 99.59-100.00%), respectively. It allowed earlier detection of IgM than the previous generation assay both in pregnant women and in newborns from mothers who seroconverted during pregnancy. In addition, agreements with the Architect Toxo IgM (Abbott Diagnostics), Platelia Toxo IgM (Bio-Rad), and Toxo-ISAGA (bioMérieux) were almost perfect (Cohen's kappa > 0.85). The new VIDAS TXMN assay improved the detection of anti-T. gondii-specific IgM in serum compared to the previous generation and displayed high agreement with commercially available comparators and ISAGA. It, therefore, appears to reliably contribute to the diagnosis of maternal and congenital toxoplasmosis.

IMPORTANCE: Toxoplasma gondii is an ubiquitous parasite, which can cause severe fetal damage when first contracted in a pregnant woman. Serology-and particularly the detection of anti-T. gondii-specific IgM antibodies-plays a key role in diagnosing recent infections and, therefore, contributes to appropriate management of pregnant women and newborns. Commercial availability of anti-T. gondii-specific IgM assays has recently evolved, with the discontinuation of the Toxo-ISAGA IgM assay (bioMérieux, France) as a gold standard and the marketing of a new version of the VIDAS TOXO IgM assay (bioMérieux, France). This study first establishes the performance of this new assay for diagnosing maternal and congenital infections, with a direct comparison with other commonly used commercial assays. This evaluation is essential for ensuring reliable diagnosis and supporting clinical decision-making, particularly in maternal and neonatal settings.

articles.title: Structural insights into West Nile virus programmed ribosomal frameshifting reveal coordinated regulation by RNA, ribosome, and nascent peptide.
articles.abstract: Programmed -1 ribosomal frameshifting (-1 PRF) is essential for West Nile virus (WNV) gene expression and generates NS1', a protein implicated in viral replication and pathogenesis. However, the structural pathway by which translating ribosomes traverse the WNV frameshift signal remains poorly understood. Here, we combined cryo-electron microscopy, RNA structural modeling, molecular dynamics simulations, and functional analyses to investigate the mechanism of WNV -1 PRF. We resolved a pre-frameshift ribosomal complex together with four translocation intermediates, including a previously uncharacterized semi-rotated state in which the 40S subunit undergoes partial rotation while tRNAs remain in near-canonical A/A-P/P configurations. This intermediate is accompanied by remodeling of conserved peptidyl-transferase-center nucleotides, suggesting that active-site rearrangements can precede canonical tRNA movement during translocation. Structural modeling and simulations further suggest that the WNV frameshift-stimulatory RNA exists as a compact but conformationally heterogeneous ensemble capable of adopting multiple stable or metastable pseudoknot architectures. In addition, we identified direct interactions between the nascent viral peptide and the ribosomal exit tunnel, and disruption of the tunnel-occupying peptide reduced frameshifting efficiency. Together, our findings suggest that WNV frameshifting is governed not by a single stimulatory element but by the coordinated coupling of RNA dynamics, ribosome remodeling, and nascent-chain interactions.IMPORTANCEViruses often rely on a process called programmed ribosomal frameshifting to produce proteins important for infection. West Nile virus (WNV), a mosquito-borne pathogen that can cause severe neurological disease in humans, uses this strategy to generate NS1', a protein linked to viral replication and pathogenesis. However, how ribosomes are redirected into an alternative reading frame remains incompletely understood. Here, we provide structural insights into ribosome movement during translation of the WNV frameshift signal. Our findings also suggest that the viral RNA can adopt alternative conformations and that the emerging viral peptide may influence frameshifting efficiency. Together, these observations contribute to our understanding of how RNA structure, ribosomal dynamics, and nascent peptides may influence viral protein expression.

articles.title: Immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome: what the intensivist needs to know.
articles.abstract: Immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS) is a significant complication of chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy, a revolutionary treatment for hematologic malignancies. This syndrome, which might affect approximately 30% of CAR-T therapy recipients, presents a wide spectrum of neurological symptoms, ranging from mild confusion to life-threatening cerebral edema. In the intensive care unit (ICU), managing ICANS is critical due to its potential severity. Pathophysiology of ICANS is driven by immune-mediated inflammation disrupting the blood-brain barrier, resulting in cerebral cytokine infiltration and glial cell activation. Its severity is associated with elevated cytokine levels in cerebrospinal fluid and serum, which points to the need for specific biomarkers and predictive tools. Standardized assessments, including the Immune Effector Cell-Associated Encephalopathy (ICE) Score, together with brain imaging and adjunctive diagnostic tests, provide clinicians with essential baseline information for the assessment and monitoring of neurological complications. ICU management focuses on supportive care and pharmacologic strategies. Corticosteroids represent the cornerstone of treatment, effectively targeting neuroinflammation while preserving the antitumor efficacy of CAR-T cell therapy. Anticonvulsants, hyperosmolar agents and advanced neurocritical care measures are also pivotal. Recent advances suggest potential benefits of alternative therapies, such as anti-cytokine agents and innovative immune cell products with reduced neurotoxic risks. Despite advancements, challenges persist, including diagnostic ambiguities, resource allocation, and variability in care protocols. This review highlighted challenges in ICANS management for ICU physicians, intending to underline the importance of early detection, rigorous monitoring, and tailored interventions to improve patient outcomes.

articles.title: Nutritional support in immunosuppressed critically ill patients.
articles.abstract: Immunosuppressed patients now make up a growing share of intensive care unit (ICU) admissions, largely as a result of advances in cancer treatment, organ transplantation, and immunomodulatory therapies. While their short-term ICU mortality may be similar to that of immunocompetent patients when illness severity is taken into account, these individuals often face longer ICU stays, more complications, and poorer long-term outcomes. In this context, artificial nutrition plays a central role in ICU management and represents a potentially modifiable intervention. Beyond meeting energy requirements, nutritional support may help sustain immune function, preserve gut integrity, and reduce the risk of infectious complications. Whenever possible, enteral nutrition should be favored, as it supports the intestinal barrier and gut-associated lymphoid tissue, even when delivered at low, trophic doses. Parenteral nutrition remains indispensable in the presence of intestinal failure but should be used cautiously, given its association with complications such as catheter-related bloodstream infections. Critical illness profoundly alters gut-immune interactions, promoting dysbiosis, increased intestinal permeability, and immune dysfunction - processes that may be further amplified by immunosuppressive therapies. This has fueled interest in immunonutrition strategies, including arginine, ω-3 fatty acids, glutamine, and nucleotides. However, evidence in immunosuppressed critically ill patients remains limited and inconsistent, preventing firm recommendations. Looking ahead, the integration of body composition assessment, immune-metabolic phenotyping, multi-omics technologies, and artificial intelligence may enable more personalized nutritional strategies. Future studies should focus on phenotype-specific randomized trials to better define the optimal route, composition, timing, and dosing of nutritional support in this complex population.

articles.title: SCN1A (C>T) rs3812718 Polymorphism and Phenytoin-Induced Adverse Drug Reactions: Genotyping Versus Therapeutic Drug Monitoring in a Prospective Cohort.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Phenytoin has a narrow therapeutic index, and therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) is routinely used to guide dosing. The SCN1A (C>T) rs3812718 polymorphism has been proposed as a pharmacogenomic marker of phenytoin response; however, whether genotyping provides additional predictive value once TDM is already available remains unclear.

METHODS: A prospective cohort of 168 adult patients with epilepsy receiving phenytoin monotherapy was recruited from the neurology outpatient department of a tertiary care center. Participants were genotyped for SCN1A (C>T) rs3812718 using real-time polymerase chain reaction and followed for 6 months to assess adverse drug reactions (ADRs). Trough plasma phenytoin concentrations were measured and categorized as subtherapeutic, therapeutic, or supratherapeutic. Associations between genotype and ADRs were assessed overall, by TDM category, and using Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel (CMH) analysis stratified by TDM category.

RESULTS: ADRs occurred in 155 of 168 participants (92.3%), predominantly involving the central nervous system (85.7%). The mutant genotype (CT/TT) was present in 81.5% of participants. No significant association was observed between SCN1A genotype and overall or system-specific ADRs (dominant model, P = 0.655; codominant model, P = 0.576). Genotype was also not associated with TDM category (dominant model, P = 0.263; codominant model, P = 0.583). CMH analysis stratified by TDM category showed no association (odds ratio, 0.37; 95% confidence interval, 0.05-2.72; P = 0.330).

CONCLUSIONS: In this cohort, SCN1A (C>T) rs3812718 genotyping did not provide additional value beyond routine TDM in predicting phenytoin-induced ADRs. Phenytoin therapy may therefore continue to be guided by TDM rather than by routine genotyping for this variant.

articles.title: Long term lithium exposure and chronic kidney disease in the elderly with bipolar disorder: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Lithium remains the most effective long-term treatment for bipolar disorder, but concern about chronic kidney disease (CKD) continues to limit its use in older adults, in whom renal reserve is already reduced and competing renal risk factors are common. Whether that concern is proportionate, and whether risk depends on serum concentration or on the comparator chosen, remains unsettled. We synthesized the observational evidence on lithium and CKD in adults aged 50 and over with bipolar disorder.

RECENT FINDINGS: Across 6 cohorts, lithium was associated with a higher risk of CKD than nonlithium exposure (pooled hazard ratio 1.62, 95% confidence interval 1.25-2.11), although heterogeneity was substantial and the prediction interval crossed the null. Risk tracked with serum concentration: a higher-versus-lower contrast across 5 cohorts gave a pooled hazard ratio of 2.07 (1.47-2.91), the least heterogeneous analysis and the only one whose prediction interval lay entirely above the null. Against valproate the association attenuated to 1.39 (0.77-2.51). Hard kidney-failure endpoints were too few to estimate reliably. No study reported cognition in relation to renal function. No study was at low risk of bias, and confounding was the dominant concern.

SUMMARY: In older adults with bipolar disorder, lithium is associated with a modest, concentration-dependent increase in CKD risk that narrows when valproate rather than nonuse is the comparator. The evidence is observational and confounding-prone, and supports minimising serum concentration and monitoring renal function against age-appropriate thresholds rather than avoiding lithium.

articles.title: Off-panel resistance determinants in a high-resistance setting: comparative evaluation of syndromic multiplex PCR, metagenomic sequencing, and phenotypic AST in bloodstream infections.
articles.abstract: Rapid syndromic molecular panels substantially reduce turnaround time for bloodstream infection diagnosis by identifying common pathogens and selected antimicrobial resistance determinants directly from positive blood cultures. However, their fixed target repertoires may limit diagnostic coverage in settings with diverse endemic resistance mechanisms and clinically relevant off-panel organisms. This retrospective comparative diagnostic study evaluated direct-from-positive-blood-culture metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS), the BioFire Blood Culture Identification 2 (BCID2) panel, and routine microbiological methods across 165 positive blood-culture episodes from 145 patients at a tertiary-care center with a high burden of antimicrobial resistance. Complete recovery of the routine-culture organism set was achieved in 155/165 episodes (93.9%) by mNGS and 142/165 (86.1%) by BCID2. Among 23 episodes with incomplete routine-set recovery by BCID2, mNGS restored complete coverage in 18 (78.3%). For meropenem resistance, sensitivity was numerically higher with mNGS than with BCID2 (90.0% versus 75.0%), whereas ceftriaxone-resistance sensitivity among Enterobacterales was numerically higher with BCID2 (97.5% versus 85.0%); neither paired difference was statistically significant. BCID2 meropenem very major errors were concentrated among non-fermenting gram-negative organisms, particularly Acinetobacter baumannii, and were frequently associated with off-panel blaOXA-23 detected by mNGS. Overall, targeted syndromic testing and mNGS demonstrated complementary diagnostic performance, with mNGS extending organism and resistance-mechanism coverage beyond predefined molecular targets, while phenotypic antimicrobial susceptibility testing remained necessary for definitive susceptibility assessment.IMPORTANCERapid molecular blood-culture panels provide clinically actionable results, but are inherently restricted to predefined pathogen and resistance targets. This limitation is particularly relevant in regions where local antimicrobial resistance epidemiology includes mechanisms not represented within commercial panel repertoires. In this study, metagenomic sequencing improved recovery of routine-culture organisms and identified off-panel carbapenem resistance determinants underlying several false-susceptible panel results, particularly OXA-23 in Acinetobacter baumannii. However, broader genomic detection did not consistently improve phenotypic resistance prediction across antimicrobial classes. These findings illustrate that diagnostic breadth and phenotypic predictive accuracy are distinct attributes and support the use of metagenomic sequencing as a complementary approach to rapid targeted testing and conventional antimicrobial susceptibility testing.

articles.title: Right heart remodeling in Sugen/hypoxia rat model of severe pulmonary hypertension.
articles.journal: American journal of physiology. Cell physiology
articles.abstract: Pulmonary hypertension (PH) directly impacts the right heart through pressure overload. Unlike well-characterized remodeling of the left ventricle in systemic hypertension, PH-induced changes in the right heart are less understood. Here, we investigate chamber-specific alterations in the right atrium (RA) and right ventricle (RV) in a rat model of PH. PH was induced in 6-week-old male Wistar rats using Sugen/hypoxia (SuHx) treatment. Right heart pressure overload was confirmed by catheterization. Cardiac remodeling was characterized by using confocal microscopy, micro-CT, optical mapping, and proteomic mass spectrometry. The increase in right-heart mass was predominantly attributable to cardiomyocyte hypertrophy, with concomitant extracellular-matrix remodeling. Hypertrophy was associated with significantly elevated right heart pressures after SuHx treatment, further progressing during the subsequent normoxia. At the end of the PH protocol, electrophysiology analysis showed significant prolongation of the action potential in both the RA and RV. Proteomic analysis revealed pronounced alterations in the RV, with substantial overlap with the RA and LV, and more upregulated than downregulated proteins. GO analysis indicated increased expression of sarcomeric and fibrillar proteins and reduced expression of proteins related to oxidative energy production. In conclusion, myocardial remodeling in PH is based on cardiomyocyte hypertrophy rather than cell proliferation. Electrophysiological changes along with increased pressure in the right atrium might contribute to phenotype progression. Changes in proteome show commonalities and differences in RA and RV pressure-induced pathways that that warrant therapeutic exploration.

articles.title: Mycoplasma genitalium extracellular vesicles and the P140 adhesin carboxyl region as high-fidelity antigens for improved serodiagnosis.
articles.abstract:
UNLABELLED: Mycoplasma genitalium (Mg) is an important etiological agent of sexually transmitted infections that has emerged as a global health threat. Despite its clinical importance, accurate serodiagnosis remains challenging due to high cross-reactivity caused by non-specific proteins. To address this limitation, we optimized Mg growth in a serum-free minimal medium to characterize the biogenesis and diagnostic applications of Mg-secreted extracellular vesicles (EVs). We demonstrate that Mg generates EVs that retain immunodominant proteins, specifically the key adhesins P140 and P110. From an initial cohort of 1,608 women (12.5% Mg-positive), we selected a longitudinal sub-study population, including 24 women who were PCR-positive at enrollment and a control group of 14 individuals who remained Mg-negative across three visits, each spaced approximately 6 months apart. Comparative ELISA and immunoblotting using sera from Mg-infected and uninfected individuals revealed that the EV-associated antigens provide superior diagnostic discrimination over conventional total-cell lysates and lipid-associated membrane protein extracts. Notably, EV-associated antigens lack common non-specific proteins, such as immunoglobulin-binding protein, MG281. Functional characterization using full-length and truncated P140 variants in cell-based ELISAs with human cervical epithelial cells identified the C-terminal region (P140-C) as the primary host-cell-interacting domain. In addition, this specific region induces an epitope-restricted antibody response in infected individuals. Within the longitudinal clinical cohort, high anti-P140-C antibody titers correlated with a trend toward Mg clearance, suggesting potential prognostic utility despite lacking statistical significance. Collectively, these results establish Mg EVs as a high-fidelity antigenic source and identify P140-C as a promising candidate for the development of next-generation serological assays.

IMPORTANCE: Serodiagnosis of Mycoplasma genitalium (Mg) faces significant challenges, especially in the context of emerging antimicrobial resistance and asymptomatic infections. This study introduces Mg-derived extracellular vesicles (EVs) as a source of refined antigens for serodiagnosis. By isolating the P140 C-terminal region, we identified a highly specific marker that overcomes antigenic variation, reduces cross-reactivity, and offers a candidate antigen that may warrant evaluation as a marker of infection clearance. By leveraging bacterial EVs as a source of purified diagnostic antigen, our findings offer a framework with broader implications for other antigenically complex pathogens.

articles.title: H. pylori induces ferroptosis and inhibits malignant progression of gastric epithelial cells via STAT1/SLC7A11 axis.
articles.abstract:
UNLABELLED: Helicobacter pylori is a primary risk factor for gastric carcinogenesis; however, an in-depth evaluation of its potential role in modulating ferroptosis to influence cancer development remains undetermined. Therefore, this study developed complementary in vitro cell models (using GES-1 and AGS gastric epithelial cells) and C57BL/6 mouse models to systematically evaluate the mechanism by which H. pylori regulates ferroptosis in gastric epithelial cells. The acquired data revealed that H. pylori infection selectively promotes ferroptotic cell death, which elevates lipid peroxidation, impairs the GPX4-GSH antioxidant axis, and causes intracellular iron overload, resulting in characteristic mitochondrial structural damage. H. pylori disrupts iron homeostasis, alters lipid composition, and impairs redox buffering ability, promoting a ferroptosis-prone microenvironment that mediates epithelial cell death via convergent pathways. Furthermore, H. pylori was found to suppress SLC7A11 expression by two distinct mechanisms: ubiquitin-proteasome-mediated protein destabilization and STAT1-driven transcriptional silencing, which disrupt the antioxidant system and promote ferroptosis. Moreover, pharmacological inhibition of ferroptosis significantly increased the proliferation, motility, and invasiveness of H. pylori-infected gastric cells. These results demonstrate a context-dependent dual role of ferroptosis in H. pylori-mediated gastric tumorigenesis: ferroptosis inhibits tumor growth by eliminating damaged epithelial cells, whereas its inhibition promotes malignant progression. This study reveals a multi-faceted mechanism by which H. pylori mediates ferroptosis, indicating the STAT1/SLC7A11 module as a key regulatory hub, and identifies the dichotomous role of ferroptosis in infection-mediated gastric oncogenesis. These results provide new insights into the pathogenic mechanisms of H. pylori-related gastric cancer and highlight the potential diagnostic and therapeutic targets against the condition.

IMPORTANCE: Helicobacter pylori infection is a major cause of gastric cancer, but how it regulates gastric epithelial ferroptosis to modulate tumor progression remains incompletely understood. This study explores the underlying mechanisms using cellular and animal models. We show that H. pylori disrupts iron homeostasis and impairs the GPX4-GSH antioxidant system, triggering lipid peroxidation and mitochondrial damage to induce ferroptosis. Mechanistically, H. pylori downregulates SLC7A11 through ubiquitin-proteasome-mediated degradation and STAT1-dependent transcriptional repression. Ferroptosis exhibits a dual role in H. pylori-associated tumorigenesis, suppressing early tumorigenesis while its inhibition promotes malignant progression. This work defines the STAT1/SLC7A11 axis as a key regulatory module and provides novel targets for H. pylori-related gastric cancer.

articles.title: GCN5L1 Depletion Promotes Left Ventricular Fibrosis in Failing Hearts via Upregulation of RAB7A.
articles.journal: American journal of physiology. Heart and circulatory physiology
articles.abstract: Pathologic cardiac fibrosis is one of the key determinants of adverse remodeling and progression to heart failure. Although GCN5-like 1 (GCN5L1) is documented to regulate cardiac metabolic homeostasis, its role in myocardial remodeling and fibrosis is unknown. In a murine transverse aortic constriction (TAC) pressure overload model, GCN5L1 protein abundance was significantly reduced in the left ventricular (LV) tissues from wild type (WT) mice. This finding was concurrent with increased collagen 1α1 expression in the same tissues. Interestingly, LVs from cardiomyocyte-specific GCN5L1 knockout (GCN5L1 cKO) mice showed exacerbated TAC-induced collagen 1α1 expression among profibrotic genes identified by bulk RNA sequencing, when compared with corresponding WT mice. These finding are consistent with our previous report of increased fibrotic tissue and decreased fractional shortening (a marker of contractile function) in GCN5L1 cKO mice under TAC stress. Consistently, analysis of human hearts with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction demonstrated reduced GCN5L1 expression accompanied by increased collagen 1α1, revealing a conserved inverse relationship. In vitro, we further demonstrate that conditioned media collected from GCN5L1-depleted AC16 human ventricular cardiomyocyte-like cells induced upregulation of collagen 1α1 expression in human cardiac fibroblasts. Proteomic profiling of WT and GCN5L1 cKO cardiac tissues aligned with our in vitro findings in WT and GCN5L1 knockout (KO) mouse embryonic fibroblasts, revealing increased expression of lysosomal, endo-lysosomal, and autophagy markers (including RAB7A) in response to GCN5L1 deficiency. In vivo, RAB7A protein was increased following TAC, which was exacerbated in GCN5L1-deficient hearts under the same conditions. Furthermore, in human ventricular fibroblasts, TGF-β1 stimulated RAB7A and collagen 1α1 expression. Importantly, RAB7A knockdown attenuated TGF-β1-induced collagen 1α1, whereas GCN5L1 knockdown altered expression of fibrosis related markers and increased RAB7A without directly altering collagen expression. Collectively, these findings identify GCN5L1 as a negative regulator of pressure overload-induced cardiac fibrosis, and implicate a GCN5L1- RAB7A axis linking lysosomal pathways to collagen deposition in ventricular remodeling. These findings highlight a potential therapeutic target to attenuate LV fibrosis.

articles.title: Direct patch-clamp recording reveals TRPML2-dependent cation conductance across pathogen-containing vacuole membranes.
articles.journal: American journal of physiology. Cell physiology
articles.abstract: Transient receptor potential mucolipin 2 (TRPML2), a cation channel encoded by MCOLN2 and localized to endolysosomal compartments, has been implicated in restricting Salmonella enterica replication through regulation of the Salmonella-containing vacuole (SCV). However, direct electrophysiological evidence of TRPML2 activity on the SCV membrane has been lacking. Using S. enterica serovar Typhi as a model, we optimized infection and patch-clamp conditions to directly access SCVs in infected THP-1 cells and record vacuolar ion currents. SCVs from wild-type cells exhibited robust inward currents at negative potentials that were reduced in TRPML2-knockout cells and enhanced by TRPML2 agonists. Under Mg2+-permeant conditions, SCVs displayed TRPML2-dependent Mg2+ conductance, supporting a role for TRPML2 in regulating Mg2+ availability during S. Typhi infection. Ca2+-permeant recordings further showed agonist-responsive inward currents on SCVs, indicating that SCV-localized TRPML2 retains broader divalent-cation conductance. Basal currents were also better maintained on SCVs than on bacteria-negative vacuoles isolated from uninfected bystander cells within the same cultures. PI3P reduced current rundown, suggesting that the phosphoinositide environment of SCVs may help sustain TRPML2 activity. Together, these findings provide the first direct electrophysiological characterization of a pathogen-containing vacuole and establish a tractable platform for investigating host ion-channel function at the host-pathogen interface.

articles.title: The magnitude and durability of immune response to the SARS-CoV-2 vaccination among children.
articles.journal: Journal of the Pediatric Infectious Diseases Society
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The declining uptake of SARS-CoV-2 vaccines, combined with evolving schedules and recurrent infections, underscores the need to monitor the durability of hybrid immunity in children. The objective of this study was to assess children's SARS-CoV-2-specific immune responses post-second vaccine dose and to compare immune responses between unvaccinated children and children vaccinated with two or three vaccine doses.

METHODS: Three observational cohorts of children aged 3-14 years were followed longitudinally from December 2021 to October 2023 in Montreal, Canada. Two had scheduled serology assessments before their second dose and at one, six and twelve months post-second dose. The other cohort included unvaccinated and vaccinated children, with 2-4 serology assessments, every 2-3 months. Linear mixed models adjusting for infection history were used to assess immune waning post-second dose and differences over time by vaccine status.

RESULTS: Controlling for recent infection, anti-spike IgG, anti-receptor binding domain (RBD) IgG, and neutralizing titers against wild-type SARS-CoV-2 declined by six months post-vaccination. For example, average IgG anti-RBD was 1 374.1 BAU/mL one month after dose two, with an estimated decline of -856.1 BAU/mL at six months (95% CI, -1 303.5 to -596.0; p<0.0001). T cell responses showed little evidence of decline over 12 months across all groups with a history of infection. Comparing children by vaccine status, the highest humoral responses were associated with three doses whereas the lowest with unvaccinated status (e.g., crude average two-dose IgG anti-RBD: 920.0 BAU/ml; unvaccinated estimated difference -515.1 BAU/mL; 95% CI, -698.0 to -444.7; p<0.0001). Spike-specific CD4+ T cell responses were lower among the unvaccinated.

CONCLUSIONS: Humoral responses declined significantly within six months of vaccination. Cellular responses were comparable across vaccine status groups, yet vaccinated children tended to maintain higher levels for more than one-year post-vaccination. Hybrid immunity could contribute to a more robust and durable cellular response.

articles.title: Post-Treatment Follow-up, Rehabilitation, and Return to Sport: Proceedings of the International Consensus Meetings on Cartilage Repair of the Ankle.
articles.abstract: BackgroundPostoperative follow-up, rehabilitation, and return to sport (RTS) are key components of recovery following surgical management of osteochondral lesions of the talus (OLT). However, substantial variability exists in postoperative protocols, with limited high-quality evidence guiding clinical practicesMethodsInternational experts convened during the International Congress on Cartilage Repair of the Ankle (ICCRA) in Pittsburgh, USA (2017), with subsequent ratification of recommendations in New York, USA (2025). The original consensus statements were developed using a modified Delphi process involving electronic surveys, structured questionnaires, and expert discussion. Consensus strength was defined as consensus (51%-74%), strong consensus (75%-99%), or unanimous (100%). The recommendations addressed postoperative follow-up, rehabilitation, and RTS following OLT management.ResultsA total of 16 consensus statements were developed and subsequently ratified, comprising 7 statements addressing post-treatment follow-up and 9 addressing rehabilitation and RTS. All statements achieved strong consensus, with agreement ranging from 75% to 98%. Follow-up recommendations emphasized standardized clinical assessment and patient-reported outcomes, with extended monitoring in select patients. Rehabilitation recommendations supported early controlled motion and progressive weightbearing, with individualized progression according to procedure and clinical performance. Return to sport recommendations emphasized functional recovery and individualized decision-making. Ten statements (63%) were classified exclusively as Grade E, highlighting the limited evidence supporting several recommendations.ConclusionThe ICCRA consensus statements establish a structured framework for postoperative follow-up, rehabilitation, and RTS following surgical management of OLT. Despite strong expert agreement, several recommendations remain supported by limited evidence, underlining the need for prospective studies to establish validated, procedure-specific rehabilitation protocols and objective RTS criteria.Level of Evidence:V, expert consensus.

articles.title: Incidence and Risk Assessment of Pulmonary Aspergillosis in Lung Cancer Survivors: A Nationwide Longitudinal Study.
articles.abstract: Lung cancer survivors may be at increased risk of pulmonary aspergillosis due to structural lung damage and treatment-related immunosuppression, yet population-based data quantifying this risk are limited. Using the Korean National Health Insurance Service database, we conducted a nationwide retrospective cohort study of 37,005 surgically treated lung cancer survivors (2010-2017) and 111,015 age- and sex-matched controls without lung cancer. Incident pulmonary aspergillosis was identified using ICD-10 codes, and its association with lung cancer survivorship was evaluated using multivariable Cox proportional hazards models adjusted for demographic factors and comorbidities, with additional analyses in a health-screening subgroup. Among 148,020 participants followed for 1,126,079 person-years, lung cancer survivors had a significantly higher incidence of pulmonary aspergillosis than age- and sex-matched controls (1.96 vs 0.39 per 1,000 person-years), with an increased adjusted risk (adjusted HR, 4.47; 95% CI, 3.83-5.21). The risk increased in a stepwise manner with treatment intensity and was highest among patients who received combined surgery, chemotherapy, and radiotherapy (adjusted HR, 15.00; 95% CI, 11.91-18.88). This elevated risk was greatest within the first year after diagnosis and remained significant at 5 years. Lung cancer survivors had a significantly increased risk of pulmonary aspergillosis compared with matched controls, particularly during the early post-treatment period and among those receiving multimodal therapy.

articles.title: Identification of soluble immune markers for the diagnosis of aspergillosis and pneumocystosis: an exploratory study.
articles.abstract: Invasive fungal diseases (IFDs) are increasingly recognized in immunocompromised patients, but diagnosis remains challenging because current pathogen-targeted perform variably across heterogeneous immune backgrounds. We investigated whether bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) immune profiling could identify disease-specific signatures for aspergillosis and Pneumocystis pneumonia. BALF samples from 27 patients were analyzed by shotgun proteomics using a Q Exactive Plus mass spectrometer coupled to an EASY-nLC1200 system. Clinical groups included invasive pulmonary aspergillosis (IPA, n = 7), chronic pulmonary aspergillosis (CPA, n = 4), Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP, n = 4), Pneumocystis colonization (PCC, n = 4), bacterial infection (BI, n = 4), and controls (n = 4). Overall, 2,278 proteins were identified, with a median of 1,000 proteins per sample (IQR 902-1,384). Within-group pairwise Jaccard similarity was high for controls (median, 0.89), PCP (0.91), PCC (0.87) and BI (0.79), but lower for IPA (0.73) and CPA (0.62), indicating greater heterogeneity in aspergillosis. Hierarchical clustering largely grouped controls, BI, PCC, and PCP according to clinical diagnosis, whereas aspergillosis profiles were more variable. Two IPA clusters emerged: kidney transplant recipients, whose proteomic profiles resembled controls, and non-neutropenic patients with hematological malignancies. Analysis of 77 soluble immune mediators produced broadly similar clustering, suggesting that immune proteins may distinguish clinically relevant disease patterns. In this exploratory analysis, BALF immune proteomic profiles differed according to clinical diagnosis, with the most pronounced heterogeneity observed within aspergillosis. Complement proteins and antimicrobial peptides emerged as candidate biomarkers that warrant validation in larger, independent cohorts before their diagnostic utility can be established.

articles.title: Satisfaction With Long-Acting Injectable Antipsychotic Treatment in People With Severe Mental Disorder: A Cross-Sectional Observational Study From the Perspective of Community Nursing Practice.
articles.journal: Journal of psychiatric and mental health nursing
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Mental health nurses play a central role in administering long-acting injectable antipsychotic treatment and developing therapeutic relationships with people with severe mental disorder. However, patients' satisfaction with this treatment modality is not routinely assessed, potentially limiting person-centred care.

AIM: To examine treatment satisfaction among people with severe mental disorder receiving long-acting injectable antipsychotic treatment in community mental health services, and to explore associations between satisfaction with this treatment and sociodemographic variables.

METHOD: Cross-sectional observational study with 81 adults attending a community mental health service in Barcelona, Spain. Treatment satisfaction was assessed using the Treatment Satisfaction Questionnaire for Medication (TSQM v.1.4), and functional independence was assessed using the Barthel Index. Data were collected through structured nurse-led interviews.

RESULTS: Participants reported high satisfaction with treatment convenience, effectiveness and global experience. One quarter reported treatment-related side effects. Convenience scores differed significantly by sex, marital status and age, with higher scores among women and older participants. Foreign-born participants reported higher effectiveness scores than Spanish participants. Most participants were functionally independent, with no significant differences in treatment satisfaction according to functional independence.

DISCUSSION: Routine assessment of treatment satisfaction by mental health nurses may provide an opportunity to identify treatment-related concerns and support communication about care.

LIMITATIONS: Single-site, cross-sectional design limits transferability and precludes causal inference.

IMPLICATIONS FOR PRACTICE: Incorporating brief, structured assessment of treatment satisfaction and perceived side effects into routine long-acting injectable antipsychotic administration may help nurses identify treatment-related concerns and support communication with patients.

RECOMMENDATIONS: Multicentre longitudinal studies are needed to examine how patient-reported satisfaction relates to clinical outcomes and therapeutic alliance. Embedding validated patient-reported outcome measures into routine nursing protocols for long-acting injectable antipsychotic administration is recommended.

articles.title: Susceptibility-weighted venous features in DWI-negative migraine with aura and transient ischemic attack presentations: A retrospective study with preliminary score derivation.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to evaluate the discriminative performance of venous asymmetry and index vein sign on susceptibility-weighted images (SWI) and to construct a preliminary, derivation-stage score for distinguishing migraine with aura (MA) from transient ischemic attack (TIA) in diffusion weighted imaging (DWI)-negative patients exhibiting lateralizable hemispheric deficits, defined by symptom-concordant clinico-radiologic features.

BACKGROUND: Distinguishing migraine with aura from transient ischemic attack in patients with acute neurological deficits remains diagnostically challenging. Imaging biomarkers may aid this differentiation.

METHODS: This study was designed as a retrospective, single-center, single-gate hypothesis-generating study with embedded preliminary score derivation and prospective blinded imaging assessment. Patients presenting with acute stroke-like symptoms between January 2023 and December 2024 to Hacettepe University Faculty of Medicine Hospitals were enrolled. Reference diagnoses had been assigned during routine clinical care using American Heart Association/American Stroke Association (AHA/ASA) criteria for transient ischemic attack (TIA) and the final International Classification of Headache Disorders, 3rd edition (ICHD-3) (2018) criteria for MA, without independent adjudication; retrospective per-patient tabulation of criterion C followed the ICHD-3 (2018) formulation. Clinical and demographic data were extracted retrospectively, and SWI images were evaluated prospectively. Clinico-radiologic characteristics of venous asymmetry and index vein sign (IVS) were examined in primary analyses along with their associations. From these analyses, a preliminary score named SVI (the symptom-concordant venous imaging) was derived.

RESULTS: Of 290 DWI-negative patients, only 21 had MA (TIA = 269). Marked or mild venous asymmetry was observed in 19/21 (90.5%) of MA and in 44/269 (16.4%) of patients with TIA (predominantly mild). The IVS was observed in 18/21 (85.7%) of MA versus 28/269 (10.4%) of patients with TIA. In a small follow-up subset, venous signs tended to resolve interictally in MA, representing a hypothesis-generating observation. Symptom-concordant venous asymmetry and the IVS, together with younger age, hypoesthesia, and speech impairment, were independently associated with MA. As derivation-cohort estimates, the SVI score yielded an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) = 0.97 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.94-0.99); at a data-derived cutoff of eight or more points, selected to prioritize specificity, sensitivity was 15/21 (71.4%, 95% CI 47.8-88.7%), and specificity 258/269 (95.9%, 95% CI 92.8-97.9%).

CONCLUSION: In this single derivation cohort, venous imaging findings were associated with MA and are potentially informative but merit further study. The preliminary SVI score requires independent prospective validation and should not presently guide diagnosis or treatment.

articles.title: Development of an accurate CRISPR/Cas13 diagnostic system for Wuchereria bancrofti.
articles.abstract: Disease surveillance is critical for WHO's Global Programme to Eliminate Lymphatic Filariasis (LF), but current field-ready diagnostics exhibit insufficient sensitivity and/or specificity in low-endemic settings. We aim to develop an ultra-sensitive and field-friendly CRISPR/Cas13-based SHERLOCK (Specific High-sensitivity Enzymatic Reporter unLOCKing) tool for point-of-care detection of Wuchereria bancrofti infection. The SHERLOCK assay, combining recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA) with CRISPR/Cas13a detection, was performed in two-step and one-pot formats, with sensitivity compared to qPCR (the emerging gold standard). The W. bancrofti SHERLOCK assays achieved a detection limit of 0.1 fg/μL gBlock DNA and showed no cross-reaction with five other filarial species. Assays were validated using 149 pooled mosquito and 185 human blood samples from Samoa, which were previously tested for LF antigen using WHO-recommended Filariasis Test Strips (FTS) and microscopically examined for microfilariae (Mf). For both mosquito and human samples, the two-step SHERLOCK assay reached 100% sensitivity and specificity, while one-pot SHERLOCK showed 94.0-96.4% sensitivity and 100% specificity. To improve the field deployability of the assay, we also used lyophilised one-pot SHERLOCK master mix and assessed its thermostability after storage at 25°C, 4°C and -20°C. The lyophilised one-pot SHERLOCK mix maintained a detection limit of 10 fg/μL W. bancrofti gBlock after 10 days at 25°C, indicating reduced reliance on cold-chain for reagent storage and transport. However, when testing human blood samples with lyophilised SHERLOCK, reduced sensitivity (59.7%) was observed. This CRISPR-based platform offers a promising field-ready next-generation approach to LF diagnostics, potentially addressing current limitations, enhancing surveillance and elimination efforts.

articles.title: Letter: Anticoagulation After Gastrointestinal Bleeding-Prognostic Associations are not Treatment Effects.
Chest physiotherapy for pneumonia in children.
articles.journal: The Cochrane database of systematic reviews
articles.abstract:
RATIONALE: Pneumonia is the single largest infectious cause of death in children aged under five years and remains a relevant cause of illness and death amongst older children and adolescents worldwide. Most pneumonia-related deaths occur in low- and middle-income countries, where access to healthcare resources, diagnostic services, and supportive treatments may be more limited than in high-income settings. Chest physiotherapy is widely used as adjuvant treatment for pneumonia. Physiotherapy is thought to help remove inflammatory exudates, tracheobronchial secretions, and airway obstructions, and reduce airway resistance to improve breathing and enhance gas exchange. This is an update of a review first published in 2013 and updated in 2019.

OBJECTIVES: To assess the effectiveness of chest physiotherapy regarding time until clinical resolution in children (from birth to 18 years) of either gender with any type of pneumonia, irrespective of aetiology or clinical classification.

SEARCH METHODS: We searched the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, LILACS, Web of Science, and PEDro and two clinical trial registries on 8 June 2026.

ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA: We included randomised controlled trials (RCTs) that compared any type of chest physiotherapy with no chest physiotherapy (i.e. usual care for pneumonia treatment) in children with pneumonia. We did not apply any eligibility restrictions based on gestational age at birth.

OUTCOMES: Our critical outcomes were mortality, duration of hospital stay, and time to clinical resolution. Adverse events was an important outcome.

RISK OF BIAS: We used the Cochrane RoB 1 tool for RCTs.

SYNTHESIS METHODS: We used standard Cochrane methodological procedures. Two review authors independently selected studies for inclusion, extracted data, and assessed the risk of bias. For dichotomous outcomes, we calculated risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). For continuous outcomes measured on the same scale, we calculated mean differences (MDs) with 95% CIs. We synthesised the results for each outcome of interest using a random-effects meta-analysis. When pooling of data was not possible, we described the results narratively. We used GRADE to assess the certainty of evidence for each outcome.

INCLUDED STUDIES: We included six new RCTs (2304 children) in this update, for a total of 12 RCTs involving 2863 children aged from 29 days to 14 years with pneumonia who were treated as inpatients. Pneumonia severity was described as moderate in two trials, severe in five trials, and was not stated in five trials. The included studies were conducted in Bangladesh, Brazil, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, Malawi, and South Africa. The studies assessed the effects of conventional (4 studies, 287 children), modern (1 study, 29 children), and instrumental chest physiotherapy (7 studies, 2547 children), comprising continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP), bubble CPAP (bCPAP), and thoracic high-frequency chest wall oscillation (HFCWO) devices, compared to no chest physiotherapy. The studies were at overall low risk of bias. Blinding of participants was not possible in most studies, but we considered that the outcomes were unlikely to be influenced by the lack of blinding.

SYNTHESIS OF RESULTS: Six studies (2294 children) reported mortality. Three studies reported no deaths. However, three studies of bCPAP reported contrasting results: one reported higher mortality in the intervention group (RR 1.52, 95% CI 1.02 to 2.27), whereas the other two found lower mortality in the bCPAP group (RR 0.14, 95% CI 0.03 to 1.16; and RR 0.28, 95% CI 0.08 to 0.90). Due to high heterogeneity amongst the studies, a pooled analysis was not possible (I² = 83%; low-certainty evidence). However, the evidence suggests that chest physiotherapy results in little to no difference in mortality. Nine studies (2069 children) evaluated the duration of hospital stay. Five studies reported no difference between groups, whilst the other four studies found a shorter hospital stay in the group receiving chest physiotherapy. Due to high heterogeneity amongst the studies, a pooled analysis was not possible (I² = 88%; low-certainty evidence). Eleven studies (2219 children) assessed time to clinical resolution. Chest physiotherapy may result in little to no difference in time to clinical resolution of increased respiratory rate (MD -1.21, 95% CI -3.55 to 1.13; 4 studies, 1446 children; low-certainty evidence). Moreover, five studies reported the time to resolution of fever; however, pooling of data was not possible due to high heterogeneity (I² = 94%; very low-certainty evidence). Five studies assessed peripheral capillary oxygen saturation (SpO2), but pooling of data was not possible due to high heterogeneity (I² = 79%; very low-certainty evidence). Two out of five studies showed that children assigned to the intervention group had a significant increase in SpO2 compared to the control group. Regarding symptom improvement, three studies (336 children) found shorter cough and sputum duration in children receiving physiotherapy, whereas one study (89 children) observed a longer coughing period. Six studies (2382 children) reported adverse events. Most studies found no serious adverse events, but mild complications such as nasal irritation, skin breakdown, or abdominal distension were more common in children receiving CPAP or bCPAP. Due to high heterogeneity amongst the studies, a pooled analysis was not possible (I² = 80%; low-certainty evidence). Overall, the evidence was limited by small sample sizes, wide CIs, high risk of reporting bias, heterogeneity across interventions, and variations in outcome definitions. The certainty of evidence ranged from very low to low.

AUTHORS' CONCLUSIONS: We could draw no reliable conclusions regarding the effectiveness of chest physiotherapy for children with pneumonia due to substantial variability in study characteristics and limitations in how data were presented and analysed across the included trials. Future research should ensure adequate methodological rigour, standardisation of physiotherapy techniques, appropriate outcome measures (such as duration of leukocytosis and airway clearance), and careful reporting of potential adverse effects.

FUNDING: The review authors declare no funding support or financial conflicts of interest.

REGISTRATION: Protocol (2012) DOI: doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD010277 Original review (2013) DOI: doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD010277.pub2 Review update (2019) DOI: doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD010277.pub3.

articles.title: A safety profile on idarucizumab for dabigatran reversal: an update.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Idarucizumab has been widely adopted since its approval as the only reversal agent for dabigatran. Since then, evidence on its effectiveness, safety, and real-world use has continued to accumulate.

AREAS COVERED: This review summarizes the pharmacological characteristics of idarucizumab, the clinical evidence supporting its use, and practical considerations for administration, including post-reversal care. We also provide expert opinion on its role as reversal agent. Key literature on clinical evidence, pharmacology, and safety was identified through PubMed searches and screening of reference lists.

EXPERT OPINION: Idarucizumab remains the only approved targeted antidote for dabigatran and is likely to retain this position in the near term. However, evidence for clinical benefit remains limited to observational data and a single-arm trial conducted without a comparator. High cost and lower dabigatran use compared with other DOACs may make routine stocking of idarucizumab impractical in rural or resource-limited settings. In our expert opinion, its indication can be complex, particularly because trial-based bleeding definitions may not align with clinical practice; therefore, multidisciplinary input may be required to support appropriate use. Furthermore, we advocate that multidisciplinary care should extend beyond hemostasis is achieved, dedicated aftercare and anticoagulation stewardship could optimize clinical outcomes.

articles.title: Evidence-Informed Recommendations for Child Sex Trafficking Identification and Response in Ontario Pediatric Emergency Departments: A Modified Delphi Method Study.
articles.abstract: Children who experience sex trafficking often access emergency departments (EDs) while they are being exploited for related health and psychosocial concerns. However, few clinical resources exist to support ED providers in identifying and responding to presentations of child sex trafficking (CST) in Canada, an internationally recognized source, destination, and transit site for trafficking. This study used a modified Delphi method to propose evidence-informed recommendations for CST identification and response in pediatric EDs. Between July 6 and October 18, 2023, N = 58 Ontario health and social service providers completed three iterative surveys on CST identification, intervention, and referral practices. Providers rated statements using a 4-point Likert scale and provided write-in responses to expand on their survey selections. We analyzed closed-ended responses using descriptive and Kappa statistics, and write-in responses using content analysis. Experts endorsed 57 of the 84 components (68%) to inform clinical practice recommendations for CST identification and response in pediatric EDs, which center on three categories: (1) assessing CST vulnerability factors and indicators, (2) intervention practices that center a culturally responsive, trauma- and violence-informed approach, and (3) in-hospital and community referrals to support the short- and long-term service needs of children who experience sex trafficking. Pediatric ED providers are encouraged to adopt a trauma- and violence-informed approach when incorporating CST identification into existing patient-interviewing methods, such as the pediatric HEADS-ED assessment tool. This population may require specialized services, such as through Sexual Assault/Domestic Violence Treatment Centres and anti-human trafficking community services. While these findings can inform the development of inter-institutional care transition protocols, readily achievable response practices in the ED include providing patient education on safer sexual health and online practices and establishing community linkages to anti-human trafficking services.

articles.title: Arylhydrazineylidene linked dimedone and acetylacetone analogs as multitarget inhibitors of α-glucosidase, α-amylase, acetylcholinesterase, butyrylcholinesterase and potential antioxidants: an integrated study based on synthesis, in vitro study, molecular docking, and ADME analysis.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Diabetes and Alzheimer diseases have the shared pathological mechanisms, thus making multitarget-directed inhibitors as a promising therapeutic approach.

METHODS: In the present study, a varyingly substituted arylhydrazineylidene linked dimedone and acetylacetone analogs 1-32 were synthesized, characterized, and first time evaluated against α-amylase, α-glucosidase, acetylcholinesterase (AChE), and butyrylcholinesterase (BChE) enzymes.

RESULTS: The dimedone-based derivatives 1-18 exhibited enhanced inhibitory activity against all four tested enzymes compared to acetylacetone analogs 19-32. Among the most active compounds, compound 13 showed the highest inhibitory potency, with IC50 values of 1.59, 1.90, 1.94, and 2.14 µM against α-amylase, α-glucosidase, AChE, and BChE, respectively. Compounds were also evaluated for antioxidant potential and luckily compound 13 was found to possess strong antioxidant potential. Other compounds also demonstrated notable activity, whereas a few were found inactive. Furthermore, the compounds were subjected to molecular docking studies to reveal their binding interactions with the target enzymes and to rationalize their observed inhibitory activities. Moreover, a comprehensive pharmacokinetics, drug-likeness, and ADME analysis was also predicted. The synthesized compounds have optimal oral absorption and bioavailability.

CONCLUSION: This study has identified promising multitarget inhibitors that could be potential therapeutics for the treatment of diabetes and Alzheimer disease.

articles.title: Neurorehabilitation as an Opportunity for Structured Post-Stroke Lipid Management: A Narrative Review.
articles.abstract: Background and PurposeIschemic stroke remains a major cause of death, disability, and recurrent vascular events worldwide. Although lipid-lowering therapy is central to secondary prevention, the transition between acute stroke care and long-term outpatient management remains a vulnerable period during which guideline-directed treatment is frequently delayed, undertitrated, or discontinued. Neurorehabilitation may provide an important opportunity to address this gap. This narrative review summarizes evidence supporting intensive low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) reduction after ischemic stroke and examines how the neurorehabilitation setting may facilitate optimized lipid management.MethodsA literature search was performed in PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and the Cochrane Library through March 2026, combining terms across three domains: (1) ischemic stroke and secondary prevention, (2) lipid-lowering therapy, and (3) neurorehabilitation and functional recovery. Included study types encompassed randomized controlled trials, systematic reviews with meta-analyses, clinical practice guidelines, observational cohort and preclinical studies addressing statin pleiotropic effects. Priority was given to landmark randomized trials, major society guidelines, and studies with direct relevance to recurrent stroke prevention, hemorrhagic risk stratification, and rehabilitation-based care delivery.ResultsEvidence from SPARCL, Treat Stroke to Target, FOURIER, and Ez PAVE shows that intensive LDL-C reduction improves secondary stroke prevention. Statins may also affect neuroinflammation, endothelial function, blood-brain barrier integrity, and neuroplasticity, with differences in hemorrhagic stroke risk and safety profiles compared with PCSK9 inhibitors.ConclusionAlthough direct rehabilitation-based randomized trials are lacking, integrating supervised medication titration, adherence monitoring, neuroimaging-guided risk stratification, and patient-centered secondary prevention strategies into neurorehabilitation may represent a practical approach for strengthening secondary stroke prevention and reducing recurrent vascular events.

articles.title: Comfort and Adverse Reactions in Immediate Mouthwash Use: A Comparative Study.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: To evaluate the immediate effects and user acceptance of mouthwashes containing different active ingredients - chlorhexidine, essential oils, and green tea/hyaluronic acid - by assessing their impact on salivary pH, sensory experiences, and potential side effects.

METHODS AND MATERIALS: This is a randomised clinical trial, including 96 students who were randomised into three groups, each using one of three mouthwashes: essential oils, chlorhexidine, and green tea/hyaluronic acid. Participants conducted a 60-s rinse and subsequently filled out questionnaires on sensory experiences, such as taste and irritation, and the potential for daily use. Salivary pH was measured immediately before and after rinsing to assess any changes.

RESULTS: All mouthwashes effectively increased salivary pH from an average of 7.0 to 8.6, indicating a shift towards a less acidic oral environment. There were no significant differences in the sensation of clean teeth across different mouthwashes. However, the green tea/hyaluronic acid mouthwash was more favourably received, causing less discomfort in the lips, tongue, and throat and showing no reports of tongue irritation. Participants expressed a significantly higher preference for this mouthwash (p = 0.04) for potential daily use, as opposed to those using essential oil or chlorhexidine mouthwashes, which commonly reported burning sensations.

CONCLUSION: Although all tested mouthwashes were effective in increasing salivary pH, the green tea/hyaluronic acid formulation stood out due to higher user comfort and acceptance, potentially due to its natural component base. These findings suggest a promising direction for future mouthwash formulations that prioritise natural ingredients and user comfort. In conclusion, green tea and hyaluronic acid mouthwash increases salivary pH with better user comfort and acceptance than chlorhexidine or essential oils.

articles.title: Machine Learning Prediction of Independent Walking 8 Weeks After Rehabilitation in Patients With Stroke: A Retrospective Study.
articles.abstract: BackgroundEarly prediction of independent walking after stroke may support rehabilitation planning, but the prognostic relevance of somatosensory pathway integrity remains unclear.ObjectivesTo compare logistic regression, used as a conventional reference model, with five machine-learning classifiers (random forest, gradient boosting, support vector machine, k-nearest neighbors, and neural network) for predicting independent walking 8 weeks after inpatient rehabilitation admission.MethodsThis single-center retrospective cohort study included 169 patients with ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke and baseline Functional Ambulation Category scores ≤3 who underwent inpatient rehabilitation. Seven baseline predictors were NIHSS, FMA-LE, BBS, TIS, MMSE-K, SEP severity, and stroke type. Six classifiers were evaluated using stratified five-fold cross-validation and pooled out-of-fold predictions. ROC-AUC was the primary measure; average precision and calibration were additionally assessed.ResultsFifty patients (29.6%) were independent walkers at 8 weeks. Complete SEP impairment was present in 36.1% of non-independent versus 4.0% of independent walkers (p < .001). AUCs ranged from 0.839 to 0.884. The neural network had the highest AUC (0.884; 95% CI, 0.832-0.937) and average precision (0.771), a calibration slope of 0.904, and the lowest Brier score (0.122). No pairwise AUC difference remained significant after Holm adjustment. BBS and SEP severity were the leading neural-network predictors by permutation importance.ConclusionsBaseline clinical and somatosensory measures showed good internally validated discrimination. The neural network had the highest AUC point estimate and average precision, but no model showed statistically superior AUC after multiplicity adjustment. External validation is required before clinical implementation.

articles.title: Effect of a dietary behaviour change education intervention on iron status and linear growth in children aged 6 to 59 months: a cluster-randomised controlled trial in rural Ethiopia.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Food insecurity and limited maternal nutrition knowledge contribute to childhood iron deficiency anaemia (IDA) and stunting. This study evaluated community-based Dietary Intake Behaviour Education (DIBE) for improving iron status and linear growth among children aged 6-59 months in rural central Ethiopia.

METHODS: A cluster-randomized controlled trial with 1:1 allocation was conducted across 16 community units from April 2021 to January 2023, enrolling 1,012 mother-child pairs. Structured assessments collected data on nutritional status, maternal nutrition knowledge, feeding practices, and related factors. IDA was defined as a haemoglobin concentration below 110 g/L, while stunting was defined as a height-for-age Z-score (HAZ) below -2 SD from the WHO child growth standards. Independent-samples t-tests and generalized estimating equations assessed intervention effects and associated factors.

RESULTS: Baseline IDA prevalence was 18.2%, higher in the intervention group (22.13%) than the control group (14.2%). At endline, IDA prevalence decreased to 6.5% in the intervention group but increased to 20.4% in controls. Baseline stunting prevalence was comparable between intervention (41.5%) and control (40.7%) groups. At endline, stunting decreased to 15.0% in the intervention group but increased to 51.8% in controls. DIBE was positively associated with HAZ (B = 0.744, p = 0.003). Maternal food-preparation practices (B = 0.242, p = 0.020) and IDA awareness (B = 0.237) were also positively associated with HAZ.

CONCLUSIONS: Community-based DIBE improved linear growth and coincided with reductions in IDA and stunting. Integrating practical nutrition education into routine child health services may improve nutritional outcomes in resource-limited settings.Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov:NCT04846062.Registered: 15 April 2021, View at: https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT04846062.

articles.title: Early childhood blood pressure in relation to umbilical cord homocysteine and folate: insights from the ENVIRonmental influence ON AGEing birth cohort Study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: High blood pressure (BP) tracks from childhood into adulthood, contributing to cardiovascular risk. How the prenatal one-carbon (1-C) metabolism, as reflected by umbilical cord homocysteine and folate, affects BP in early childhood is unknown.

METHODS: The prospective population-based birth cohort ENVIRonmental influence ON early﻿AGEing (ENVIRONAGE) comprised 500 mother-offspring pairs. Umbilical cord and maternal homocysteine and folate were measured by electrochemiluminescence immunoassay. The association of the offspring BP and risk of high BP was assessed by linear and logistic regression and by mediation analysis. Association sizes were expressed per doubling of the biomarkers and adjusted for the children's sex, age and weight and maternal age at delivery and parity.

RESULTS: At 4.5  years (median), cord homocysteine was associated with higher diastolic and mean BP (MBP), but not SBP with association sizes of 1.67  mmHg [95% confidence interval (CI), 0.36-2.99] and 1.19  mmHg (0.01-2.38), respectively. The odds ratio for high childhood DBP with normotension as reference was 2.22 (1.34-3.68). Associations of BP with cord folate were not significant. Cord folate had only an indirect effect on DBP and MBP with effect sizes amounting to -3.04 (P = 0.027) and -2.30 (P = 0.061)  mmHg. Maternal biomarkers were not associated with the offspring's BP.

CONCLUSION: In this prospective birth cohort study, higher cord plasma homocysteine was associated with higher DBP in early childhood, whereas cord folate was only via homocysteine associated with the offspring's BP. The 1-C metabolism provides a mechanism for preventing high BP in childhood, which is a forerunner of hypertension in adolescence and adulthood.

articles.title: The relationship between cardiac output and postexercise hypotension differs according to resting blood pressure status: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To examine whether postexercise blood pressure (BP) reductions are associated with changes in cardiac output (CO) and its components and whether these relationships depend on baseline BP status.

METHODS: This systematic review and meta-analysis (PROSPERO: CRD42021256569) included studies assessing BP and central hemodynamic responses at least 30 min after aerobic exercise. Random- and mixed-effects models and meta-regression examined associations between BP and CO, stroke volume (SV), and heart rate (HR), stratified by baseline BP status.

RESULTS: Fifty-six trials were included (101 interventions; 1026 participants, 31.2 ± 5.1 years, 120.4 ± 8.9/72.3 ± 7.6 mmHg). Aerobic exercise reduced systolic, diastolic, and mean arterial pressure. Meta-regression analyses revealed that the association between BP reduction and central hemodynamic responses differed according to baseline BP. In individuals with normal BP, no associations between BP and CO, SV, or HR remained significant after correction for multiple testing. In contrast, in individuals with elevated BP, greater reductions in SBP were associated with greater reductions in CO [slope = 0.659; 95% confidence interval (95% CI), 0.268-1.051; P < 0.001], and this association remained significant after false discovery rate and Bonferroni corrections. No other associations between BP and CO, SV, or HR remained significant.

CONCLUSION: Greater postexercise reductions in SBP were associated with reductions in CO in individuals with elevated BP, whereas no consistent association was observed in individuals with normal BP. These findings indicate that the relationship between postexercise BP and hemodynamic responses differs according to baseline BP status, with a stronger association between SBP and CO responses in individuals with elevated BP, without establishing a causal relationship.
