While some vaccine candidates exist, such as the live-attenuated ΔNSsΔNSm vaccine, most immunogenicity studies do not consider the contribution of the Fc region to antibody quality. In this study, multiplexed Fc array assays were developed to assess the Fc profile of antigen-specific antibodies following RVFV vaccination. These assays proved to be useful in identifying a Th1-biased response induced by RVFV ΔNSsΔNSm and ΔNSs and in identifying the contribution of innate immunity to this response. These assays can be applied to other RVFV vaccine platforms, such as mRNA and protein vaccines, to fully characterize the quality of an antibody response following vaccination.

articles.title: Pharmacokinetic interactions of azithromycin and ethambutol with or without SPR720 in healthy participants.
articles.abstract: SPR720 is an aminobenzimidazole prodrug that is rapidly converted in vivo to SPR719, an inhibitor of the DNA gyrase B ATPase subunit in mycobacteria. SPR719 demonstrates potent in vitro activity against clinically relevant Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) species. This study evaluated the pharmacokinetics (PK), safety, and tolerability of SPR720, azithromycin, and ethambutol administered alone and in combination in healthy adults. Participants were assigned to one of five groups and received the following oral regimens daily for 7 days: (1) SPR720 1,000 mg, (2) azithromycin 500 mg, (3) ethambutol 800 mg, (4) SPR720 plus azithromycin and ethambutol, or (5) azithromycin plus ethambutol. PK and safety analyses included 39 participants. Between-group PK comparisons were descriptive, and no formal statistical hypothesis testing was performed. On Day 7, mean SPR719 AUC0-τ was 15% higher with SPR720 plus azithromycin and ethambutol than with SPR720 alone, indicating a modest difference in SPR719 exposure. Azithromycin exposure increased from Day 1 to Day 7, consistent with its long half-life. On Day 7, mean azithromycin AUC0-τ was 56% higher with azithromycin plus ethambutol than with azithromycin alone but was 47% lower with the three-drug regimen than with azithromycin plus ethambutol. Mean ethambutol AUC0-τ was 19% lower with azithromycin plus ethambutol and 48% lower with the three-drug regimen than with ethambutol alone. Macrolides remain the cornerstone of MAC pulmonary disease (MAC-PD) therapy. These descriptive findings highlight the importance of evaluating PK within multidrug regimens for MAC-PD rather than extrapolating from single- or dual-agent studies.CLINICAL TRIALSThis study is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov as NCT05966688.

articles.title: Neisseria gonorrhoeae: a historical model for host adaptation.
articles.abstract: Research into Neisseria gonorrhoeae (Gc) physiology, genetics, and pathogenicity remains deeply shaped by its history. Long before molecular tools were available, early clinical observations, human inoculation studies, and initial vaccine trials defined the field's primary experimental questions and limitations. Key features of gonococcal infection, including restriction to the human host, rapid phenotypic alteration during culture, and the absence of durable protective immunity, were documented empirically decades before researchers understood their underlying biological mechanisms. As a result, contemporary gonococcal research has largely developed in response to these early empirical findings. Modern genomic and molecular studies have provided mechanistic explanations for long-standing clinical observations, turning historical paradoxes into defined areas of investigation. From designing vaccines that target variable surface structures to surveilling horizontally acquired resistance determinants, the questions driving current research directly continue the experimental challenges investigators identified.

articles.title: Integrating QSAR, molecular dynamics and MM-GBSA to re-rank natural product-derived DPP4 candidates from virtual screening.
articles.journal: SAR and QSAR in environmental research
articles.abstract: Dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP4) is a validated target for type 2 diabetes, and virtual screening of natural product libraries is a common route to new chemotypes. We asked whether a top docking rank survives independent scrutiny. From COCONUT, 85,600 compounds were filtered to 32,008 and docked against DPP4; 873 outscored the crystallographic ligand N7F (-10.01 kcal/mol), with Lig_771 first at -12.5 kcal/mol. Across four 300 ns simulations (two replicas per complex, 1.2 μs) Lig_771 stayed bound but never reproduced the gliptin recognition motif: the control held its salt bridges to Glu205 and Glu206 in over 93% of frames, whereas Lig_771 formed no persistent hydrogen bond to these residues and sampled two distinct poses. MM-GBSA gave -15.6 kcal/mol for Lig_771 against -23.9 for the control. A QSAR model built on 4327 measured DPP4 inhibitors (scaffold-based external R2 = 0.415; random split 0.669) predicted a pIC50 of 6.59 for Lig_771, below linagliptin (8.29), sitagliptin (7.39) and vildagliptin (6.96). None of the three analyses corroborated the docking ranking. The study is computational and does not establish DPP4 inhibition. Lig_771 occupies largely unexplored chemical space (maximum Tanimoto similarity 0.316) and merits testing, but selecting hits on docking score alone would have been misleading here.

articles.title: Pregnancy considerations in women with uncorrected tetralogy of Fallot.
articles.journal: International journal of gynaecology and obstetrics: the official organ of the International Federation of Gynaecology and Obstetrics
articles.abstract: Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) is the most common cyanotic congenital heart disease, accounting for approximately 7-10% of all congenital cardiac malformations. Although early surgical repair has transformed its natural history in high-income settings, with contemporary long-term survival exceeding 90%, uncorrected TOF continues to be encountered in pregnancy, particularly in women from resource-limited regions or those with previously undiagnosed disease. The physiological adaptations of pregnancy, including reduction in systemic vascular resistance, plasma volume expansion, and a 30-50% rise in cardiac output, are poorly tolerated in the presence of a non-restrictive ventricular septal defect and fixed right ventricular outflow tract obstruction, leading to progressive cyanosis, right ventricular strain, and uteroplacental hypoperfusion. Current European Society of Cardiology (ESC) guidance classifies unrepaired cyanotic heart disease without Eisenmenger syndrome as mWHO 2.0 class III, while Eisenmenger syndrome is classified as mWHO 2.0 class IV. Contemporary data from the ESC EORP Registry of Pregnancy and Cardiac Disease (ROPAC) report maternal mortality of 0.7% and heart failure in 8.7% of pregnancies with uncorrected congenital heart disease, with markedly worse outcomes in cyanotic subsets. This narrative review synthesizes the pathophysiology, risk stratification, obstetric management, intrapartum anesthetic considerations, comparative outcomes of uncorrected versus corrected disease, and key evidence gaps that continue to constrain care for this population, providing a physiology-driven framework for the pregnancy heart team.

articles.title: Gene-by-Sleep Duration Interaction for Glycemic Traits in More Than 480,000 Individuals.
articles.abstract: The biological mechanisms of how sleep duration impacts type 2 diabetes pathogenesis and glycemic control are unclear. This study reveals 16 loci (11 novel) that interact with either short or long sleep duration to influence hemoglobin A1c, fasting glucose, or fasting insulin. Short and long sleep duration loci were nonoverlapping. Regulation of copper and diacylglycerol levels appear as distinct cellular mechanisms implicated by long and short sleep duration loci, respectively. Identified gene targets present insight for potential type 2 diabetes therapeutic design approaches related to JIP1-c-Jun N-terminal kinase interaction disruption, pericyte health, N-methyl-d-aspartate receptor activity, anti-inflammatory and leptin-enhancing dietary supplements, and serpins.

articles.title: A Pilot Study of PMHNP Students' Knowledge, Confidence, and Attitudes to Inform Telemental Health Curriculum Enhancement.
articles.journal: Journal of the American Psychiatric Nurses Association
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Telemental health (TMH) has been shown to improve access to mental health services. However, a lack of formal telehealth education may be a significant barrier to the widespread effective use of this technology.

AIMS: This pilot study explored psychiatric mental health nurse practitioner (PMHNP) students' knowledge, confidence, and attitudes about delivering telemental healthcare following a telemental health curriculum enhancement.

METHODS: A multi-faceted evidence-based TMH curriculum was integrated into the PMHNP graduate program. To inform future curriculum enhancement, a mixed-methods descriptive study was conducted using a 22-item tele-OSCE (objective structured clinical exam) questionnaire to assess students' knowledge, confidence, and attitudes toward telehealth competencies. Narrative questions were included to gain greater insight into the curriculum's impact. Descriptive statistics and content analysis were used to evaluate the results.

RESULTS: A sample of 11 students showed high knowledge scores except in the areas of understanding laws and regulations for the discipline and policies for their organization. Confidence scores were high in many areas, with a few aspects showing lower scores, such as building rapport and communicating using TMH. Attitude scores were primarily strong. Narrative data indicated some students were able to develop more knowledge of laws and regulations than others. Finally, simulation and clinical aspects of the curriculum enhanced learning.

CONCLUSIONS: Formal TMH education can enhance PMHNP students' knowledge, confidence, and attitudes toward this healthcare delivery modality. The development and integration of standardized telehealth education in nurse practitioner (NP) programs is critical in promoting widespread telehealth use and improving patient outcomes.

articles.title: SEPSIS-INDUCED COAGULOPATHY ATTENUATES THE PROGNOSTIC VALUE OF THE HEMOGLOBIN-ALBUMIN-LYMPHOCYTE-PLATELET (HALP) SCORE IN SEPSIS.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The hemoglobin-albumin-lymphocyte-platelet (HALP) score predicts outcomes in sepsis, but its platelet denominator is also a core component of sepsis-induced coagulopathy (SIC), and may distort its prognostic meaning. We examined whether SIC modifies HALP's association with 28-day mortality.

METHODS: We analyzed 6,218 adults meeting Sepsis-3 criteria in MIMIC-IV. HALP was calculated from first ICU measurements; SIC was defined by the 2017 ISTH criteria (score ≥4). Analyses included multivariable regression, interaction testing, propensity-score methods, and platelet-independent coagulopathy definitions, and evaluation of modified HALP (m-HALP; platelets in the numerator).

RESULTS: Twenty-eight-day mortality was 25.6%; SIC incidence was 26.1%. HALP showed a J-shaped association with mortality (P for nonlinearity <0.001). The lowest quartile independently predicted death (adjusted OR 1.43, 95% CI 1.20-1.70; HR 1.24, 95% CI 1.10-1.39). This association persisted in non-SIC patients (OR 1.51, 95% CI 1.28-1.79) but was attenuated and non-significant in SIC patients (OR 1.14, 95% CI 0.82-1.60; interaction P=0.006). Albumin carried HALP's discrimination in non-SIC patients, whereas platelets dominated in SIC (OR 0.51 per SD, P=0.001). When coagulopathy was redefined without platelets, the modification was no longer significant (P=0.295), indicating it partly reflects the shared platelet component. m-HALP was inversely associated with mortality in both strata (interaction P=0.691). Results were robust to weighting, 90-day mortality, and alternative Cox models.

CONCLUSIONS: HALP is an independent prognostic marker mainly in septic patients without coagulopathy; once SIC develops, thrombocytopenia both raises mortality risk and arithmetically inflates HALP. Coagulation status should be assessed before HALP-based risk stratification; m-HALP may offer a platelet-consistent alternative.

articles.title: The effect of music listening to mothers of premature babies in the neonatal intensive care unit on mothers' stress levels and amount of breast milk: A randomized controlled trial.
articles.abstract: We aimed to examine the effects of music listening on stress levels and breast milk volume among mothers of premature infants in the neonatal intensive care unit. We conducted a randomized controlled trial between 15.11.2023, and 22.04.2024. A total of 59 mothers of premature infants completed the study. When comparing the mean 'State-Trait Anxiety Inventory (STAI)' scores between the experimental and control groups, there was no significant difference between the groups on the third and fourth days. However, in the experimental group, the amount of breast milk on day 4th was statistically significantly higher than on day 1st. Listening to music may contribute to increased breast milk production in mothers of preterm infants during the early postpartum period. Based on these findings, we suggest that music may be considered a supportive, non-pharmacological intervention in neonatal intensive care settings.

articles.title: A temperate phage acts as a symbiotic fitness enhancer for UPEC but surrenders to combination therapy through lysogeny suppression.
articles.abstract:
UNLABELLED: Temperate phages are increasingly recognized as key drivers of bacterial evolution. Here, we isolated a myoviral prophage, vB_EcoM_P899, from a clinical uropathogenic Escherichia coli (UPEC) isolate and characterized how lysogenization shapes host biology. Lysogenization significantly enhanced biofilm formation, swarming motility, oxidative stress resistance, and adhesion to macrophages (up to 100-fold) without altering antibiotic susceptibility or overall 72-h lethality in the Galleria mellonella larval infection model. Mechanistically, this is associated with upregulation of the fimbrial gene FimA and enhanced inducibility of the oxidative stress response genes KatE and OxyR under oxidative stress. Crucially, combining P899 with ciprofloxacin or kanamycin produced synergistic killing and suppressed new lysogen formation in an antibiotic-class-dependent manner. In contrast, ceftazidime, while synergistic, failed to prevent lysogeny. Our findings demonstrate that while prophage vB_EcoM_P899 promotes bacterial niche adaptation, its lysogenization frequency is significantly reduced under specific antibiotic pressure, facilitating clearance of the challenged UPEC population. This work provides a strong rationale for optimizing phage-antibiotic combination therapies to treat drug-resistant infections by simultaneously enhancing bacterial killing and limiting lysogenic survivors.

IMPORTANCE: This study reveals that lysogenization by a temperate phage can enhance the niche adaptation of uropathogenic Escherichia coli without increasing its virulence in the Galleria mellonella larval model or altering antibiotic resistance. Crucially, we demonstrate that combining this phage with select antibiotics (e.g., kanamycin and ciprofloxacin) not only kills the bacteria effectively but also actively suppresses the formation of new lysogens in an antibiotic-class-dependent manner. These findings uncover a novel role for temperate phages as symbiotic regulators within the host and provide direct experimental evidence for a phage-antibiotic combination strategy. This approach holds promise for combating chronic, recurrent urinary tract infections and offers a clinically viable pathway to address antibiotic tolerance in chronic, recurrent urinary tract infections.

articles.title: Exercise chronotropic inefficiency in patients with heart failure across distinct left ventricular ejection fraction phenotypes.
articles.abstract:
AIMS: To characterize the pattern of chronotropic incompetence (CI) response to exercise in patients with heart failure (HF) across distinct phenotypes of the left ventricular ejection fraction and to explore the extent to which heart rate (HR) response should be prioritized as a therapeutic target within personalized HF management strategies.

METHODS: Patients with HF with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), HF with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), and healthy controls underwent incremental exercise testing with simultaneous gas exchange and echocardiography assessments. Stroke volume (SV), HR, cardiac output (CO), and arteriovenous oxygen difference [C(a-v)O2] were assessed from rest to peak exercise. Graphical analyses explored relationships amongst determinants of oxygen uptake (V̇O2).

RESULTS: Both HF phenotypes exhibited CI and a blunted increase in CO during exercise compared with controls. Peak HR was similarly reduced by 20% in HFpEF and 23% in HFrEF. HFpEF, however, exhibited a steeper HR-VO2 relationship. HFrEF demonstrated a greater compensatory increase in peripheral O2 extraction, with peak C(a-v)O2 73% higher than controls and 21% higher than HFpEF. In contrast, HFpEF showed limited ability to augment C(a-v)O2 and presented the lowest relative peak V̇O2 (-39% vs. controls and -16% vs. HFrEF), despite similar peak V̇O2%pred between HF phenotypes.

CONCLUSION: CI can contribute to exercise intolerance in both HF phenotypes, with distinct compensatory mechanisms. An integrated cardiopulmonary exercise testing-echocardiography approach may support identifying phenotype-specific physiological profiles that might address therapeutic strategies targeting CI, SV reserve, and peripheral O2 utilization to improve functional capacity in HF. Addressing the kinetics of HR slope and ΔHR metrics seems relevant to implement knowledge on the fundamental CI contribution in HF phenotypes.

articles.title: Interpregnancy interval and adverse live-birth outcomes after a non-live-birth prior pregnancy: A 2024 U.S. population-based analysis.
articles.journal: International journal of gynaecology and obstetrics: the official organ of the International Federation of Gynaecology and Obstetrics
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To examine whether the association between interpregnancy interval and adverse live-birth outcomes differs by the outcome of the preceding pregnancy.

METHODS: We conducted a retrospective population-based cohort study of singleton live births in the 50 U.S. states and the District of Columbia in 2024 (final Natality Public Use File) with at least one previous pregnancy and a classifiable most recent prior pregnancy outcome (live birth vs other outcome). Derived interpregnancy interval was categorized as <6, 6-11, 12-17, 18-23 (reference), 24-59, and ≥60 months. The primary outcome was preterm birth (<37 weeks); secondary outcomes were low birth weight, very low birth weight, neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) admission, and a composite adverse outcome. Modified Poisson regression with robust variance estimated adjusted risk ratios (aRRs) and tested the interval × prior-outcome interaction.

RESULTS: Of 1 995 754 births, 420 882 (21.1%) followed a non-live-birth outcome. The association between interval and preterm birth differed by prior outcome (interaction P < 0.001). After a prior live birth, risk was U-shaped (<6 months: aRR 1.61, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.57-1.66; ≥60 months: 1.30, 1.27-1.33). After another outcome, intervals <6 months were not associated with increased risk (aRR 0.90, 0.87-0.94), although risk exceeded that after a live birth at every interval of 6 months or longer. Findings were similar for secondary outcomes and robust in sensitivity analyses, including adjustment for parity.

CONCLUSION: The association between interpregnancy interval and adverse outcomes of the subsequent live birth depends on the outcome of the preceding pregnancy and should not be interpreted uniformly across prior pregnancy outcomes.

articles.title: Consensus-derived clinical sepsis profiles and mortality across six international cohorts.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Clinical phenotyping may help characterize sepsis heterogeneity, but the applicability of derived profiles across healthcare settings remains uncertain. We evaluated consensus-derived clinical profiles and their associations with mortality across six international cohorts.

METHODS: We analyzed 62,458 adults from six critical care databases in four countries. In the MIMIC-IV discovery cohort (n = 28,733), six clustering algorithms were applied to 24 routinely available clinical variables to derive consensus profiles. The profiles were assigned in five external cohorts using fixed discovery-cohort templates. We examined clinical characteristics, mortality associations, and exploratory treatment-outcome associations.

RESULTS: Three profiles were selected based on the Calinski-Harabasz peak and clinical interpretability. Profiles 1, 2, and 3 comprised 32.6%, 20.0%, and 47.4% of the discovery cohort, with in-hospital mortality of 30.3%, 13.8%, and 9.3%, respectively. Profile 1 showed greater multiorgan dysfunction, Profile 2 relatively preserved hemodynamics, and Profile 3 greater ventilatory support with less extrapulmonary dysfunction. Profile 1 had the highest mortality in all five external cohorts, with a decreasing mortality gradient across profiles in most cohorts. After adjustment for age and SOFA score, Profile 3 was associated with lower 1-year mortality than Profile 1 (hazard ratio 0.62, 95% CI 0.57-0.67). Treatment-outcome associations were exploratory.

CONCLUSIONS: Consensus-derived profiles characterized clinically interpretable patterns of sepsis heterogeneity with mortality differences across the evaluated cohorts. These findings support further evaluation of clinical profiling for risk stratification and phenotype-informed research.

articles.title: Impact of Social Vulnerability on Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the association between the Social Vulnerability Index (SVI) and pediatric obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) outcomes, including comorbidities, diagnostic timing, and surgical intervention.

METHODS: A retrospective review of our institution's TriNetX Research Enterprise Data Warehouse assessed patients aged 0-18 years diagnosed with OSA from 2014 to 2024. Patients were grouped into four SVI quartiles: Low, Low-Medium, Medium-High, and High. Extracted variables included polysomnography (PSG), Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP), tonsillectomy and adenoidectomy (T&A) surgeries, secondary complications, and the time elapsed between diagnosis and procedures or complications.

RESULTS: The study included 5753 patients with an average age of 7.69 years, and 43.9% were in the High SVI quartile. Black or African American patients comprised 75.9% of this highly vulnerable cohort. Overall, 8.7% of the cohort underwent PSG, with no significant differences in testing or time to PSG. There was a significant stepwise increase in comorbid asthma across vulnerability tiers, peaking at 9.4% in the High SVI group (p = 0.001). High SVI patients underwent T&A at significantly higher rates compared to those in the Low (p = 0.008) and Low-Medium (p = 0.002) quartiles. The mean time to surgery was 166.5 days, which did not significantly differ between SVI groups.

CONCLUSION: Children in highly vulnerable neighborhoods experienced a disproportionate burden of comorbid asthma and underwent surgical management for OSA at significantly higher rates. This suggests that socially vulnerable patients may present with more severe disease requiring surgery. Incorporating metrics like SVI into clinical pathways can better guide patient-centered care and equitable resource allocation.

articles.title: Lesion side influences the effects of bilateral upper-limb robotic-assisted training on motor recovery in chronic stroke.
articles.journal: European journal of physical and rehabilitation medicine

articles.title: Bictegravir/Lenacapavir: A 2-Drug Regimen for the Treatment of HIV-1 Infection.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the efficacy and safety of bictegravir/lenacapavir for the treatment of HIV-1 infection.

DATA SOURCES: A literature search was conducted in PubMed and Google Scholar (January 2016-August 2026) using the search terms bictegravir and lenacapavir. Other data sources included abstracts presented at recent conferences and the prescribing information.

STUDY SELECTION AND DATA EXTRACTION: All English-language studies assessing the efficacy and safety of bictegravir/lenacapavir for the treatment of HIV-1 infection were considered for inclusion.

DATA SYNTHESIS: Bictegravir is an established second-generation integrase strand transfer inhibitor (INSTI), whereas lenacapavir is a novel capsid inhibitor. Both antiretrovirals are highly active against HIV-1. Bictegravir/lenacapavir 75 mg/50 mg was shown to be safe and effective in two phase 3 clinical trials after switching from complex antiretroviral therapy (ART) or bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide. The Food and Drug Administration approved this combination for the treatment of HIV-1 infection in adults who are virologically suppressed on stable ART with no resistance to the individual components. It is available as a single-tablet regimen (STR) taken orally once daily.Relevance to Patient Care and Clinical Practice in Comparison With Existing Drugs:Bictegravir/lenacapvir is the first INSTI-capsid inhibitor 2-drug STR indicated for the treatment of HIV-1 infection. The combination could be useful for patients who want to simplify their regimen and/or those who cannot use a nucleos(t)ide or a non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor. It is not active against hepatitis B virus coinfection.

CONCLUSIONS: Bictegravir/lenacapvir is safe and efficacious as a 2-drug regimen for the treatment of adults with HIV-1 infection.

articles.title: Single-incision mini-sling (SIMS) under local anesthesia for stress urinary incontinence: A single-center prospective cohort study-12 months of follow-up.
articles.journal: International journal of gynaecology and obstetrics: the official organ of the International Federation of Gynaecology and Obstetrics
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Stress urinary incontinence (SUI) is a prevalent and costly condition, with an estimated lifetime risk of surgery reaching 20% by the age of 80 years. Single-incision mini-slings (SIMS) represent the latest advancement in midurethral sling technology, offering a minimally invasive alternative to traditional retropubic and transobturator tapes (TOT). Studies indicate comparable subjective and objective cure rates between SIMS and TOT, with potential advantages in postmenopausal women owing to earlier mobilization and reduced morbidity. The study aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of SIMS under local anesthesia in the management of SUI.

METHODS: A prospective cohort study was conducted in a tertiary academic urogynecology unit from December 2019 to December 2024. Consecutive patients meeting the inclusion criteria were enrolled following a standardized diagnostic and treatment protocol. Informed consent was obtained, and ethical approval was granted by the institutional review board. All patients underwent SIMS placement (Altis©, Coloplast) performed by two experienced urogynecologists under local anesthesia. Sling tensioning was performed via a standardized cough stress test at bladder volumes equal to normal voiding volume, as per pre-operative urodynamics. Patients were followed for 3 weeks and 12 months post-surgery. Data analysis was conducted using Microsoft Excel. Descriptive statistics were applied, and paired t-tests compared pre- and post-operative results. Statistical significance was set at P < 0.05.

RESULTS: A total of 124 women underwent SIMS for SUI, with a mean age of 63.8 ± 11.1 years and a body mass index (BMI, calculated as weight in kilograms divided by the square of height in meters) of 29.0 ± 4.3. Among them, 21.8% had severe and 78.2% had moderate SUI, while 30.6% presented with mixed urinary incontinence (MUI). Pre-operatively, mean International Consultation on Incontinence Questionnaire (ICIQ) Urinary Incontinence Short Form (ICIQ-UI-SF) and Female Lower Urinary Tract Symptoms (ICIQ-FLUTS) scores were 14.3 ± 2.4 and 19.0 ± 6.0, respectively. All surgeries were performed in an ambulatory setting, with 95.2% discharged the same day. The mean surgical time was 31.5 ± 8.0 min, and peri-operative pain was 2.8 ± 1.8/10. At discharge, all but one patient had a negative stress test, and 99.2% would recommend the procedure. At 12 months, the composite outcome was successful for 103 (83.1%) patients, with an objective cure rate of 94.3% and a subjective cure rate of 83.1%. A clinically important difference in ICIQ-FLUTS was observed in 92.7% of cases. Patient Global Impression of Improvement (PGI-I, scores 1 or 2) was reported by 93.5%, and Patient Global Impression of Severity (PGI-S, score 1) was reported by 83.9%. There were no cases of bladder perforation, major bleeding, mesh erosion, or reoperation.

CONCLUSION: The present study evaluates SIMS under local anesthesia as a minimally invasive and effective treatment for SUI, highlighting its potential benefits in post-operative recovery and resource optimization. The findings contribute to the ongoing advancements in SUI management, particularly in addressing modern healthcare challenges.

articles.title: Barriers and facilitators to implementing self-management programs for stroke survivors: a systematic review.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: This systematic review aimed to identify the barriers and facilitators to implementing self-management programs with stroke survivors.

METHODS: Studies describing stroke survivors', carers', and health professionals' perspectives on the barriers and facilitators to implementation in real-world settings were included. Exclusion criteria included publication prior to 2014, conference abstracts, editorials, or non-English publications. MEDLINE, PsycINFO, CINAHL, and grey literature were searched in November 2025. Risk of bias was assessed using the Mixed Methods Assessment Tool. A narrative synthesis, with barriers and facilitators mapped to the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research, was conducted.

RESULTS: Twenty-four studies describing 23 programs were included in the review, including quantitative, qualitative, and mixed methods designs. Interventions were implemented across hospital, community, home-based, and online settings. Barriers and facilitators were frequently reported for characteristics of the innovation, in particular the need for flexible and person-centred approaches. Factors related to individuals' characteristics were also highly reported, including the impact of stroke-related symptoms on participation, the need for social supports, and workforce challenges.

CONCLUSIONS: The studies included possessed high levels of heterogeneity, limiting the ability to determine the relative importance of barriers and facilitators. Future implementation efforts require consideration of the challenges in sustaining self-management programs long-term.

articles.title: The Ferret as a Companion Animal: A Welfare Analysis of Husbandry, Health and Behavior Across Regions.
articles.journal: Journal of applied animal welfare science : JAAWS
articles.abstract: Regional variation in companion-ferret management and owner-reported welfare indicators is poorly documented. We compared acquisition, nutrition, housing, behavior, health, preventive care, and reproductive management across Slovakia/Czech Republic (SK/CZ), the United States/Canada (USA/CAN), and other countries (O-C) using 422 owner questionnaires (one per ferret). Acquisition source, feeding, housing, preventive care, behavior, and reproductive management differed among groups. Breeders were the most common acquisition source in SK/CZ and O-C, whereas pet shops predominated in USA/CAN. Biting was reported most often in SK/CZ, whereas "exploratory" and "friendly" were selected most often in USA/CAN. Diagnosed adrenal disease was reported most frequently in USA/CAN. Age > 4 years (adjusted OR = 3.85, 95% CI: 1.99-7.44) and USA/CAN membership (adjusted OR = 5.06, 95% CI: 1.67-15.37) were associated with higher odds of reported adrenal disease; neutering status was not independently associated (adjusted OR = 1.73, 95% CI: 0.42-7.02). Findings demonstrate geographical differences in ferret management and selected owner-reported health and behavioral indicators but do not establish causality or overall welfare rankings.

articles.title: Glycosaminoglycans Recruit IAPP Oligomers on Lipid Bilayers.
articles.journal: The journal of physical chemistry. B
articles.abstract: Glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) are anionic polysaccharides that coexist with cell membranes in the extracellular matrix and have been shown to cooperatively enhance the aggregation of islet amyloid polypeptide (IAPP) at zwitterionic lipid surfaces─a process implicated in β-cell death in type 2 diabetes. However, the molecular mechanisms by which GAGs and lipids concertedly promote IAPP aggregation remain poorly understood. Here, we develop a coarse-grained model for the GAG chondroitin-4-sulfate (CS) and employ molecular dynamics simulations to investigate the aggregation of the IAPP11-29 fragment in environments containing CS, a 1-palmitoyl-2-oleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine (POPC) bilayer, or both. By comparing simultaneous and sequential assembly pathways, we show that the order of molecular encounters reshapes the aggregation landscape. CS drives rapid peptide consolidation at the bilayer surface through GAG-chain flexion and peptide crawling on the GAG chain, yielding ternary aggregates in which hydrophobic residues anchor into the bilayer, a globular peptide body extends above the membrane plane, while the CS chain forms a corona. CS further stabilizes helical intermediates through dipole-charge interactions, with helix half-lives four- to five-fold greater than in the bilayer-only system. When introduced to dispersed, bilayer-bound oligomers, CS recruits them into larger, more orientationally ordered aggregates that may serve as superior seeds for downstream fibrillation. Together, these results provide a molecular basis for the experimentally observed cooperative enhancement of IAPP aggregation by GAGs and zwitterionic lipids.

articles.title: Persistent pseudolysogeny of bacteriophage phiSASD1 in Streptomyces avermitilis and its extrachromosomal plasmid-like DNA form.
articles.abstract: Pseudolysogeny represents a distinct phage-host interaction mode that differs from the classical lytic and lysogenic cycles, yet it remains poorly characterized in filamentous actinomycetes. In this study, bacteriophage phiSASD1 infecting Streptomyces avermitilis was investigated. Three phiSASD1-carrying strains exhibiting pseudolysogenic characteristics were obtained through a plaque survival assay combined with PCR verification. Physiological characterization revealed that these strains exhibited stable resistance to superinfection by the homologous phage, while SAPL-1 continuously released high titers of infectious phage particles (up to 4.62 × 10⁷ PFU/mL) and maintained substantial mycelial biomass during the tested cultivation period. Adsorption assays showed that the representative strain SAPL-1 displayed markedly reduced adsorption capacity for phiSASD1, and mitomycin C treatment did not induce significant phage production, suggesting an atypical infection pattern distinct from classical integrative lysogeny. Southern blot analysis showed that the phiSASD1 genome was present in both total DNA and plasmid DNA fractions, with restriction patterns consistent with those of the free phage genome. Pulsed-field gel electrophoresis further supported the presence of an extrachromosomal phage-derived DNA molecule, while transmission electron microscopy revealed population heterogeneity, including intact and lysing cells. Functional assessment of the putative recombinase-associated region did not detect chromosomal integration under the tested conditions. Collectively, these results support a persistent pseudolysogenic association in which phiSASD1 is maintained as an extrachromosomal plasmid-like DNA form. This study provides new insights into alternative survival strategies of actinobacteriophages and provides a basis for further mechanistic studies and for phage monitoring and control in industrial fermentation systems.IMPORTANCETo our knowledge, this study provides systematic evidence that bacteriophage phiSASD1 can establish a persistent pseudolysogenic association with the industrially important actinomycete Streptomyces avermitilis, while its genome persists outside the host chromosome as an extrachromosomal plasmid-like DNA element. These findings extend the classical lytic-lysogenic framework by illustrating a persistent phage-host coexistence mode characterized by non-integrated phage DNA maintenance, continuous production of infectious phage particles, and population heterogeneity. The study therefore provides a basis for further investigation of the molecular mechanisms underlying phage persistence and phage-host coexistence and may inform phage monitoring and contamination control strategies in industrial fermentation systems.

articles.title: Ablation of a maternal Cryptosporidium mRNA-binding protein results in sterile sporozoites.
articles.abstract: Infection with Cryptosporidium is a leading cause of diarrheal disease and early childhood mortality. This apicomplexan parasite undergoes asexual and sexual replication within the same host, and recent studies have shown an intrinsic developmental program of obligate transition to male and female gametes and sex. While factors were identified that control male fate and development, how female gene expression is orchestrated remains largely unknown. Here, we use the Cryptosporidium Single Cell Atlas to discover an RNA-binding protein (F-RBP) as one of the earliest markers of female identity in C. parvum. Reporter parasites engineered based on this gene allowed us to calibrate transcriptional pseudotime against the real time of female development, revealing a significant window of transcriptional fate ambiguity. While F-RBP is an early transcript, the protein persists throughout female development and into the zygote. Conditional ablation of the F-RBP gene showed it to be dispensable for sex determination and early female development in vitro. However, the gene is essential in vivo, and its loss results in rapid cure. Cell biological experiments link this loss to the production of oocysts that release sporozoites incapable of host-cell invasion. F-RBP binds transcripts highly expressed in the female gamete, enriched for a sequence motif recognized by a Y-box protein family member, and forms mRNA-protein complexes in late females akin to processing or P bodies. We propose F-RBP's essential role to be in the regulation of long-term homeostasis of maternally inherited RNA required for sporozoite infectivity.IMPORTANCEThe parasite Cryptosporidium is responsible for millions of cases of severe diarrheal disease in young children, and the infection is both a consequence of and a risk factor for chronic malnutrition. There are no vaccines available, and a single approved treatment is largely ineffective. Infection relies on ingestion of the oocyst, an environmentally stable spore, which contains an invasive form of the parasite, the sporozoite. Oocysts and sporozoites are the products of parasite sex and the fusion of female and male Cryptosporidium parasites. Here, we report the critical role of an RNA-binding protein in female mRNA homeostasis. Maternal transcripts orchestrate the complex process of sexual replication and oocyst formation. Loss of the protein results in spores that fail to initiate the next round of the life cycle, and conditional ablation using a small-molecule trigger quickly cures infected animals, demonstrating the essential role of parasite sex in continued infection.

articles.title: Targeted CPSF6 recoding reveals global fitness advantages of SPAD integration targeting and cell type-specific roles for capsid binding in HIV-1 DNA synthesis and nuclear import.
articles.abstract: As part of the CFIm complex, CPSF6 regulates cellular gene expression via alternative polyadenylation. CPSF6 binds primate lentiviral capsids and has been implicated in HIV-1 reverse transcription, nuclear import, and integration targeting. However, interpretations of the role(s) of CPSF6 during HIV-1 replication are complicated by the transcriptional changes that occur when the protein is depleted from cells. To disentangle the role of CPSF6 in HIV-1 replication from alternative polyadenylation, we selectively recoded its capsid-binding phenylalanine-glycine motif to alanine-alanine in CD4-positive Jurkat T cells, CEM12D7 T cells, and THP-1 myeloid/macrophage cells using CRISPR/Cas9-based homology-directed repair. While large variations in single-round HIV-1 infection were observed among isolated T cell clones, en masse comparisons of recoded T cells to cloned control T cells failed to reveal any significant differences in infection levels. Consistent with an overall fitness advantage provided by DNA integration in speckle-associated domains, which was ablated by recoding across cell types, HIV-1 replicated more robustly in control T cell populations. Single-round infection, in addition to spreading replication, was reduced in recoded myeloid/macrophage cells, which correlated with reductions in reverse transcription, and more robust blocks to HIV-1 nuclear import. Recoded monocytes/macrophages, however, did not reveal any evidence for enhanced type I interferon production or sensing of HIV-1 nucleic acids. Altogether, we define endogenously recoded cell lines to uncouple capsid binding from CPSF6's role in RNA metabolism, which highlights a global fitness advantage of targeted DNA integration and cell type-specific roles for CPSF6 in HIV-1 reverse transcription, nuclear import, and virus replication proficiency.IMPORTANCEHIV-1 usurps cellular factors to effectively replicate and avoid innate immune sensing. HIV-1 capsid binds CPSF6, but the consequences of this virus-host interaction on HIV-1 biology are necessarily complicated by the cellular role of CPSF6 in pre-RNA processing. By endogenously recoding CPSF6 to selectively disrupt capsid binding while preserving its RNA-processing activity, we demonstrate in two different T cell lines that CPSF6-mediated targeting of HIV-1 DNA integration into nuclear speckle-associated domains correlates with optimal viral replication. Recoded THP-1 myeloid/macrophage cells revealed additional single-round and multi-round infection defects, which correlated with reductions in reverse transcription and HIV-1 nuclear import. These defects, however, did not correlate with enhanced type I interferon production or detection of HIV-1 nucleic acids by known innate immune sensors. Our work clarifies diverse roles for the capsid-CPSF6 interaction in HIV-1 infection of T lymphocytic versus myeloid cell lines and provides novel cell reagents for future research studies.

articles.title: Resensitization of colistin-resistant bacteria by the combination of colistin and L-arginine.
articles.abstract: Colistin is the last-resort antibiotic for the clinical treatment of infections caused by multidrug-resistant Gram-negative bacteria. However, the emergence of colistin-resistant bacteria, particularly those harboring the mcr-1 gene, has severely compromised the therapeutic efficacy of colistin. Herein, we demonstrated that L-arginine restores colistin susceptibility in colistin-resistant bacteria, including those with intrinsic or acquired resistance. The combination of colistin and L-arginine effectively treated murine acute peritonitis caused by a colistin-resistant bacterial infection, with no toxicity observed in either in vitro or in vivo assays. Mechanistically, we revealed that the combination enhances the permeability of the cell membrane, thereby promoting the influx of colistin, ATP efflux, and the level of reactive oxygen species (ROS), ultimately leading to the death of colistin-resistant bacteria. Furthermore, the combination downregulates membrane lipid-related genes fabZ and fadL, consequently suppressing fatty acid synthesis. This inhibition resulted in the uneven distribution of membrane lipids and lipopolysaccharide (LPS), which further increased membrane permeability. In sum, our findings indicate that the combination of colistin and L-arginine successfully reverses the colistin resistance phenotype, providing a potential therapeutic strategy to combat infections caused by colistin-resistant bacteria.IMPORTANCEThe global spread of colistin-resistant bacteria has eroded one of the last lines of defense against life-threatening infections that no longer respond to conventional antibiotics. Here we show that L-arginine, a natural and safe amino acid, is an agent that can restore colistin susceptibility in strains with intrinsic or acquired resistance, and is effective in a murine peritonitis model without observable toxicity. Mechanistically, the combination increases membrane permeability and compromises the integrity of the membrane, leading to altered membrane lipid and LPS distribution that further amplifies membrane disruption. These findings establish that colistin combined with L-arginine constitutes a readily translatable therapeutic strategy to overcome colistin resistance and preserve the clinical utility of this critical last-resort antibiotic.

articles.title: Advancing NTM research with citizen science.
articles.abstract: Nontuberculous mycobacteria (NTM) is a generic term for the >200 species of environmental mycobacteria. NTM are ubiquitous, but there is extensive variation in the distribution of individual species. In a recent article published in Applied and Environmental Microbiology, Wilsey et al. describe how community-based citizen science efforts helped map the distribution of NTM in Hawai'i (R. N. Wilsey, L.-H. Ding, S. N. Dawrs, C. K. Raulerson, et al., Appl Environ Microbiol 92:e00269-26, 2026, https://doi.org/10.1128/aem.00269-26). Mycobacterium chimaera, an opportunistic pathogen and the leading cause of NTM pulmonary disease in Hawai'i, was among the most common species isolated.

articles.title: Association of Preoperative Psychiatric Medication Use With Complication Rates After Total Ankle Arthroplasty.
articles.journal: The Journal of the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Psychiatric medications are widely used in the United States, yet their effect on outcomes in patients undergoing total ankle arthroplasty (TAA) remains unclear. The purpose of this study was to determine the effect of preoperative psychiatric medication use on postoperative medical and surgical complications after TAA.

METHODS: The TriNetX database (2005 to 2023) was queried to retrospectively identify patients who underwent TAA. Patients were stratified into two cohorts: one with preoperative psychiatric medication use within 1 year before operation (C1) and one without preoperative psychiatric medication use (C2). Propensity score matching was conducted using a 1:1 ratio to control for demographics and comorbidities. After matching, the psychiatry medication cohort consisted of 1,164 patients ,of whom 42.8% were female, with a mean age of 58.9 years, body mass index (BMI) of 30.8 kg/m2, and follow-up duration of 828.0 days (range, 730 to 1,095 days). The control cohort consisted of 1,164 patients, of whom 40.9% were female, with a mean age of 59.0 years, BMI of 30.5 kg/m2, and follow-up duration of 790.5 days (range, 730 to 1,095 days).

RESULTS: At 6 months, patients in the psychiatric medication cohort had a significantly higher risk of acute respiratory failure compared with control subjects (risk differences [RD] = 0.009; 95% confidence intervals [CI], 0.003 to 0.014; P = 0.002). Conversely, treatment for wound dehiscence was more frequent among control subjects (RD = -0.009; 95% CI, -0.014 to -0.003; P = 0.002). At 2 years, the psychiatric medication cohort demonstrated higher risks of mechanical loosening (RD = 0.086; 95% CI, 0.060 to 0.112; P < 0.001), implant-related pain (RD = 0.021; 95% CI, 0.005 to 0.036; P = 0.008), and periprosthetic fracture (RD = 0.009; 95% CI, 0.003 to 0.014; P = 0.002).

CONCLUSION: Preoperative psychiatric medication use is associated with markedly higher rates of long-term implant-related complications after TAA. Additional research is needed to elucidate mechanisms underlying these associations.

LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, Retrospective Cohort Study.

articles.title: Slowly burning down the house: the role of calcium in spotted fever rickettsiosis pathogenesis.
articles.abstract: Spotted fever group rickettsiae (SFGR) infect microvascular endothelial cells, increasing vascular permeability, a major pathophysiological effect with unclear underlying factors. To accurately model this disease feature, we used a microvascular barrier model that continuously monitors transendothelial electrical resistivity in brain microvascular endothelial cell barriers. Using this model, we previously showed that Rickettsia parkeri-infected microvascular endothelial cells treated with voltage-gated L-, T-, and N-type calcium channel blocker (VGCCb) benidipine delayed in vitro vascular permeability. This study aimed to investigate whether host calcium signaling modulation and metabolic stress with SFGR infection are primary drivers of rickettsial fitness and the subsequent loss of vascular integrity. We hypothesize that SFGR infections, while consuming host cell energy resources such as ATP, lead to modulation of microvascular endothelial cell calcium transport that enhances bacterial fitness, prefacing collateral barrier dysfunction. We confirmed that benidipine, the L-type VGCCb nifedipine, and the membrane-active divalent ion chelator DP-b99 have dose-dependent effects on vascular permeability, as measured by electric cell-substrate impedance sensing, which result in delayed rickettsial growth, as measured by qPCR, without direct bactericidal activity. During R. parkeri infection, intracellular calcium concentrations increased and ATP concentrations decreased simultaneously; these effects were mitigated by benidipine. VGCCb and DP-b99 treatment sustained VE-cadherin junctions, seen with immunofluorescence microscopy, similar to uninfected microvascular endothelial cells, corresponding to barrier integrity preservation. In addition to delayed rickettsial growth, VGCCbs and DP-b99 inhibited rickettsial actin tail formation, reduced cell-to-cell spread, and increased bacterial length by impacting FtsZ-ring localization, evaluated by immunofluorescence microscopy and plaque assay. Furthermore, bacterial protein synthesis is required, as replicating but not heat-killed R. parkeri caused microvascular endothelial cell barrier dysfunction, and a subinhibitory doxycycline dose delayed R. parkeri-induced microvascular endothelial cell dysfunction without impacting R. parkeri growth. Limiting calcium access disrupts R. parkeri growth by interrupting bacterial elongation and division, actin tail formation, and cell-to-cell spread, mitigating R. parkeri-induced microvascular endothelial cell barrier permeability in vitro. This suggests that rickettsial interference with host cell metabolism triggers calcium entry and accessibility, key in rickettsial fitness, and pathogenicity.IMPORTANCEThis work investigated pathogen- and host-associated factors contributing to SFGR disease pathogenesis, as measured by vascular permeability. Our findings demonstrate that SFGR disrupts endothelial cell homeostasis by causing intracellular calcium influx, a process that is critical for rickettsial fitness and pathogenesis. Rickettsial growth and cell-to-cell spread are dependent on host cell calcium, underscoring the essential role of Ca²+ access and linking bacterial fitness to calcium-dependent host processes. Although blocking calcium channels suppresses immune cell activation in vitro and increases mortality in an SFGR murine model in vivo, these findings warrant further investigation into whether selectively targeting endothelial cell-specific calcium signaling could reduce SFGR-associated vascular permeability without compromising innate immune responses. Such an approach may improve SFGR-related morbidity and mortality. Elucidating the role of calcium signaling in the obligate intracellular lifestyle of rickettsiae provides deeper insight into fundamental rickettsial biology and the mechanisms driving severe disease.

articles.title: Development and optimization of self-collected, field-stable, saliva-based immunoassays for scalable epidemiological surveillance of pathogen-specific immunity.
articles.abstract:
UNLABELLED: Serological surveillance is fundamental to infectious disease research and informed public-health decision-making. Immunoassays used in the study of pathogen-specific immunity have historically relied on the collection of venous blood. While critical for many public-health applications, this sample collection method is invasive and resource-intensive. The costs and logistical barriers associated with venous blood collection are exacerbated in resource-limited regions, and the shift to less invasive sampling methods would increase sample availability for pathogen surveillance and study of pathogen-specific immunity. To this end, we have developed and optimized a self-collected, saliva-based immunoassay capable of quantifying pathogen-specific antibody binding in saliva samples. Using samples collected from geographically and epidemiologically diverse regions of the world, we compared antigen-specific IgG levels in paired plasma and saliva samples. We observed that levels of IgG against multiple pathogens of public health concern-including SARS-CoV-2 and dengue virus-were highly correlated in plasma and swab-collected saliva. In addition, the decay of maternally derived antibodies in saliva samples collected from infants was readily observed using this immunoassay, demonstrating the assay's sensitivity and potential for use in measuring antibody kinetics. We posit that this assay represents a climate-stable, non-invasive tool that can aid in the surveillance and study of pathogen-specific immunity across a broad range of public-health indications.

IMPORTANCE: Traditional serological surveillance relies on venous blood collection, which is invasive, resource-intensive, and particularly burdensome in low-resource settings. To address these limitations, our team has developed and validated a self-collected, saliva-based immunoassay for quantifying pathogen-specific antibody levels. Testing paired plasma and saliva samples from geographically diverse populations, the authors found that IgG levels against SARS-CoV-2 and dengue virus were highly correlated between the two sample types. The assay was sensitive enough to detect the decay of maternally derived antibodies in infant saliva, demonstrating its utility for tracking antibody kinetics over time. The authors conclude that this non-invasive, climate-stable platform offers a practical alternative for broad pathogen surveillance and immune monitoring across a variety of public health contexts.

articles.title: Light-induced phyB-NPR1 interaction activates systemic acquired resistance.
articles.abstract: Light perception by phytochromes controls different aspects of plant-environment interactions including plant immunity; however, the underpinning molecular mechanisms are less well-understood. Upon localized attack on leaves by avirulent pathogens, the systemic accumulation of salicylic acid (SA) is required for the establishment of systemic acquired resistance (SAR) throughout the plant to curtail pathogen spread. We demonstrate that light-mediated Small Ubiquitin-like Modifier 1 (SUMO) conjugation to phytochrome B (phyB) is critical for increasing cellular SA levels to orchestrate SAR upon avirulent bacterial infection. SA promotes SUMOylation of phyB, which enables it to interact with the SA receptor, Nonexpressor of Pathogenesis-Related 1 (NPR1) via its SUMO1-interacting motif. SUMOylation of phyB is enhanced by the accumulation of SUMO-Conjugating Enzyme (E2) (SCE1) and the degradation of SUMO protease Overly Tolerant to Salt 1 (OTS1) in SAR-induced systemic tissues. Using confocal imaging, we show that SUMOylated phyB undergoes liquid-liquid phase separation together with NPR1 in nuclear bodies. We further validated through immunoprecipitation, ChIP and RNA-seq analysis that SUMOylated phyB associates with NPR1 and TGA transcription factors in nuclear photobodies to induce the expression of PR1 gene. We reveal a post-translational modification mechanism in which light-induced SUMOylation of photoreceptors promotes SAR by regulating NPR1 function.

articles.title: Does Pain Level Change When Receiving Multiple Intravitreal Injections?
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: The aim of this study was to evaluate differences in pain intensity among patients receiving their first and those receiving multiple (≥10) intravitreal injections (IVIs), and to identify demographic, systemic, and ocular factors associated with pain perception.

MATERIALS AND METHODS: This cross-sectional study included 86 eyes of 86 patients treated with intravitreal anti-VEGF agents or corticosteroids for retinal vascular and neovascular diseases. Pain was assessed within 5 min after injection using the Visual Analog Scale (VAS), ranging from 0 (no pain) to 10 (worst pain imaginable). Patients were grouped according to injection number: group 1 (first injection, n = 19) and group 2 (≥10 injections, n = 67; subdivided into 2a, 2b, 2c).

RESULTS: The median VAS pain score among all included patients was 2 (range 0-10). Median VAS score increased with the number of injections, female sex, and urban residence, whereas it decreased with diabetes, arterial hypertension, and smoking habits. However, multiple regression analysis showed that only female sex (p = 0.038) and a greater number of intravitreal injections (p = 0.020) were significant independent predictors of higher VAS scores, whereas urban residence showed a marginal association (p = 0.058).

CONCLUSIONS: Pain intensity after intravitreal injections was generally low but tended to increase with the number of injections. Female sex and a greater number of injections were independent predictors of higher VAS scores, while urban residence showed a marginal association. These findings suggest that patient-related characteristics and cumulative treatment burden may influence pain perception, highlighting the importance of individualized counseling and comfort-oriented strategies during chronic intravitreal therapy.

articles.title: Levodopa or dopamine agonists for enhancing motor function after stroke.
articles.journal: The Cochrane database of systematic reviews
articles.abstract:
RATIONALE: Stroke is a leading cause of mortality and disability worldwide. There is a lack of evidence regarding pharmacological enhancement of stroke recovery with dopamine agonists or levodopa, in particular in terms of motor deficits.

OBJECTIVES: To assess the effects of dopaminergic agents, defined as levodopa or dopamine agonists, on improving motor function after stroke.

SEARCH METHODS: We conducted an extensive database search on the Cochrane Stroke Group trials register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, PsycINFO, Science Citation Index Expanded, CPCI-S, BIOSIS Citation Index, ProQuest Dissertation and Theses Global up to November 2025.

ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA: We included randomised controlled trials (RCTs) that enrolled participants with a clinical diagnosis of stroke, irrespective of age or stroke aetiology and without a pre-existing indication for the use of levodopa or dopamine agonists. Eligible trials compared levodopa or dopamine agonists with a comparator group who received placebo or no medication, with equivalent rehabilitative care in both groups, and aimed at enhancing motor function after stroke.

OUTCOMES: Motor function was the critical benefit outcome. As a critical harm outcome, we assessed serious adverse events. Important outcomes consisted of death, recurrent stroke, disability, dependence, health-related quality of life, activities of daily living, total number of adverse events, and psychiatric adverse events.

RISK OF BIAS: Two review authors independently assessed the risk of bias for each trial using the Cochrane Risk of bias tool (RoB 1).

SYNTHESIS METHODS: We synthesised results for each outcome using a standardised mean difference (SMD) or mean difference (MD) for continuous data and risk ratio (RR) for dichotomous results, with a random-effects model due to heterogeneity between the trials. For non-extractable trials due to missing numerical data, we synthesised the results narratively. We used GRADE to assess the certainty of evidence for each outcome.

INCLUDED STUDIES: We included 12 parallel-group RCTs involving 1860 participants. The trials were conducted in Europe, the USA and Asia, and were published between 2001 and 2025. All trials included participants with either ischaemic strokes only or both haemorrhagic and ischaemic strokes. The mean age of all included participants ranged from 55 to 78 years. Of the included trials, 10 were placebo-controlled and two compared levodopa or dopamine agonists against usual care. Eleven trials investigated levodopa as the intervention and one examined the dopamine agonist ropinirole.

SYNTHESIS OF RESULTS: Across 12 included trials, complete data on motor function were available for six trials with continuous data (1258 participants) and for two trials with dichotomous data (615 participants), of which one trial assessed both continuous and dichotomous data. We detected no difference in motor function scores between levodopa or dopamine agonists and the comparator groups for continuous outcomes (SMD 1.42, 95% confidence interval (CI) -0.20 to 3.05; 6 trials, 1258 participants; very low-certainty evidence). The wide confidence intervals indicate substantial imprecision in the effect estimate. Consistent with those results, we detected no difference for dichotomous motor function outcomes either (RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.06; 2 trials, 615 participants; anticipated absolute event rate of having a favourable outcome of 581/1000 in the comparator group versus 540/1000 with levodopa/dopamine agonists; low-certainty evidence). Heterogeneity for the critical outcome motor function (continuously measured) was high (I2 = 99%). However, a sensitivity analysis including only two trials with a low risk of bias in all domains, that accounted for the majority of the included patient population (1025 of 1258), showed no heterogeneity (I2 = 0%), and a smaller confidence interval (SMD 0.02, 95% CI -0.10 to 0.14; 2 trials, 1025 participants), implying no difference between groups. Six trials assessed serious adverse events, including 1281 participants. There was no notable difference in the risk of serious adverse events between groups (RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.83 to 1.27; anticipated absolute event rate of 302/1000 events in comparators versus 311/1000 events with levodopa/dopamine agonists; low-certainty evidence). All important outcomes showed no notable between-group differences. The certainty of evidence, according to GRADE, was very low for continuously measured scores of motor function, low for dichotomous motor function outcomes, and low for serious adverse events. Together with heterogeneity in both interventions and outcomes, inconsistency of findings, imprecision related to small sample sizes in some trials, and imprecision of summary effect, there are major limitations of the current evidence.

AUTHORS' CONCLUSIONS: Based on limited data, we did not find evidence that the use of levodopa or dopamine agonists improves motor function after a stroke. Given the low certainty of evidence due to limited data, wide confidence intervals, and heterogeneity across trials, further research may change this assessment and explore whether effects are different in specific subgroups of patients.

FUNDING: Science funds [Wissenschaftsfonds] Department of Rehabilitation and Neurology, University Department of Geriatric Medicine, Felix Platter, University of Basel, Switzerland. This review had no external funding.

REGISTRATION: Protocol available via https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD013416.

articles.title: Maternity versus non-maternity healthcare settings for the diagnosis of gestational diabetes or diabetes in pregnancy.
articles.journal: The Cochrane database of systematic reviews
articles.abstract:
RATIONALE: Substantial uncertainty exists regarding how healthcare system factors, especially care setting types, affect the uptake and implementation of gestational diabetes or diabetes in pregnancy screening in practice. Evidence suggests that the care environment may influence diagnostic processes.

OBJECTIVES: To assess the effectiveness of maternity and non-maternity healthcare settings for the diagnosis of gestational diabetes mellitus or diabetes in pregnancy.

SEARCH METHODS: We searched CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature (CINAHL) for randomised controlled trials (RCTs) up to April 2026, and for controlled non-randomised studies of interventions (NRSIs) up to December 2025. We also searched CENTRAL to identify ongoing trials.

ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA: We included RCTs and planned to include cluster-RCTs and NRSIs, but we did not find any. Eligible participants were pregnant women being screened for gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) or diabetes in pregnancy. We defined maternity healthcare settings as those specialising in care for pregnant, birthing, and postpartum individuals, with appropriate screening protocols, and non-maternity healthcare settings as general medical environments lacking a focus on pregnancy and women's care. We considered any screening format (e.g. risk-factor-based screening) and any diagnostic test (e.g. one- and two-step oral glucose tolerance tests (OGTT)).

OUTCOMES: Critical health service outcomes were compliance with screening and follow-up guidelines, diagnosis of gestational diabetes or diabetes in pregnancy, maternal emergency department visits during pregnancy, maternal antenatal hospitalisation, length of maternal hospitalisation, length of neonatal hospitalisation, and care accessibility. Critical maternal outcomes included hypertensive disorders, maternal death, intensive care admissions, hyperglycaemia requiring pharmacological treatment, infections, and postpartum glucose intolerance, including progression to diabetes, within 15 years after birth. Critical child-related outcomes encompassed perinatal death, neonatal intensive care admissions, preterm birth, neonatal hypoglycaemia, large-for-gestational-age, shoulder dystocia, and birth trauma. Further critical and important outcomes not included in the summary of findings tables can be found in the full text.

RISK OF BIAS: We used the Cochrane RoB 2 tool to assess bias in the RCTs. We had planned to use ROBINS-I version 2 to assess bias in the NRSIs if we had identified any.

SYNTHESIS METHODS: We used standard Cochrane methodology. We planned to synthesise results for each outcome using meta-analysis where possible (inverse-variance or Mantel-Haenszel approaches; fixed-effect model). We used GRADE to assess the certainty of the evidence for each outcome.

INCLUDED STUDIES: We included one RCT with 781 participants: 390 were randomised to screening in a maternity healthcare setting and 391 were randomised to screening in a non-maternity healthcare setting. Except for screening compliance, trialists evaluated all outcomes using a per-protocol analysis instead of by original randomised groups. This approach created substantial disparities in sample sizes between settings and largely nullified the methodological protections typically provided by a randomised design. The trial evaluated screening for GDM only. We did not identify any ongoing studies or studies awaiting classification.

SYNTHESIS OF RESULTS: Health service outcomes Screening in a maternity healthcare setting may increase compliance with screening and follow-up guidelines (risk ratio (RR) 1.69, 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.53 to 1.87; 781 participants) and may improve care accessibility, assessed as time to access antenatal diabetes care, measured in days (mean difference (MD) -4.70, 95% CI -6.03 to -3.37; 690 participants), both with low-certainty evidence. We are very uncertain about the effect of screening in a maternity healthcare setting versus a non-maternity healthcare setting on diagnosis of gestational diabetes or diabetes in pregnancy (RR 1.10, 95% CI 0.60 to 2.01; 690 participants; very low-certainty evidence) and length of neonatal hospitalisation (MD 0.04, 95% CI -0.57 to 0.65; 690 participants; very low-certainty evidence). No direct evidence was available on screening for diabetes in pregnancy as distinct from GDM. No data were reported on maternal emergency department visits, maternal antenatal hospitalisation, length of maternal hospitalisations, and costs. Maternal outcomes We are very uncertain about the effect of screening in a maternity healthcare setting versus a non-maternity healthcare setting on pre-eclampsia (RR 1.24, 95% CI 0.56 to 2.75; 690 participants; very low-certainty evidence). The following outcomes were not reported: eclampsia, HELLP syndrome, maternal death, admission to intensive care, hyperglycaemia requiring pharmacological treatment, infections, and postpartum glucose intolerance. Child-related outcomes We are very uncertain about the effect of screening in a maternity healthcare setting versus a non-maternity healthcare setting on: stillbirth or foetal death (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.08 to 9.93), admission to neonatal intensive care (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.59 to 1.71), preterm birth (RR 1.06, 95% CI 0.41 to 2.71), neonatal hypoglycaemia (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.23 to 3.59), large-for-gestational-age (RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.51 to 1.04), shoulder dystocia (RR 0.15, 95% CI 0.01 to 3.70), and birth trauma (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.08 to 9.93), all with 690 participants each and very low-certainty evidence. An effect estimate for neonatal death was not estimable (maternity setting: 0/475; non-maternity setting: 0/215).

AUTHORS' CONCLUSIONS: There is insufficient evidence to determine whether screening for gestational diabetes or diabetes in pregnancy in maternity healthcare settings compared with non-maternity healthcare settings improves health service, maternal, or child-related outcomes. Low-certainty evidence from a single study indicates that screening in maternity healthcare settings may result in a reduction in time to access antenatal diabetes care and may increase compliance. The effects on other outcomes remain unknown. Conducting studies using intention-to-treat analyses could bridge existing research gaps, enhancing effect estimates and certainty.

FUNDING: This Cochrane review was funded by the World Health Organization (WHO) and the UNDP-UNFPA-UNICEF-WHO-World Bank Special Programme of Research, Development and Research Training in Human Reproduction (HRP).

REGISTRATION: Protocol available via PROSPERO: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251108692.

articles.title: Italian guidelines for speech and language therapy in patients with stroke or primary progressive aphasia. Recommendations from the Italian neuropsychological society.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Aphasia can be frequently observed after left hemisphere stroke, but also in neurodegenerative diseases, as in primary progressive aphasia (PPA). Aphasia strongly impacts on quality of life, and rehabilitation of People with Aphasia (PWA) presents clinicians with complex challenges.

AIMS: An ad-hoc Scientific Panel, including 20 members (neurologists, physiatrists, psychologists, therapists, nurses, PWA representatives), selected 4 questions not addressed by current international guidelines: (1) effectiveness of SLT for post-stroke aphasia provided by professionals vs non-specialized personnel; (2) effectiveness of SLT in the chronic phase vs no treatment; (3) effectiveness of non-invasive neuromodulation combined with SLT vs stand-alone SLT for PWA after stroke; (4) effectiveness of non-invasive neuromodulation combined with SLT vs stand-alone SLT for PPA patients.

METHODS: The Scientific Panel and experienced methodologists followed common guidelines for systematic reviews and the PICO framework for scrutinizing several databases (last search: March 2023). Recommendations were based on evidence analysis according to the GRADE methodology.

KEY FINDINGS: The Scientific Panel suggested one strong and three conditional recommendations, although quality of evidence was low or very low.

CONCLUSIONS: The present guidelines, published by the Italian Higher Institute for Health on December 19, 2023, supplement the most recent international guidelines, particularly in tackling PPA.

articles.title: Timing of Corticosteroid Injection Before Endoscopic Carpal Tunnel Release Influences Wound Complication Rates.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Endoscopic carpal tunnel release (CTR) is an alternative to open CTR, which may have improved wound healing. Corticosteroid injections (CSIs) may increase postoperative wound complications and are commonly used for nonoperative management. Given these competing effects, this study sought to determine whether the timing of CSI prior to endoscopic CTR would influence postoperative wound-complication rates.

METHODS: A national claims database was retrospectively queried for patients undergoing endoscopic CTR between 2010 and 2023. Patients were stratified based on preoperative CSI timing: <1, 1 to 3, 6 to 12 months, with no preoperative CSI within 1 year as a comparator. These were propensity score matched, using demographic and comorbidity factors. Primary outcomes included a composite of infectious and noninfectious wound complications and irrigation and debridement within 3 months postoperatively. Multivariable logistic regression compared patients with and without a recent history of CSI and their association with wound complications.

RESULTS: In total, 24 013 patients with a history of preoperative CSI were matched to 70 918 patients without a CSI history with good balance. When compared with patients without a CSI history, patients who were administered a CSI < 1 month (1.72 [95% confidence interval (CI): 1.21-2.38, P = .002]) and 1-3 months (1.48 [95% CI: 1.16-1.86, P = .001]) before their endoscopic CTR were at significantly greater adjusted odds of composite wound complications.

CONCLUSIONS: Endoscopic CTR is associated with equivalent wound complications when compared with those without a preoperative CSI if performed ≥3 months after CSI.

articles.title: Prevalence and prognostic impact of valvular heart disease in transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis.
articles.journal: Amyloid : the international journal of experimental and clinical investigation : the official journal of the International Society of Amyloidosis
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Significant valvular heart disease (VHD) is associated with adverse prognosis in transthyretin amyloidosis cardiomyopathy (ATTR-CM). However, data is limited to isolated VHD. We aimed at evaluating the difference in outcome between isolated and multiple VHD, and particularly with and without aortic stenosis (AS).

METHODS: Patients with ATTR-CM were retrospectively included in a multicentric registry. The endpoint was a composite of heart failure hospitalizations and all-cause death.

RESULTS: Of the 694 patients (mean age 75 ± 13 years,74%male), 302(44%) presented with significant VHD. Of these, 98 had VHD including AS (isolated AS in 45%;multiple VHD with AS in 55%), while 204 had VHD without AS (isolated in 64%, multiple VHD in 36%). During a median follow-up of 22(8-38) months, 217(31%) patients reached the endpoint. Significant VHD was associated with worse outcomes than no-VHD (log-rank p < 0.001; HR:3.275; 95%CI (2.472-4.337), remaining significant after adjustment (HR2.006 (1.193-3.047);p = 0.007). Stratification by the presence of AS, and according to isolated or multiple VHD, revealed that isolated significant AS ((HR: 2.462; 95%CI (1.233-4.917); p = 0.011), and multiple VHD including significant AS, had the highest risk for adverse outcomes ((HR: 3.385; 95%CI (1.744-6.573);p < 0.001).

CONCLUSION: In ATTR-CM, significant VHD is strongly associated with poor prognosis, with the highest risk for adverse events in significant multiple VHD including AS.

articles.title: Tibial Tuberosity Osteotomy for Patellar Instability Has Low Complication Rates and Favorable Patient-Reported Outcomes: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
articles.journal: Arthroscopy : the journal of arthroscopic & related surgery : official publication of the Arthroscopy Association of North America and the International Arthroscopy Association
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: To identify complications in patients who undergo tibial tubercle osteotomy (TTO) for patellar instability and secondarily to summarize patient-reported outcomes across patients who underwent TTO.

METHODS: In accordance with Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines, PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane Library databases were searched in November 2025 for studies published in the past 20 years. Studies were included if they met these criteria: evaluated complications after primary TTO and were written in English. Data was pooled for analysis using inverse-variance random-effects models.

RESULTS: The initial screen identified 5619 studies, 12 of which were included in this systematic review and meta-analysis. A total of 1110 patients were included in this study, with 866 (78.0%) female patients. Mean age across studies ranged from 15.8 to 27.7 years. Mean follow-up times across studies ranged from 15.0 to 81.6 months. Demographics were similar across studies, and each study had a low risk of bias per Methodological Index for Non-Randomized Studies criteria. Favorable postoperative clinical outcomes were observed, with mean Kujala scores of 78.1 to 96.0, International Knee Documentation Committee scores of 83.0 to 88.4, and Lysholm scores of 76.7 to 94.0. Overall, 149 complications were reported from the 1110 patients analyzed (13.4%). Reoperation to remove painful hardware was observed in up to 38.9% (range 0%-38.9%), rates of arthrofibrosis ranged from 0% to 12.5%, postoperative infection rates ranged from 0% to 5.6%, and bony complication rates, including malunion/nonunion and fracture, ranged from 0% to 1% reoperation. The failure-associated reoperation rate ranged from 0% to 25% across studies.

CONCLUSIONS: TTO performed for the treatment of patellofemoral instability has low associated bony and soft-tissue complication risk, but it can potentially require reoperation to address hardware-related discomfort, postoperative stiffness, or failure.

LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, systematic review and meta-analysis of Level II and III studies.
