The stimulation of these cytokines is associated with the activation of the NF-κB pathway. Altogether, this is the first report on the putative oxidoreductase Rv1714 of M.tb, highlighting its structural features and its key immune-modulatory function involved in shaping host inflammatory responses during infection.

articles.title: Glycyrrhizic acid-Cu2+ reinforced chondroitin sulfate/carboxymethyl chitosan injectable dual-network hydrogel with multi-bioactivity and enhanced mechanical strength for burn wound healing.
articles.abstract: The effective recovery of burn wounds is a major clinical challenge. Since available wound dressings are limited, rapid wound healing is still difficult to achieve. Injectable hydrogels present remarkable advantages over traditional hydrogels in dealing with irregular wounds, which have attracted extensive research. However, injectable hydrogels face the challenges of insufficient mechanical strength and poor adhesion. To address the issues, a dual-network hydrogel (DOCGC) with levodopa-modified oxidized chondroitin sulfate (L-Dopa-OCS) and carboxymethyl chitosan (CMC) as the matrix, combined with glycyrrhizic acid (GA) and Cu2+ for self-assembly, was designed. This strategy not only optimized the mechanical properties of the hydrogel, but also achieves synergistic effect of anti-inflammation, angiogenesis and anti-infection for burn wounds. The in vitro experiments confirmed that the introduction of levodopa enhanced the tissue adhesion ability of hydrogel. Meanwhile, with the support of GA and Cu2+, the DOCGC hydrogel exhibited enhanced mechanical strength. Crucially, the DOCGC hydrogel showed favorable biocompatibility and antibacterial activity. In the mouse deep second-degree burn model, the application of DOCGC hydrogel achieved a more rapid progression of wound healing. Overall, our results suggested that DOCGC hydrogel with multi-bioactive and excellent gel properties presented a promising solution for treating burn wounds.

articles.title: Lipid Profile and Liver Enzyme Alterations in HIV-Positive Patients Receiving Highly Active Antiretroviral Therapy in South-Eastern Nigeria: A Cross-Sectional Analysis and Implications for Pharmacogenetic Research.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) improves survival in HIV infection but has been linked to metabolic and hepatic alterations that vary across populations.

METHODS: This cross-sectional study compared serum lipid profile and liver enzyme activities between HIV-positive adults receiving HAART continuously for at least six months (n = 50) and HIV-negative controls (n = 50) in South-Eastern Nigeria, using independent-samples t-tests.

RESULTS: Total cholesterol, LDL-C, and VLDL-C were significantly lower in the HAART group (p < 0.05). ALT was lower (p < 0.001) and AST was higher (p = 0.005) in the HAART group; triglycerides and HDL-C did not differ significantly between groups.

CONCLUSION: HAART was associated with altered lipid and liver enzyme profiles in this population. The pattern differs from reports in predominantly European-ancestry cohorts. Nutritional, regimen-related, and host genetic factors are all plausible contributors; the genetic explanation remains speculative in the absence of pharmacogenetic testing. Routine biochemical monitoring and dedicated pharmacogenomic studies in African populations are warranted.

articles.title: Venous thromboembolism reporting in fusion-positive NSCLC treated with tyrosine kinase inhibitors: A systematic review of safety reporting and protocol-level provisions in phase I-IV clinical trials.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) is increasingly recognized as a clinically relevant complication in patients with fusion-positive non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). However, the completeness and consistency of thromboembolic safety reporting in clinical trials of tyrosine kinase inhibitors remain poorly characterized.

METHODS: We performed a systematic review of phase I-IV clinical trials evaluating targeted therapies in fusion-positive NSCLC. Protocols, publications, and online trial registry updates were systematically reviewed to assess thromboembolic event ascertainment, reporting practices, protocol-level anticoagulant therapy provisions, and VTE-related eligibility criteria.

RESULTS: A total of 108 reporting sources from 61 study entries (58 unique trials) were reviewed. Pulmonary embolism and deep vein thrombosis were the predominant reported events. VTE-related information was highly fragmented across reporting sources: 14 study entries reported events exclusively through full-text publications, 19 exclusively through online trial updates, and 15 through both sources. Study protocols rarely prespecified thromboembolic events as dedicated safety outcomes, more commonly addressing them in eligibility criteria, anticoagulant therapy provisions, or differential diagnosis guidance. More than 40% of study entries lacked protocol-level anticoagulant therapy provisions and nearly 60% lacked VTE-related eligibility restrictions. Marked heterogeneity was observed in event definitions, reporting practices, safety ascertainment, and observation periods.

CONCLUSIONS: In fusion-positive NSCLC trials, heterogeneity in event ascertainment and reporting, rather than a true scarcity of thromboembolic events, represents a major limitation of the available evidence. Greater standardization of safety reporting and integration of trial registry and publication data may improve the completeness, comparability, and interpretability of future studies.

articles.title: Multi-institutional assessment of practice patterns in the use of cardiovascular magnetic resonance and computed tomography for pulmonary valve replacement planning: A survey-based study.
articles.journal: Journal of cardiovascular magnetic resonance : official journal of the Society for Cardiovascular Magnetic Resonance
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Consensus documents provide recommendations on using cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) and cardiovascular computed tomography (CCT) in pulmonary valve replacement (PVR) planning in congenital heart disease (CHD). However, clinical practice patterns across institutions remain unclear, particularly with the increase in transcatheter PVR options and multi-modality imaging use. We aimed to characterize practice variation in cross-sectional imaging using CCT and CMR.

METHODS: A REDCap survey was distributed to Society for Cardiovascular Magnetic Resonance and Society of Cardiovascular Computed Tomography members to assess imaging practices for PVR planning in CHD, including imaging volumes, acquisition protocols, right ventricular outflow tract (RVOT) measurement techniques, and reporting times, with one response per institution. Wilcoxon rank sum tests, Fisher's exact tests, and analysis of variance were used.

RESULTS: Forty-three institutions (84% US and 16% international) responded. Most centers (29/43, 67%) reported performing CMR first, adding CCT only if the Harmony valve or Alterra pre-stent was under consideration. Only two centers (5%) used CCT without CMR as their standard practice. CCT was performed instead of CMR in patients with pacemakers or intracardiac leads (28/38, 74%). 88% of centers perform functional CCT, with 44% reporting ventricular volumes and function. Eight centers (19%) used a focused field of view on the RVOT, and branch pulmonary arteries, excluding the ventricles. RVOT measurement techniques varied: 84% of centers used angulated multiplanar reformats (MPR) and 28% used centerline technique/curved planar reformats (CPR). 88% used MPR-derived diameters and 24% used perimeter-derived area and average diameters. For CMR, only six centers (14%) reported using a non-gadolinium-based superparamagnetic iron oxide contrast agent. 30% of centers reported performing dedicated RVOT short-axis cine sequences and 16% reported utilizing 4D flow or 3D models. Median reporting times were 60minutes (IQR 60-90) for CCT and 120minutes (IQR 80-142) for CMR with dedicated technologist support available in 14 (33%) for CCT, and 15 (35%) for CMR. Overall, 84% favored a standardized imaging protocol and/or reporting template for PVR planning.

CONCLUSION: This survey highlights wide variations in imaging practices for PVR planning, with most respondents supporting standardization, which may improve efficiency, quality, and potentially reduce radiation burden in this specific patient population.

articles.title: Depressive and Anxiety symptoms associated with ICU admission in hypertensive disorders of pregnancy: a prospective cohort study.
articles.journal: Journal of the Academy of Consultation-Liaison Psychiatry
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (HDP) are a leading cause of maternal morbidity and mortality, particularly in Latin America. Depression and anxiety are frequent during pregnancy and may influence HDP severity, yet their impact on clinical outcomes remains unclear.

OBJECTIVE: To determine whether depressive and anxiety symptoms are associated with obstetric intensive care unit (ICU) admission and hospital length of stay among women with HDP.

METHODS: A prospective cohort study was conducted at a Colombian tertiary-care referral hospital (July 2024-January 2025). Women aged ≥16 years in their third trimester hospitalized for HDP completed the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) and Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7). Multivariable Firth penalized logistic regression and Cox regression models assessed associations with ICU admission and length of stay RESULTS: Among 234 participants (median age 25 years), 61.1% required ICU care; only 14 of the 143 ICU patients (9.8%) were assessed before ICU transfer. An EPDS score ≥10 or a positive response to item 10 was independently associated with ICU admission (OR 4.83 , 95% CI 1.56 -14.94, p=0.006) and longer hospitalization (HR 0.69 , 95% CI 0.48 -1.00, p=0.048). In an exploratory finding, a GAD-7 score ≥10 showed an inverse association with ICU admission (OR 0.29, 95% CI 0.09-0.88, p=0.029). Hemoglobin <11 g/dL and a post hoc mean arterial pressure threshold ≥102.5 mmHg were also significantly associated with ICU admission.

CONCLUSIONS: Depressive symptoms were associated with obstetric ICU admission and prolonged hospitalization in patients admitted for HDP, whereas anxiety appeared protective, which seems counterintuitive and requires future research to confirm its association; however, because most assessments took place after ICU transfer, causality could not be established. Integrating mental health screening into HDP management may improve maternal outcomes.

articles.title: Metabolic Burden, Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease, and Cognitive Performance Among Older Adults: Analysis of 1,387 Participants from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey.
articles.journal: The American journal of the medical sciences
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is prevalent in older adults, yet its independent contribution to cognitive decline beyond cardiometabolic risk factors remains uncertain.

METHODS: We performed a cross-sectional analysis of 1,387 NHANES 2011-2014 participants aged ≥60 years. MASLD was defined using hepatic steatosis index ≥36 plus ≥1 cardiometabolic risk factor, excluding excessive alcohol use. Cognitive performance across memory, verbal fluency, and processing speed was summarized as a global z-score composite. Advanced fibrosis likelihood was assessed using validated non-invasive scores. Weighted multivariable linear regression adjusted for demographic, lifestyle, and cardiometabolic covariates.

FINDINGS: MASLD was not associated with global cognition (β = 0.027; p=0.526) or individual domains after full adjustment. Advanced fibrosis risk was unrelated to cognition except for lower CERAD memory with high FIB-4 (β = -0.319; p=0.016). Greater metabolic risk factor burden showed graded associations with poorer cognition: ≥2 risk factors linked to lower global cognition (β = -0.23; p=0.036) and memory (β = -0.33; p=0.003); ≥3 showed borderline memory impairment (β = -0.24; p=0.049). In MASLD participants, ≥2 risk factors were associated with lower global cognition (β = -0.19; p=0.021) and ≥3 with reduced verbal fluency (β = -0.27; p=0.045). Processing speed declined only at highest metabolic burden in fibrosis-stratified models (e.g., DSST β = -0.51; p=0.015).

CONCLUSION: MASLD and related fibrosis risk were not independently linked to cognitive impairment. Metabolic risk factor burden primarily drove poorer cognition, especially memory, in both the overall sample and those with MASLD, with processing speed affected only at the highest burden.

articles.title: Clinical Utility of Plasma Microbial Cell-Free DNA Sequencing in Adult Immunocompromised Patients: A Real-World Cohort Study.
articles.journal: The American journal of the medical sciences
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Plasma metagenomic next generation sequencing (mNGS) enables noninvasive pathogen detection independent of organism viability. Although analytic performance has been described, the real-world clinical impact in immunocompromised hosts remains incompletely defined.

METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of immunocompromised adults undergoing plasma mNGS testing from January 2022 through November 2024 at the Medical University of South Carolina. Immunocompromised conditions included solid organ transplantation, hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, active hematologic malignancy, HIV, or biologic immunosuppressants. Clinical impact was adjudicated by infectious disease physicians as positive, negative, or neutral. Positive results were classified as definite, probable, possible, or unlikely infectious based on clinical correlation and concordance with conventional microbiologic testing (CMT).

RESULTS: Ninety-eight patients were included (median age 60 years [range 18-76]; 63% male), including solid organ transplant (31%), hematopoietic stem cell transplant (8%), HIV (13%), active malignancy (42%), corticosteroids (3%), and biologic therapy (10%). At testing, 85% were receiving antimicrobials and 88% were hospitalized. Plasma mNGS was positive in 62% of cases, with CMT concordance in 30%. Thirty-two percent of tests had positive clinical impact, identifying unrecognized infection or antimicrobial optimization. Sixty-six percent had no treatment impact and 2% had potential negative impact. More than half of discordant positives were deemed possible or unlikely infections. False-negative cases included invasive mold and nontuberculous mycobacterial infections.

CONCLUSIONS: In this antimicrobial-exposed immunocompromised cohort, plasma mNGS frequently detected organisms but less often influenced clinical management. Discordant positives were common, and false negatives occurred in selected syndromes, supporting cautious interpretation and stewardship-guided use.

articles.title: Associations between Global Immune-Nutrition-Inflammation Index and Risk of Mortality in Intensive Care Unit Patients.
articles.journal: The American journal of the medical sciences
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: This retrospective study aimed to evaluate the association between the newly developed Global Immune-Nutrition-Inflammation (GINI) index and the risk of all-cause mortality among patients admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU).

METHODS: Data were extracted from the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV version 3.0 (MIMIC-IV-3.0) database. Associations between the GINI index and all-cause mortality were assessed using Kaplan-Meier survival curves and multivariate weighted Cox regression models. Additionally, restricted cubic spline (RCS) analyses were performed to explore potential non-linear relationships between the GINI index and hazard ratios (HRs). Subgroup analyses were conducted to evaluate possible interactions between the GINI index and selected clinical features.

RESULTS: A total of 970 patients were included, of whom 11.75% (N = 114) experienced all-cause mortality. A significant association was observed between a higher GINI index and increased risk of all-cause mortality. This association remained consistent when the GINI index was treated as a continuous variable (HR = 1.12; P = 0.03) and when categorized into groups (Group 2 vs. Group 1: HR = 1.97; P = 0.02; Group 3 vs. Group 1: HR = 2.17; P = 0.01). The RCS analysis supported a linear, rather than a non-linear, relationship between the GINI index and all-cause mortality (P > 0.05 for non-linearity).

CONCLUSIONS: The GINI index is associated with elevated all-cause mortality risk among ICU patients and may serve as a promising candidate for mortality risk stratification, which highlights the potential benefit of timely targeted intervention.

articles.title: Beyond Traditional Risk: Does Systemic Inflammation Drive Accelerated Atherosclerosis in Rheumatoid Arthritis?
articles.journal: The American journal of the medical sciences
articles.abstract: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the primary cause of morbidity and mortality in individuals with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and other rheumatic diseases (RDs), contributing to an approximate 50% increased cardiovascular risk relative to the general population. In addition to conventional cardiovascular risk factors, disease-specific processes such as chronic inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, and immunological dysregulation substantially accelerate atherosclerosis. This thorough analysis brings together the most recent information on how to measure cardiovascular risk, how to understand the underlying causes of RA and other rheumatic diseases, and how to treat them all together. In RA, long-term inflammation throughout the body causes atherosclerosis through several different mechanisms that are not related to common risk factors. To lower the risk of heart disease, rheumatologists, cardiologists, dietitians, physiotherapists, and immunologists must all work together. Evidence supports the targeting of disease activity, the management of conventional cardiovascular risk factors such as hypertension, dyslipidemia, diabetes, and the use of non-pharmacological therapies.

articles.title: Clinician- and researcher-identified barriers and enablers to general population screening for type 1 diabetes in Canada.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Early identification of risk for type 1 diabetes (T1D) can reduce diabetic ketoacidosis at diagnosis and delay disease onset through disease-modifying therapies. While international population-based screening initiatives have demonstrated feasibility, Canadian efforts have focused on first-degree relatives, leaving uncertainty about broader implementation and capacity. As part of the Canadian Population Screening for Risk of Type 1 Diabetes (CanScreen T1D) initiative, this study assessed readiness across Canada to provide follow-up care, conduct clinical trials, and deliver immunotherapies to individuals identified through general population screening.

METHODS: We conducted a national needs assessment including a cross-sectional survey and follow-up qualitative interviews. The survey assessed institutional capacity for clinical care and research related to individuals at risk for or newly diagnosed with T1D. Interviews were conducted to contextualize survey findings. Quantitative data were analyzed descriptively, and qualitative data were analyzed using thematic content analysis.

RESULTS: Eighteen survey responses (39% response rate) revealed substantial variability in institutional capacity. While most institutions reported moderate to high capacity to care for individuals newly diagnosed with T1D, fewer reported sufficient capacity to support at-risk individuals or participate in prevention trials. Interviews highlighted broad support for population screening. However, participants identified major barriers, including limited space, staffing shortages, inadequate psychological supports, and challenges to equitable access for equity-deserving populations.

CONCLUSION: Canadian clinicians and researchers support population-based T1D screening in principle, but have reservations due to current healthcare and research infrastructure. Addressing capacity limitations and equity considerations will be critical to developing a coordinated national screening and follow-up strategy.

articles.title: Assessing reproducibility of CGM-derived postprandial phenotypes without discordance-based exclusion.
Wastewater-informed agent-based modelling of hepatitis E transmission dynamics.
articles.abstract: Hepatitis E virus (HEV) is considered a predominantly foodborne pathogen in developed settings. During COVID-19 lockdown periods, however, HEV concentrations in wastewater at a treatment plant in Munich, Germany decreased, suggesting that pandemic-related behaviour changes inadvertently influenced transmission. In contrast, reported cases and wastewater data from a smaller catchment showed no comparable decline. To assess whether the observed reduction is compatible with a near-exclusively foodborne infection and to reconcile the contrasting signals across surveillance modalities, we developed a stochastic, individual-level model of HEV transmission, shedding, and ascertainment in Munich. Using Approximate Bayesian Computation, we calibrated this model to wastewater and case data from 2020-2023, first separately and then jointly. Posterior parameter estimates indicated a substantial decline in transmission during lockdowns to about 35-40% of the non-lockdown level, with the 95% credible interval entirely below 1 (no change). Joint inference suggested that possible modest lockdown-associated increases in diagnosis probabilities and higher measurement variability in the smaller catchment masked this effect in clinical and small-scale wastewater data, respectively. These findings demonstrate how wastewater-based surveillance, used alongside reported cases, can enable more robust parameter inference for models of under-reported pathogens like HEV, thereby supporting informed public health risk assessments.

articles.title: Vaccination-driven suppression, stochastic variability, and contact saturation in HPV-cervical cancer transmission in India: A Black-Karasinski perturbation model.
articles.abstract: This study develops two stochastic models (one representing the pre-vaccination era and the other representing the vaccination era) describing human papillomavirus infection and its progression to cervical cancer in India. Both models incorporate Holling type-II incidence, with transmission dynamics perturbed by the Black-Karasinski stochastic process. A rigorous theoretical analysis is conducted for these models. The existence and uniqueness of global positive solutions are established, followed by the derivation of threshold quantities governing persistence and extinction. When Ris>1(i=1,2), each model admits at least one stationary distribution, indicating long-term persistence of infection. In contrast, when Rie<1(i=1,2), the infection undergoes exponential extinction. The non-vaccination model is fitted to annual cervical cancer incidence data from India for the period 2003 to 2017. Substituting the fitted parameter values within the specified time horizon implies that the system remains persistent under the current conditions. Subsequently, for the vaccination model, the remaining parameters are estimated from reliable scientific data, and simulations are carried out from 2025 onward. For the vaccination period, the estimated parameter values indicate eventual eradication of infection. Extensive numerical simulations support the theoretical findings. A global sensitivity analysis using Latin hypercube sampling and partial rank correlation coefficients identifies the most influential parameters. Finally, extinction time distributions and survival probabilities are examined to provide policy-relevant insights toward achieving an HPV-free India within the next 50 years.

articles.title: Effects of prehospital blood pressure on 90-day functional outcomes in patients with acute ischemic stroke due to large vessel occlusion.
articles.journal: Journal of stroke and cerebrovascular diseases : the official journal of National Stroke Association
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Prehospital blood pressure (BP) could influence cerebral circulation and outcomes in acute large vessel occlusion (LVO). We investigated the association between prehospital BP and 90-day functional outcomes and explored effect modification by endovascular thrombectomy (EVT).

METHODS: We analyzed 1,106 patients with acute LVO transported by emergency medical services between 2018 and 2024. Prehospital systolic BP (SBP, mmHg) measured at the scene was categorized into four groups: <120, 120-149, 150-179, and ≥180 groups. The primary outcome was a 90-day modified Rankin Scale (mRS) score of 0-2. Secondary outcomes included mRS 0-3 and hemorrhagic complications. Subgroup analyses for the primary outcome were also conducted.

RESULTS: Mean age was 79 years, and 51% were male; 60% underwent EVT. The SBP <120, 120-149, 150-179, and ≥180 groups included 120, 403, 403, and 180 patients, respectively. Cardioembolic stroke was most common and decreased with increasing SBP. Compared with SBP <120 mmHg, SBP ≥180 mmHg was associated with lower odds of mRS 0-2 (adjusted OR, 0.43; 95% CI, 0.22-0.84; p=0.01), with similar trends for mRS 0-3. This association was significant in EVT-treated patients but not in non-EVT patients (interaction p=0.007). Hemorrhagic complications were similar across groups.

CONCLUSIONS: Elevated prehospital SBP (≥180 mmHg) was associated with worse 90-day functional outcomes in acute LVO, especially following EVT. These findings highlighted the potential clinical relevance of prehospital BP assessment in patients with LVO. Further investigation should be considered for prehospital BP status in addition to the in-hospital managements.

articles.title: Quantitative in vitro PET/MRI and kinetic modelling of imaging agent release from a thermoreversible intranasal sol-gel.
articles.journal: European journal of pharmaceutics and biopharmaceutics : official journal of Arbeitsgemeinschaft fur Pharmazeutische Verfahrenstechnik e.V
articles.abstract: Intranasal phase-transforming thermoresponsive gels can prolong nasal residence and enable controlled release of diagnostic or therapeutic payloads. However, quantitative real-time release characterisation of multimodal imaging probes remains limited. Here, we developed a poloxamer-based sol-gel and established a hybrid PET/MRI framework to quantify the release of PET tracers and an activatable MnO2 nanoflower into simulated nasal fluid. The formulations transformed from solution-to-gel at ∼ 28-29 °C with a storage modulus of 8.2-9.5  kPa attained at typical nasal cavity temperature (34 °C), while maintaining a nasal-compatible pH. PET imaging with an extended time window demonstrated diffusion-dominated release with clear size dependence: ionic [64Cu]Cu2+ reached 30.0 ± 3.0 % cumulative release at ∼42  h, whereas [64Cu]Cu-Sar-OP showed 15.6 ± 3.1 % cumulative release under the same simulated conditions. PEGylated MnO2 nanoflowers exhibited negligible apparent release in simulated nasal fluid without reductant due to the absence of redox-triggered MnO2 dissolution to soluble Mn2+ and electrolyte-induced nanoparticle aggregation trapping, which restricts diffusion out of the gel; but with GSH-supplementation, quantitative T1/T2 mapping enabled relaxivity-calibrated tracking of apparent Mn-equivalent accumulation, reaching 13.9 ± 0.7 % of the nominal loaded Mn (T1-based) at ∼24  h. The cytocompatibility of MnO2 NFs-PEG was also evaluated in an RPMI 2650 human nasal epithelial cell model following 24-h exposure. Kinetic modelling (Higuchi and Korsmeyer - Peppas) supported diffusion-dominated transfer of the PET tracers, whereas the MnO2 profile reflected coupled redox and transport processes under limited-GSH conditions. Overall, our integrated PET/MRI approach provides a quantitative framework for comparing in vitro depot release kinetics and informing intranasal PET/MRI formulation design; however, the findings should not be interpreted as direct evidence of mucosal retention or in vivo nose-to-brain transport.

articles.title: Convergent Cardioprotection through Distinct Nitric Oxide and Carbon Monoxide Signaling Pathways after Myocardial Infarction.
articles.abstract: Reduced nitric oxide (NO) bioavailability contributes to endothelial dysfunction and increases myocardial susceptibility to ischemic injury. In addition to NO, carbon monoxide (CO) functions as an important endogenous gasotransmitter that regulates vascular tone, mitochondrial respiration, and cellular defense mechanisms. Although NO- and CO-related interventions activate distinct proximal signaling pathways, it remains unclear whether they converge on a common anti-inflammatory and antioxidant mechanism under conditions of chronic NO deficiency. We therefore investigated cardioprotective signaling induced by the NO donor Nicorandil and the CO-releasing molecule CORM-3 in L-NAME-induced hypertensive rats subjected to myocardial infarction. Male Wistar Kyoto rats received L-NAME (20 mg/kg/day) for four weeks to induce chronic NO-deficient hypertension. Myocardial infarction was induced by left coronary artery occlusion followed by reperfusion. Before reperfusion, Nicorandil or CORM-3 was administered intramyocardially. Seven days later, blood pressure, infarct size, collagen deposition, inflammatory markers, NO synthase (NOS) activity, protein expression of eNOS, iNOS, NF-κB, Nrf2, HO-1, and antioxidant enzymes were assessed. Both Nicorandil and CORM-3 significantly reduced myocardial infarct size and attenuated fibrotic collagen deposition compared with untreated infarcted animals. Furthermore, both treatments reduced circulating TNF-α and IL-6, suppressed myocardial NF-κB activation, decreased iNOS expression, and restored antioxidant enzyme levels. However, the interventions exhibited distinct upstream molecular signatures. Nicorandil preferentially enhanced NO-related signaling, increased total NOS activity and eNOS expression, whereas CORM-3 produced stronger activation of the Nrf2/HO-1 pathway. Nicorandil and CORM-3 produce a common structural, antioxidant, and anti-inflammatory cardioprotective phenotype associated with distinct molecular signaling profiles under conditions of chronic NO deficiency.

articles.title: Gonadectomy Practices in a Multidisciplinary Differences of Sex Development Clinic Support a Risk-Stratified Approach.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate gonadal management practices among pediatric patients with differences of sex development (DSD) at increased risk for gonadal tumors cared for in a multidisciplinary setting.

MATERIALS AND METHODS: Patients evaluated within the multidisciplinary clinic for gonadectomy between 2013-2024 were retrospectively reviewed. Eligible patients were stratified into tumor risk categories: high, intermediate, and low. Descriptive statistics characterized gonadectomy practices for the cohort, including stratification by tumor risk category and study year.

RESULTS: Eighty-one patients were included. The most common diagnoses were Turner syndrome with Y chromosome material (TS+Y) (N=23), Complete Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome (CAIS) (N=15), and Mixed Gonadal Dysgenesis (N=12). The proportion undergoing gonadectomy differed significantly by tumor risk: 96% for high-risk (24/25), 63% for intermediate-risk (20/32), and 38% for low-risk (9/24). Median age at gonadectomy was significantly different, with younger ages observed among higher-risk patients (median: 6.7 years in high-risk, 9.7 years in intermediate-risk, and 16.4 years in low-risk diagnoses). Tumors were present in nine patients (7 gonadoblastoma, 2 dysgerminoma, all high- or intermediate-risk). Two-thirds of tumors occurred in patients with complete gonadal dysgenesis [CGD]).

CONCLUSIONS: Gonadectomy frequency and age at surgery differed by tumor risk category, with higher-risk patients with DSD undergoing gonadectomy more often and younger. Across study years, there was no significant change in the proportion undergoing gonadectomy or in age at surgery. These findings support risk-stratified gonadal management, including deferring gonadectomy until after puberty in CAIS, and emphasizing discussion rather than default removal in TS+Y. Gonadectomy remains important for high-risk DSD diagnoses, particularly CGD.

articles.title: Preparing humanoid robots for the operating room: Infection prevention requirements for clinical deployment.
Plasma proteomics enhances genetic risk prediction and biological understanding of venous thromboembolism.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) is a leading cause of morbidity and the third most common vascular cause of death globally. While clinical and genetic risk factors have improved VTE risk stratification, they do not fully capture underlying disease biology. We hypothesized that integrating large-scale plasma proteomics with a validated polygenic risk score (PRSVTE) would reveal novel biological understanding and improve risk stratification.

METHODS: In 44,138 UK Biobank participants, we examined associations between PRSVTE and 2,911 plasma proteins using multivariable linear regressions. We evaluated proteins as predictors of incident VTE using Cox regression models. We employed bidirectional Mendelian randomization (MR) using cis-acting protein quantitative trait loci (cis-pQTLs) instruments and genome-wide association summary statistics to infer potential causality. A protein-based risk score (ProteinRS) was developed with Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO) logistic regression and compared against a clinical risk model.

RESULTS: PRSVTE associated with 265 proteins after false-discovery-rate correction (FDR < 0.01). Pathway enrichment analysis of these proteins highlighted cell adhesion, cell-junction organization, and transmembrane receptor signaling. Time-to-event analyses identified 354 proteins that predicted incident VTE (FDR < 0.01). MR implicated 14 proteins in potential causal pathways to VTE, while genetic liability to VTE affected the levels of 44 proteins. A 60-protein ProteinRS improved discrimination beyond clinical factors (area under the curve (AUC) 0.664 vs 0.647; P = 0.024). Participants above the 80th percentile of ProteinRS had a 49% higher hazard of VTE (hazard ratio (HR) = 1.49, 95% confidence interval (CI): 1.17-1.90) and those below the 20th percentile had a 48% lower hazard (HR = 0.52, 95% CI: 0.34-0.79) relative to the 20-80th percentile.

CONCLUSIONS: Integrating genetic and proteomics data uncovered molecular pathways that link genetic susceptibility to VTE, highlighted actionable protein targets, and modestly enhanced risk prediction. Plasma proteomics therefore holds promise for precision prevention of VTE.

articles.title: The Population-based Rate of Hospitalizations for Scurvy in the United States from 2005-2016.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND & AIMS: Scurvy, the disease state caused by a deficiency of ascorbic acid, had a high incidence during pre-industrial times but its incidence and prevalence in modern industrial societies are unknown. We sought to present the annual population-based rate for scurvy-associated hospitalizations in the United States.

MATERIAL & METHODS: RESULTS: There were an estimated 8,964 scurvy-associated hospitalizations in United States hospitals between 2005-2016. The mean age of scurvy patients was age 56.9 years old; 57.7% of patients were female. The population-based rate of hospitalizations carrying an ICD diagnosis of scurvy in the United States increased during the study period, from 0.08 scurvy-associated hospitalizations per 100,000 Americans in 2005 to 0.54 scurvy-associated hospitalizations per 100,000 Americans in 2016. Trend analysis demonstrated statistically significant increases in scurvy-associated hospitalizations year-to-year (annual rate ratio of 1.19 [95% CI 1.16-1.22; p<0.001]), or an average annual increase of 18.9%. Prediction analysis of the 2016 rate of scurvy-associated hospitalizations utilizing only ICD-9 data projected 0.520 hospitalizations per 100,000 population (95% CI 0.407-0.664), which is similar to the observed rate of 0.535 per 100,000 population derived from ICD-10 data. The mean mortality rate for scurvy-associated hospitalizations during the study period was 2.2%, with annual mortality ranging from 0% to 6.7%. In all years, scurvy was rarely the primary admission diagnosis (1.8% of cases). The most common primary diagnosis among scurvy patients was septicemia/sepsis (3.7% of cases).

CONCLUSION: Based on annual US hospital admissions, scurvy occurs significantly more frequently than is commonly believed and its population-based rate of hospitalizations is increasing over time. Further work is needed to clearly understand the burden of disease and associated health care costs related to scurvy.

articles.title: Shock Teams May Improve Outcomes of Patients with Cardiogenic Shock (STOP-CS): a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: A multidisciplinary team-based approach became one of the main paradigms in health care. Current evidence regarding the efficacy of Shock Teams and related advanced shock care models in cardiogenic shock (CS) comes from observational studies, with limited synthetic data available. We aimed to assess the association between advanced shock care models and short- and mid-term outcomes of CS patients.

MATERIALS AND METHODS: This systematic review and meta-analysis (PROSPERO registration: CRD42024581904) were conducted according to the PRISMA 2020 Statement. We included observational studies of at least 25 adult CS patients managed with or without a Shock Team or related advanced shock care models. We searched Embase, Medline Ultimate, PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science from 01.01.2016 to 13.08.2024. Risk of bias was assessed with the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. Meta-analyses were performed with a random-effects model. The primary outcome was in-hospital mortality.

RESULTS: Nine studies with a total of 658,708 patients met the inclusion criteria. For medium-term mortality, follow-up ranged from 60 to 365 days. Treatment of patients within the included models was associated with lower in-hospital mortality (OR: 0.81, 95%CI: [0.74, 0.90], p<0.0001, I2=58%), lower intensive care unit mortality (OR: 0.58, 95%CI: [0.43, 0.78], p=0.0004, I2=45%), and lower medium-term mortality (HR: 0.59, 95%CI: [0.48, 0.72], p<0.00001, I2=0%). These associations remained significant in sensitivity analyses, although clinical and methodological heterogeneity persisted.

CONCLUSIONS: Advanced shock care models may be associated with improved short- and mid-term outcomes in CS patients including lower in-hospital and medium-term mortality. Prospective studies are needed to confirm these results.

articles.title: Preoperative Predictors of Outcome for Adults Undergoing Congenital Cardiac Surgery: Multicenter Model Validation.
articles.journal: The Journal of thoracic and cardiovascular surgery
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Adults with congenital heart disease (ACHD) undergoing cardiac surgery represent a growing population in whom conventional surgical risk models perform suboptimally. We externally validated a previously described ACHD-specific preoperative risk model and evaluated whether performance could be improved through recalibration/model updating.

METHODS: We conducted a prospective, multicenter observational study of patients ≥16 years undergoing congenital cardiac surgery at four centers (March 2020-April 2023). The primary composite adverse outcome (CAO) comprised in-hospital death, prolonged ventilation >7 days, or new-onset dialysis. We evaluated discrimination and calibration of the original preoperative model (including MELD-XI, cognitive impairment, body-mass index [BMI], prior chest wall incisions, and complex anatomy) and then performed bootstrap-based model updating (200 resamples) to derive refined models with and without the Adult Congenital Heart Surgery (ACHS) procedural mortality score.

RESULTS: Among 538 patients, CAO occurred in 4.3% (n=23). In external validation (n=383 complete cases), the original model preserved discrimination (AUC=0.729, 95% confidence interval: 0.602-0.855) but systematically overestimated risk, indicating need for recalibration. The refined model retained BMI, prior chest incisions, cognitive impairment, age, serum albumin level, and ventricular systolic dysfunction. Discrimination was good without procedural complexity (AUC=0.799; 0.697-0.900) and improved with inclusion of the ACHS score (AUC=0.857; 0.779-0.935).

CONCLUSIONS: In this prospective multicenter external validation, an ACHD-specific preoperative risk model maintained discrimination but required recalibration. Incorporating procedural complexity enhanced discrimination, supporting a hybrid patient- and procedure-based approach to guide perioperative planning.

articles.title: Baicalin alleviates Renal interstitial fibrosis by targeting SIRT1/HIF-1α Signaling Pathway.
articles.abstract:
UNLABELLED: RENAL INTERSTITIAL FIBROSIS IS A DEFINING FEATURE OF PROGRESSIVE CHRONIC KIDNEY DISEASE: (CKD) with no effective therapeutic drugs in the clinic. Baicalin (BA) is a natural product sourced from Scutellaria baicalensis and has been proven to treat renal fibrosis and multiple kidney diseases. However, the anti-renal fibrosis effects of BA have not been systematically studied, and its underlying mechanisms remain unclear.

AIM OF STUDY: This study aims to investigate the role of BA in renal interstitial fibrosis and its potential pharmacological mechanism.

MATERIALS AND METHODS: The model of unilateral ureteral obstruction (UUO) mouse and TGF-β-induced cells were employed to evaluate the anti-fibrotic effect of baicalin in vivo and in vitro, respectively. The molecular docking, surface plasmon resonance (SPR), and cellular thermal shift assay (CETSA) were used to verify the relationship of BA and its specific target, Sirtuin 1 (SIRT1). The gene-knockdown cells, RNA-sequence analysis, western blotting assay, and RT-qPCR analysis were performed to clarify the BA-SIRT1 interaction and explore its underlying pharmacological mechanisms.

RESULTS: BA significantly ameliorated renal fibrosis and promoted renal function in UUO mice, with suppressing fibroblast activation in cultured cells. The results of molecular docking, SPR, and CETSA suggested that SIRT1 is a specific target of BA. The anti-fibrotic effects of BA were abolished after SIRT1 was knocked down. The following RNA sequencing and western blotting analysis revealed that BA inhibits the TGF-β1-induced HIF-α signaling pathway via targeting SIRT1.

CONCLUSIONS: This study indicated that BA is a SIRT1 agonist in suppressing the HIF-1α signaling pathway to quell renal fibroblast activation and improve renal function in renal interstitial fibrosis.

articles.title: Awareness without actionable knowledge: understanding physical activity recommendations among people with COPD.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Physical activity (PA) promotion is a cornerstone of non-pharmacological Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) management. Recognising the benefits of PA may not be sufficient to guide behaviour if people with COPD do not know the specific PA recommendations. This actionable knowledge may support PA engagement. This study aimed to characterise awareness of PA benefits, inactivity risks and knowledge of the WHO recommendations among people with COPD, exploring associations with participants' characteristics.

METHODS: A cross-sectional survey-based study with community-dwelling adults with COPD was conducted. Four hospitals and a patient association recruited participants to complete an online questionnaire on sociodemographic/clinical data, PA levels, barriers/benefits to exercise, knowledge of PA guidelines and perceived benefits/risks.

RESULTS: Among the 126 participants (mean age of 66.5±12 years), 36.5% had completed higher education. Although 72.2% reported having previously seen, heard or read information about PA recommendations, specific knowledge of the minimum targets was low. Correct responses were observed for 16.7%, 11.9% and 9.5% of participants regarding moderate-intensity PA (MPA), vigorous-intensity PA (VPA) and strength training, respectively. Participants commonly recognised general benefits of PA and risks of inactivity. In multivariable analysis, educational level and PA levels were associated with MPA knowledge.

CONCLUSIONS: Despite recognising PA benefits and inactivity risks, participants lacked specific knowledge of WHO recommendations. This mismatch may indicate a potential psychological capability gap between general awareness and the knowledge required to integrate PA into daily life. These findings support the inclusion of clear, literacy-sensitive guidance on PA frequency, intensity, duration and type in COPD care.

articles.title: Transitioning from Pharmacist-led to Informatics-Integrated Antimicrobial Stewardship: An Interrupted Time Series Study in a Chinese Tertiary Hospital.
articles.abstract: This study aimed to assess and compare the effects of two Antimicrobial Management System (AMS) phases in a tertiary hospital in China on the rational utilization of antimicrobial drugs: Pharmacist-led Manual Intervention (Phase I) and the Addition of Informatics-based Clinical Medication Pathway Intervention (Phase II). An interrupted time series study was adopted to analyze the immediate level changes and long-term trend shifts of multiple indicators covering antimicrobial use, quality control, nosocomial infection, and clinical treatment efficiency after the interventions. After the intervention, the average monthly defined daily doses (DDDs) of antibiotics decreased by 6.06% (P=0.029) and the average monthly cost decreased by 38.59% (P<0.001). The structure of drug use was significantly optimized: DDDs for intravenous drug use decreased by 20.04%, while oral drug use increased by 22.10%. The DDDs of restricted antibiotics decreased by 35.14%, and that of unrestricted antibiotics increased by 33.02%. The ITS analysis showed that the combined approach in Phase II provided additional immediate reductions in antimicrobial use intensity and expenditure proportions beyond the initial Phase I implementation. In terms of clinical outcomes, the nosocomial infection rate and the positive culture rate of carbapenem-resistant bacteria were significantly decreased (P<0.05). The 24-hour antibiotic withdrawal rate for Class I surgical incisions was significantly increased from 8.09% to 41.62% (P<0.001), and the average treatment duration of infectious diseases was shortened. The AMS strategy led by clinical pharmacists, especially when integrated with the intelligent clinical medication pathway system, was associated with a significant reduction in the overall drug consumption and cost, optimized the medication structure, and improved key clinical outcomes.

articles.title: LEFT BUNDLE BRANCH AREA PACING IN A POST TRANSPLANT HEART WITH MILD LV DYSFUNCTION- A CASE REPORT.
articles.abstract: Left bundle branch pacing (LBBP) is increasingly used as a physiological alternative to right ventricular pacing, with stable thresholds and synchronized left ventricular activation. Its use in a transplanted heart is rarely described, and data on conduction system pacing in this setting is limited. We describe a 38-year-old woman who developed complete atrioventricular dissociation with a wide, LBBB-morphology escape rhythm immediately after orthotopic cardiac transplantation performed for peripartum cardiomyopathy with biventricular dysfunction. Baseline echocardiography showed global LV hypokinesia with an ejection fraction of 45%. Given high-grade AV block with LV dysfunction, we implanted a left bundle branch optimized dual-chamber pacemaker. The paced QRS showed a right bundle branch delay pattern with left axis deviation, in keeping with left posterior fascicular capture, and thresholds remained low and stable at follow-up. The patient has done well since, with a ventricular pacing burden of 100%, no device-related complications, and recovery of LV ejection fraction from 45% to 60% on serial echocardiography. As far as we are aware, this is the first reported instance of left bundle branch pacing in a post-transplant heart. The case suggests that LBBP is feasible in the transplanted heart and may support recovery of LV function even when the heart is denervated, though longer follow-up and further cases will be needed to confirm this. Written informed consent was obtained from the patient for publication of this report and the accompanying images.

articles.title: Reversible cardiomyopathy due to ventricular arrhythmias in a |highly unusual syndrome. A novel phenotypical presentation.
articles.abstract: We present a 16-year-old female with multisystemic disorder characterized by cutaneous hyperpigmentation, hypertrichosis, hepatosplenomegaly, hearing loss, heart anomalies, hypogonadism, low height (short stature), hyperglycemia and hallux valgus and pathogenic variant in SLC29A3 gene (encoding the human equilibrate nucleoside transporter (hENT3), was referred for evaluation due to recurrent non-sustained pleomorphic ventricular tachycardia refractory to amiodarone and catheter ablation. Two-dimensional echocardiography and cardiac magnetic resonance with late-gadolinium enhancement showed reduced biventricular ejection fraction without signs of inflammation or fibrosis. The administration of propranolol and flecainide controlled her ventricular arrhythmias and improved ventricular function. To our knowledge, this the first time that this arrhythmic phenotype has been demonstrated in this unusual syndrome presenting probably as a cardiomyopathy secondary to recurrent non-sustained pleomorphic ventricular tachycardia that was reversed with administration of flecainide and propranolol.

articles.title: SGLT2 Inhibitors and risk of bacteriuria, candiduria, and UTI-related hospitalization: A Nationwide Cohort Study.
articles.journal: Clinical microbiology and infection : the official publication of the European Society of Clinical Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: SGLT2 inhibitors induce glycosuria; however, pathogen-specific real-world data on UTI risk are scarce, particularly in individuals without diabetes. We compared positive urine cultures, UTI-related hospitalizations, and Gram-negative, Gram-positive, and yeast-positive cultures after the initiation of SGLT2 inhibitors vs. GLP-1 receptor agonists in adults with and without type 2 diabetes.

METHODS: We conducted parallel propensity score-matched, active-comparator, new-user cohort studies within Clalit Health Services, Israel (2015-2024). Matching and Poisson regression were performed separately in all patients and in the strata with and without documented UTI in the preceding two years.

RESULTS: We analyzed 153,660 SGLT2 inhibitor initiators (134,060 with diabetes) and 172,262 GLP-1 receptor agonist initiators (93,086 with diabetes). Yeast-positive cultures were markedly more frequent with SGLT2 inhibitors (diabetes IRR 3.31, 95% CI 2.79-3.94; no diabetes 7.76, 2.34-47.99), as were Gram-positive uropathogens (1.34, 1.23-1.45; 1.53, 1.13-2.10), whereas Gram-negative uropathogens were not (0.74, 0.72-0.77; 1.05, 0.94-1.18). Overall culture positivity was lower with SGLT2 inhibitors in patients with diabetes (0.84, 0.81-0.86), but not in those without prior UTI (1.00, 0.96-1.04), and higher in patients without diabetes (1.14, 1.03-1.27). UTI-related hospitalization was uncommon (0.85, 0.74-0.97; 1.01, 0.58-1.83).

CONCLUSIONS: Compared with GLP-1 receptor agonists, SGLT2 inhibitor initiation was associated with a marked increase in yeast-positive urine cultures irrespective of diabetes status, a smaller increase in Gram-positive uropathogens, and no increase in Gram-negative uropathogens. Culture positivity was higher in patients without diabetes, and UTI-related hospitalization remained uncommon. These findings support the continued use of SGLT2 inhibitors when indicated, with candiduria as a specific safety signal warranting further characterization.

articles.title: EZH2 lactylation: a key epigenetic regulator and potential therapeutic target for sepsis-associated lung injury.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Sepsis-associated lung injury (SALI) is a lethal infection-induced complication with high mortality and limited targeted therapies. Dysregulated lactate metabolism is closely linked to SALI, yet the underlying mechanisms remain unclear.

OBJECTIVES: This study aims to investigate the role and molecular mechanism of EZH2 (Enhancer of zeste homolog 2) lactylation in SALI development, thereby uncovering a novel exploitable therapeutic target.

METHODS: A total of 209 ICU patients were enrolled and divided into the SALI group (n = 104) and non-SALI group (n = 105) to detect serum lactate levels. Cecal ligation and puncture (CLP) mouse models and endothelial cell-specific Ezh2 knockout (Ezh2ECKO) mouse models were established. Combined with lactate and lactate dehydrogenase inhibitor intervention, multi-omics analysis, ChIP, qPCR, immunofluorescence and other techniques were used in the study.

RESULTS: Serum lactate levels were significantly elevated in patients with SALI and model mice, and lung tissue lactate levels were elevated in model mice. Lactate levels were positively associated with inflammatory markers and lung injury severity. EZH2 underwent site-specific lactylation at lysine 30 and 406 (EZH2 K30/K406la) in SALI, which was enhanced with disease progression. Inhibiting lactate production or EZH2 lactylation improved pulmonary function, reduced inflammatory infiltration and pathological lung tissue damage. EZH2 K30/K406la downregulated CITED2 (CBP-p300 interacting transactivator with Glu/Asp-rich carboxy-terminal domain 2) expression by reducing its occupancy at the CITED2 promoter and altering CITED2 promoter activity, relieving the inhibition of the NF-κB (Nuclear Factor-kappa B) pathway and exacerbating inflammatory responses and endothelial dysfunction.

CONCLUSION: EZH2 lactylation aggravates SALI via the CITED2/NF-κB axis, highlighting this epigenetic modification as a promising therapeutic target that opens a new pharmacological avenue for developing site-specific inhibitors to combat SALI.

articles.title: A neutral epidemic model of tick-borne pathogen transmission with co-infection and co-transmission.
articles.abstract: With a single circulating tick-borne pathogen in a population of ticks and vertebrate hosts, the basic reproduction number incorporates contributions from tick-to-tick, tick-to-vertebrate host, and vertebrate host-to-tick transmission routes. With two co-circulating tick-borne pathogens, resident and invasive, and under the assumption that tick-to-tick is the only transmission route in a tick population feeding on vertebrate hosts, the invasion reproduction number is a measure of the ability of the invasive strain to take over the population at the resident-strain equilibrium. Predicting whether an invasive strain, that is identical to the resident one, will dominate depends on whether the mathematical model characterising the system possesses the neutrality property. However, even if a model is neutral and the strains not identical, its associated invasion reproduction number depends on model structure. We propose a two-slot model for tick-borne pathogen transmission in the presence of tick co-feeding, co-infection, and co-transmission, which is an extension of a previous co-infection and co-transmission model proposed by Alizon in 2013. Our two-slot model, with one population of susceptible (not infected) ticks, two populations of ticks infected with a single strain (resident or invasive), one population of co-infected (infected with both strains) ticks, and two populations doubly-infected with the same strain (resident or invasive), satisfies the neutrality property. We analyse the invasion reproduction number with the next-generation method and numerical simulations. We apply the two-slot model to compute the fraction of co-infected questing adult ticks at the end of a season as a function of the co-transmission probability, and discuss the potential risk posed to humans by such co-infected ticks.

articles.title: Incretin and nutrient-sensing GPCR therapeutics in type 2 diabetes: what target-modality-formulation matching explains.
articles.abstract: Receptor-directed therapeutics now dominate type 2 diabetes, yet their clinical value depends on more than target biology. This review proposes a pharmaceutics-centered framework spanning the receptors for glucagon-like peptide-1, glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide and glucagon, amylin co-agonism and selected nutrient-sensing receptors, it then tests against a defined cohort of 49 programs that reached Phase II in type 2 diabetes. Among arrests with a disclosed scientific cause, modality predominates; two-thirds of arrests were unexplained or attributed to portfolio decisions. Deliverability discriminates among comparable mechanisms, cannot raise a low receptor ceiling and is poorly served by the public record.

articles.title: Delayed presentation of intraocular pentastomiasis resulting in unilateral blindness in a Congolese child.
articles.journal: Journal of AAPOS : the official publication of the American Association for Pediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus
articles.abstract: We report the case of a 6-year-old girl who presented with a motile larva in the anterior chamber of the right eye, associated with anterior uveitis, secondary glaucoma, and blindness. The larva was identified macroscopically as Armillifer grandis, a pentastomid parasite with snakes and other reptiles as definitive hosts. Intraocular pressure normalized and intraocular inflammation resolved within days following removal. This case is reported because ocular pentastomiasis is exceptionally rare compared with visceral pentastomiasis. It underscores the vision-threatening potential of intraocular pentastomiasis and the importance of early recognition and prompt surgical extraction to prevent visual impairment. Ocular pentastomiasis is a rare parasitic infection of the eye caused by larval stages of pentastomid arthropods, most commonly Armillifer and less frequently Linguatula species. Although pentastomiasis has historically been considered an endemic zoonosis in some areas of Africa, Asia, and the Middle East, imported cases have been reported in nonendemic regions (Europe and North America) as a result of increased travel and migration.1-4.

articles.title: Mechanisms of cetuximab resistance in head and neck squamous cell Carcinoma: Focus on the EGFR-ERK pathway.
articles.abstract: Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) is the sixth most common cancer worldwide. Major risk factors include tobacco use, excessive alcohol consumption, and infection with oncogenic human papillomaviruses (HPV). Despite advances in treatment, HNSCC remains associated with poor outcomes, particularly in patients with advanced or recurrent/metastatic disease. The epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) has been recognized as a key oncogenic driver in HNSCC, as it is frequently overexpressed and promotes activation of multiple pro-tumorigenic signaling pathways, including ERK and PI3K/Akt. Cetuximab remains the only approved molecularly targeted agent directed against a tumor-associated receptor in HNSCC. However, its clinical benefit is limited by low response rates and the frequent development of resistance even in initially responsive tumors. Understanding the molecular basis of resistance to EGFR-targeted therapy is therefore critical for developing more effective pharmacological strategies and improving the clinical utility of cetuximab. In this review, we summarize EGFR alterations, activation of parallel compensatory pathways, and the reactivation of downstream signaling cascades, including PI3K/Akt and Ras/ERK, as major mechanisms underlying resistance to EGFR-targeted therapy in HNSCC. We focus particularly on the ERK signaling pathway as a central integrator of genetic, epigenetic, and adaptive resistance mechanisms. Sustained ERK activity restores downstream EGFR outputs, promotes feedback ligand production, drives epithelial-mesenchymal transition and cellular plasticity, and engages parallel oncogenic pathways, thereby enabling tumor cells to evade cetuximab-mediated EGFR blockade. Combined targeting of ERK and EGFR may therefore represent a promising strategy for overcoming cetuximab resistance in selected molecular contexts.

articles.title: Ultrasound-assisted catheter-directed thrombolysis versus anticoagulation alone in intermediate-high risk pulmonary embolism.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Ultrasound-assisted catheter-directed thrombolysis (USAT) may enhance right ventricular recovery in intermediate-high-risk pulmonary embolism, but evidence is limited.

OBJECTIVES: We compared the safety, efficacy, and net benefit of USAT versus standard anticoagulation.

METHODS: We analysed a propensity-matched prospective cohort of 432 intermediate-high-risk patients (216 USAT vs 216 anticoagulation) from the Italian USAT-HI and OPTIRAPE registries. Outcomes included all- cause, cardiovascular (CV) and PE-related death, major bleedings, and a composite net clinical benefit (NCB), with a day-7 landmark analysis distinguishing early (0-7 days) from late (8-30 days) events. Time-to-event analyses used Kaplan-Meier estimates and Cox regression with Hazard ratios (HRs) and relative 95% confidence intervals (CIs).

RESULTS: Baseline demographics (mean age 64 ± 12 years; 48% female) and comorbidities were balanced between cohorts. USAT was associated with lower all-cause (7.4% vs 13.9%; HR 0.52, 95% CI 0.28-0.85; p = 0.01), cardiovascular (3.2% vs 8.3%; HR 0.39; p < 0.001), and PE-related mortality (2.3% vs 6.5%; HR 0.34; p = 0.02) compared with anticoagulation. Major bleeding was similar (2.7% vs 1.9%; p = 0.56). USAT significantly improved net clinical benefit (13.4% vs 25.9%; HR 0.48, 95% CI 0.30-0.75; p = 0.001), mainly driven by reductions in early mortality and clinical deterioration. Landmark analysis indicated that benefits were largely confined to the first 7 days, with favourable but non-significant effects during days 8-30.

CONCLUSIONS: In intermediate-high-risk PE, USAT was associated with lower early mortality, improved net clinical outcomes, and a safety profile comparable to standard anticoagulation.

articles.title: Which spontaneous breathing trial should be used to reproduce post-extubation respiratory effort in COVID-19-related ARDS? A multicenter randomized crossover study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Spontaneous breathing trials (SBT) guide extubation decisions in intensive care unit (ICU), predicting the respiratory effort required by the patient after extubation. Different SBTs exist and should be adapted to critical illness. Viral pneumonias such as COVID-19 combine lung injury, sepsis-induced systemic inflammation, and encephalopathy, making classification challenging. The objective was to assess which SBT could be used to reproduce postextubation respiratory effort in COVID-19-related acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) patients.

METHODS: In this multicenter randomized crossover study, COVID-19-related ARDS patients mechanically ventilated at least 24 hours and ready for extubation underwent 3 different 15-minute SBT at random order: pressure support ventilation of 7-cmH2O with positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) of 0-cmH2O (PSV7PEEP0), PSV 0-cmH2O with PEEP 0-cmH2O (PSV0PEEP0) and T-piece trial. At baseline, end of each SBT, and 20 minutes after extubation, surrogates of respiratory effort were measured: esophageal pressure-time-product (PTPes), PTPes per minute (PTPes.min), swing esophageal pressure (SwingPes), and SwingPes per minute (SwingPes.min).

RESULTS: Sixty measurements of respiratory effort from 12 patients were analyzed. Median PTPes.min increased from 193.8 [170.8-227.2] cmH2O.s/min at baseline to 236.6 [192.1-313.6] after extubation, with no significant differences between SBTs and postextubation. SwingPes and SwingPes.min were lower during PSV7-PEEP0 than after extubation, with median paired differences of 4.7 (95% CI 0.6-9.8) and 115.3 (95% CI 4.8-297.8), but these differences did not remain significant after correction for multiple comparisons.

CONCLUSION: No SBT modality differed significantly from post-extubation respiratory effort, suggesting that none could be excluded in COVID-19-related ARDS patients.

articles.title: Genomic Investigation of a Carbapenem-Resistant Chromobacterium haemolyticum Cluster Reveals Environmental Introduction and Nosocomial Transmission.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To investigate the source and transmission dynamics of a cluster of four Chromobacterium haemolyticum infections in an intensive care unit (ICU) and to characterize their antimicrobial resistance profiles.

METHODS: An epidemiological investigation was conducted involving four ICU patients identified between July 2024 and August 2025. Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) was performed on eight isolates, and core-genome single-nucleotide polymorphism (cgSNP) analysis was used to assess their genetic relatedness. Antimicrobial resistance genes were identified using the Comprehensive Antibiotic Resistance Database (CARD), while resistance-associated point mutations were detected using AMRFinderPlus. A maximum-likelihood phylogenetic tree was constructed based on 26 genomes to investigate the genomic relationships among the isolates.

RESULTS: Two distinct epidemiological events were identified. Three patients harbored closely related isolates forming a clonal cluster with 0-10 SNP differences, linked to an index case with a history of near-drowning. In contrast, an isolate recovered from a patient with independent environmental exposure was genetically unrelated to the cluster, differing by >38,000 SNPs. All cluster isolates carried the chromosomal blaCRH-2 gene, encoding a class A carbapenemase related to Klebsiella pneumoniae carbapenemase (KPC), and displayed carbapenem resistance, unlike previously reported carbapenem-susceptible C. haemolyticum strains. Transmission ceased during the winter, with Patient 2 serving as a potential long-term reservoir.

CONCLUSIONS: This study provides the first genomic evidence supporting nosocomial transmission of C. haemolyticum. The concordant resistance profiles observed in the outbreak and unrelated isolates suggest that blaCRH-2 may be a key determinant of carbapenem resistance in C. haemolyticum, challenging the assumption that empirical carbapenem therapy is reliably effective against this pathogen.

articles.title: Hypofractionated Radiation Therapy for Localized Prostate Cancer: An ASTRO Clinical Practice Guideline.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: This guideline provides evidence-based recommendations on the use of hypofractionated external beam radiation therapy (EBRT) in patients with localized prostate cancer, including indications for moderate hypofractionation (MHF) and ultrahypofractionation (UHF), appropriate dose-fractionation regimens, target volumes, and treatment planning and delivery techniques.

METHODS: The American Society for Radiation Oncology convened a multidisciplinary task force to address 5 key questions related to hypofractionated EBRT in localized prostate cancer. Recommendations were based on a systematic literature review and developed using a predefined consensus-based methodology with grading of quality of evidence and strength of recommendation.

RESULTS: MHF is recommended over conventional fractionation for patients receiving EBRT across all risk groups, supported by high-quality randomized data demonstrating equivalent oncologic outcomes, toxicity, and quality of life, with shorter treatment duration that may reduce overall treatment burden. UHF is recommended as a standard treatment option for patients with low- and intermediate-risk disease electing for definitive EBRT and may be considered in selected patients with high-risk disease, preferably in the context of clinical trials. Selection of fractionation should generally be independent of patient age, comorbidity, and use of androgen deprivation therapy, although MHF may be preferred over UHF for patients with significant baseline urinary dysfunction. Evidence supports the use of contemporary image-guided, conformal treatment techniques to optimize target coverage and minimize toxicity. Guidance is also provided regarding appropriate dose-fractionation regimens, including commonly used MHF and UHF schedules, as well as target volumes and integration of pelvic nodal irradiation.

CONCLUSIONS: Hypofractionated EBRT has become the predominant form of definitive radiation therapy for localized prostate cancer, supported by mature randomized evidence demonstrating comparable outcomes to conventional fractionation and reduced treatment burden. Ongoing studies will further refine patient selection, the role of UHF in higher-risk disease, and integration of advanced imaging and adaptive technologies. These evidence-based recommendations inform best clinical practices in the use of hypofractionated EBRT for localized prostate cancer.

articles.title: Mental Health Must Become Central in Periprosthetic Joint Infection Care.
articles.abstract: Current management of periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) has traditionally focused on infection eradication and implant survivorship. However, emerging evidence demonstrates that PJI is associated with a substantial psychological burden and long-term impairment in quality of life. Despite the profound psychosocial effects associated with prolonged treatment and increasing evidence that these effects impact a major percentage of patients, mental health considerations remain largely absent from standard PJI treatment algorithms, since they often ignore depression, anxiety, social isolation, and psychological distress. This disparity draws attention to a critical difference between the patient's perception of their recovery and the surgeon's definition of success. This commentary examines the limitations of existing definitions of treatment success and advocates for integration of routine mental health screening and multidisciplinary care into PJI management pathways. Recognition of psychological recovery as a fundamental component of treatment success may improve patient-centered outcomes, optimize recovery trajectories, and better align orthopaedic practice with modern value-based care models.

articles.title: Prospective Evaluation of an Intraoperative Synovial Calprotectin Point-of-Care Lateral Flow Test for Periprosthetic Joint Infection in Hip and Knee Revisions.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Synovial calprotectin measured by lateral flow assay (LFT) has emerged as a promising point-of-care (POC) biomarker for periprosthetic joint infection (PJI). However, existing studies are limited by retrospective designs, frozen sample use, off-label stool test application, and small sample sizes. This prospective study evaluated the diagnostic accuracy of an intraoperative synovial calprotectin POC-LFT in hip and knee revision arthroplasty.

METHODS: A consecutive cohort of 80 patients undergoing revision total hip or knee arthroplasty (THA, TKA) was prospectively enrolled between March 2022 and February 2026. The 2018 International Consensus Meeting (ICM) criteria served as the reference standard. Among 55 THA revisions, 24 patients had PJI and 31 had aseptic failure. Among 25 TKA revisions, eight had PJI and 17 aseptic failure. Synovial fluid was aspirated intraoperatively and tested fresh using a dedicated calprotectin LFT. Using a threshold of ≥ 50 mg/L, sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) were calculated.

RESULTS: Median calprotectin was 138 mg/L in infected versus seven mg/L in aseptic THA patients. Sensitivity was 91.7% (95% confidence interval (CI), 73.0 to 99.0), specificity 90.3% (95% CI, 74.2 to 98.0), and AUC 0.894 (95% CI, 0.81 to 0.98). Median calprotectin was 106.5 mg/L in infected versus seven mg/L in aseptic TKA patients. Sensitivity was 87.5% (95% CI, 47.3 to 99.7), specificity 100% (95% CI, 80.5 to 100), and AUC 0.930 (95% CI, 0.84 to 1.00). There were three false-positive cases (metallosis, recent dislocation, and unexplained inflammation), while three false-negatives were associated with fungal pathogen and culture-negative PJI with sinus tract.

CONCLUSION: The intraoperative synovial calprotectin POC-LFT demonstrated high diagnostic performance in both THA and TKA revisions using a threshold of 50 mg/L. Its rapid turnaround time and high negative predictive value make it a reliable adjunct for real-time surgical decision-making within a comprehensive diagnostic framework.

articles.title: The 10-Year Revision Risk of Dual-Mobility Versus Standard Cups in Primary Total Hip Arthroplasty for Osteoarthritis: A Population-Based Study from the Danish Hip Arthroplasty Register.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Dislocation is the leading cause of first-time revision following total hip arthroplasty (THA). Dual-mobility (DM) cups have been used to reduce this risk, but data on 10-year revision outcomes with DM compared with standard cups remain limited. We aimed to compare the 10-year risk of all-cause and cause-specific revision between DM cups and standard cups with 32 or 36 mm femoral heads.

METHODS: This was a nationwide register-based cohort study using data from the Danish Hip Arthroplasty Register and the Danish National Patient Register. We included patients who underwent primary THA for osteoarthritis (OA) between 2007 and 2019 receiving either a monoblock DM cup or a standard cup with a 32 mm (SC32) or 36 mm (SC36) femoral head. We identified 5,187 patients who have DM, 35,162 with SC36, and 15,702 with SC32. The primary outcome was revision within 10 years for any cause. The secondary outcomes included cause-specific revision within 10 years. We estimated standardized risk differences using direct standardization to the covariate distribution of the combined population.

RESULTS: The standardized 10-year risk of all-cause revision was 6.6% (95% confidence interval [CI] 5.7 to 7.4) for DM, 5.9% (95% CI 5.6 to 6.3) for SC36, and 6.9% (95% CI 6.4 to 7.4) for SC32. The standardized risk difference was -0.6 percentage points (95% CI -1.5 to 0.3; P = 0.16) for DM versus SC36 and 0.3 percentage points (95% CI -0.6 to 1.3; P = 0.50) for DM versus SC32.

CONCLUSION: The 10-year standardized risk of all-cause revision did not differ between DM and SC36 or SC32. The DM was associated with a lower standardized risk of revision due to dislocation, but a higher standardized risk of revision due to infection compared with both SC32 and SC36.

articles.title: Effect of Horizontal Medialization of the Hip Center of Rotation on Clinical Outcomes After Total Hip Arthroplasty in Crowe Types I and II Developmental Hip Dysplasia.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The objective of our study was to investigate the effect of horizontal medialization of the hip center of rotation (COR) on clinical outcomes after primary unilateral total hip arthroplasty (THA) in patients who had Crowe types I and II developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH).

METHODS: A total of 189 patients who had Crowe types I and II DDH and underwent primary unilateral THA between January 2017 and December 2024 were retrospectively included. According to the postoperative horizontal COR difference, patients were divided into a horizontal COR reconstruction group (-five millimeters (mm) ≤ horizontal COR difference ≤ five mm, n = 108) and a COR medialization group (horizontal COR difference < -five mm, n = 81). Clinical scores, pain, postoperative limping, and radiographic parameters were compared between groups, whereas complications were summarized descriptively.

RESULTS: Harris Hip Score (HHS), Oxford Hip Score (OHS), and Visual Analog Scale (VAS) pain scores improved significantly after surgery in both groups. There were no significant differences observed between groups in postoperative HHS, OHS, VAS score, or limping. Radiographic analysis showed no significant differences in vertical COR difference, leg-length difference, or femoral offset difference. There was no statistically significant difference in the proportion of patients who had a global offset difference within ± five mm. There were three dislocations in the horizontal COR reconstruction group and two in the medialization group, and no nerve injury, aseptic loosening, periprosthetic fracture, or periprosthetic joint infection was observed.

CONCLUSION: In patients who have Crowe types I and II DDH, when the acetabular cup remained within the true acetabulum, a certain degree of horizontal COR medialization after THA was not observed to be associated with poorer clinical outcomes. With adequate cup coverage and initial stability, a certain degree of horizontal COR medialization may be a clinically acceptable reconstruction strategy.

articles.title: Lactylation at the crossroads: a metabolic-epigenetic-immune integrator in intestinal homeostasis and disease.
articles.journal: Journal of genetics and genomics = Yi chuan xue bao
articles.abstract: Lysine lactylation (Kla) is a metabolite-sensitive post-translational modification implicated in DNA repair, tumorigenesis, chemoresistance, and innate immunity. Recent studies also implicate Kla in intestinal disorders. This review synthesizes current evidence on protein lactylation in intestinal inflammation, inflammatory bowel disease, colorectal cancer, irritable bowel syndrome, intestinal fibrosis, radiation-induced injury, and enteric infection. We distinguish lactate-mediated receptor signaling and metabolic effects from covalent Kla, compare evidence across cell types and disease stages, and assess preclinical strategies targeting the lactate-lactylation axis. We also discuss microbiota-host metabolic crosstalk and mucus-penetrating nanodelivery, including the cross-border emulsification effect, an oil-in-water double-emulsion concept that describes traversal of the mucus barrier rather than a biochemical form of lactylation. Collectively, the available evidence supports a metabolism-epigenetics-immunity framework for gut pathophysiology, while highlighting unresolved questions concerning stereochemistry, site specificity, causality, safety, and prospective clinical validation.

articles.title: Distinct Localization of Leishmania tarentolae and Trypanosoma platydactyli in the Putative Natural Vector Sergentomyia minuta: Does This Reflect Co-evolution?
articles.abstract: Leishmania tarentolae and Trypanosoma platydactyli are reptile parasites that naturally share the same vertebrate hosts and are presumed to be transmitted by the sand fly Sergentomyia minuta.
